papers.title: Sustained hepatitis D virus-ribonucleic acid negativity after self-discontinuation of short-term bulevirtide therapy: a case report
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection represents the most severe form of viral hepatitis and is associated with accelerated progression to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Bulevirtide (BLV), an entry inhibitor targeting the NTCP receptor, has recently emerged as the standard treatment for chronic HDV infection. Although its efficacy and safety have been demonstrated in clinical trials and real-world studies, the optimal duration of therapy and criteria for treatment discontinuation remain undefined. Case report We report the case of a 60-year-old man with long-standing HIV/HBV/HDV coinfection and previous hepatitis C virus infection successfully treated in 1993. He had previously undergone two courses of pegylated interferon alpha without achieving virological response. BLV monotherapy (2 mg/day) was started alongside tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine/rilpivirine for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Treatment was discontinued after 6 months due to mild headache and myalgia. Despite early treatment interruption, HDV-RNA continued to decline after drug withdrawal, becoming undetectable 10 months later. Viral suppression was confirmed in multiple assessments and remained undetectable for nearly 1 year of follow-up. Throughout this period, liver enzymes remained within the normal range, quantitative HBsAg progressively declined, and liver stiffness decreased from 14 to 7.8 kPa. Conclusions This case illustrates a rare example of sustained HDV-RNA suppression after short-term BLV monotherapy in a non-cirrhotic individual with controlled HIV and HBV infection. The continued decline in viral load after treatment discontinuation may reflect a host mediated-immune control of HDV replication, possibly favored by low HBsAg levels. As the decline in HBsAg preceded BLV initiation, spontaneous clearance and a BLV-associated effect remain competing explanations. While this single observation does not support shortening BLV therapy in clinical practice, it highlights the need to identify predictors of durable virological control after treatment withdrawal to guide more individualized treatment strategies.

papers.title_zh: 自行停止短期布列韦肽治疗后持续丁型肝炎病毒核糖核酸阴性:病例报告
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Background Chronic hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection represents the most severe form of viral hepatitis and is associated with accelerated progression to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Bulevirtide (BLV), an entry inhibitor targeting the NTCP receptor, has recently emerged as the standard treatment for chronic HDV infection. Although its efficacy and safety have been demonstrated in clinical trials and real-world studies, the optimal duration of therapy and criteria for treatment discontinuation remain undefined. Case report We report the case of a 60-year-old man with long-standing HIV/HBV/HDV coinfection and previous hepatitis C virus infection successfully treated in 1993. He had previously undergone two courses of pegylated interferon alpha without achieving virological response. BLV monotherapy (2 mg/day) was started alongside tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine/rilpivirine for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Treatment was discontinued after 6 months due to mild headache and myalgia. Despite early treatment interruption, HDV-RNA continued to decline after drug withdrawal, becoming undetectable 10 months later. Viral suppression was confirmed in multiple assessments and remained undetectable for nearly 1 year of follow-up. Throughout this period, liver enzymes remained within the normal range, quantitative HBsAg progressively declined, and liver stiffness decreased from 14 to 7.8 kPa. Conclusions This case illustrates a rare example of sustained HDV-RNA suppression after short-term BLV monotherapy in a non-cirrhotic individual with controlled HIV and HBV infection. The continued decline in viral load after treatment discontinuation may reflect a host mediated-immune control of HDV replication, possibly favored by low HBsAg levels. As the decline in HBsAg preceded BLV initiation, spontaneous clearance and a BLV-associated effect remain competing explanations. While this single observation does not support shortening BLV therapy in clinical practice, it highlights the need to identify predictors of durable virological control after treatment withdrawal to guide more individualized treatment strategies.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 背景 慢性丁型肝炎病毒(HDV)感染代表最严重的病毒性肝炎形式,与加速进展至肝硬化、肝功能失代偿和肝细胞癌相关。Bulevirtide(BLV)是一种针对NTCP受体的进入抑制剂,最近已成为慢性HDV感染的标准治疗方案治疗。尽管其在临床试验和真实世界研究中已显示出疗效和安全性,但最佳治疗持续时间和治疗停药标准仍未明确。病例报告 我们报告了一例60岁男性患者的病例,该患者长期患有HIV/HBV/HDV共感染,并曾于1993年成功治疗过丙型肝炎病毒(HCV)感染。他之前接受了两疗程的聚乙二醇干扰素α治疗,但未达到病毒学反应。在开始使用tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine/rilpivirine治疗人类免疫缺陷病毒(HIV)和乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)感染的同时,开始使用BLV单药治疗(2 mg/天)。由于轻度头痛和肌痛,治疗在6个月后被停用。尽管早期治疗中断,但药物停用后HDV-RNA仍持续下降,并在10个月后检测不到。病毒抑制在多次评估中得到确认,并在近1年的随访中保持检测不到状态。在此期间,肝酶水平保持在正常范围内,定量HBsAg逐渐下降,肝硬度从14降至7.8 kPa。结论 该病例展示了在非肝硬化且HIV和HBV感染得到控制的个体中,短期使用BLV单药治疗后持续HDV-RNA抑制的罕见例子。治疗停药后病毒载量的持续下降可能反映了由宿主介导的HDV复制免疫控制,可能受到低HBsAg水平的促进。由于HBsAg水平下降先于BLV治疗开始,因此自发清除和BLV相关效应仍是竞争性解释。尽管这一单一观察结果不支持在临床实践中缩短BLV治疗时间,但它强调了在治疗停药后识别持久病毒学控制预测因子的必要性,以指导更具个性化的治疗策略。

papers.title: Awareness, Risk Factors and Prevalence of Viral Hepatitis B and C among Antenatal Attendees in Federal Medical Centre, Asaba: A Cross-sectional Study
papers.abstract: Aim: To evaluate the level of awareness, risk factors, and prevalence of viral hepatitis B and C among antenatal attendees at Federal Medical Centre, Asaba. Place and Duration of Study: Federal Medical Centre, Asaba, Delta State, from June to October 2025. Methodology: This hospital-based descriptive cross-sectional study involved 145 pregnant women attending the antenatal clinic at Federal Medical Centre, Asaba, from June to October 2025. Ethical approval was obtained before the commencement of the study, and informed consent was secured from all participants prior to enrolment. Data on participants’ sociodemographic characteristics, level of awareness, knowledge, and possible risk factors associated with hepatitis B and C infection were collected using a pretested structured questionnaire. Approximately 3 mL of venous blood was collected aseptically from each participant and analysed for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis C virus antibodies using standard rapid diagnostic test kits. The data obtained were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics, with both descriptive and inferential statistical methods applied. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Results: Of the 145 pregnant women who attended the antenatal clinic, most were between 21 and 30 years old (72.4%), and almost all were married (96.6%). Awareness of hepatitis B was relatively high, with about three-quarters of participants having heard of it (75.2%), while awareness of hepatitis C was lower (58.6%). Overall, participants demonstrated a moderate understanding of how these infections are transmitted (52.4%). Healthcare professionals were the most commonly reported source of information on viral hepatitis (46.9%). Although a large proportion of the women acknowledged the importance of hepatitis B vaccination (77.9%), only a small number had received the vaccine (13.1%). Screening results showed that 2.8% of the participants tested positive for hepatitis B, while none tested positive for hepatitis C. Conclusion: The findings indicate that although awareness of viral hepatitis among pregnant women was fairly encouraging, the low uptake of hepatitis B vaccination remains a major concern. This highlights the need for stronger health education during antenatal visits, regular screening, and improved preventive measures to reduce the burden of hepatitis infections among pregnant women.

analysis.study_design_and_population: A hospital-based descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted at Federal Medical Centre, Asaba, Delta State, involving 145 pregnant women attending the antenatal clinic from June to October 2025.
analysis.methods: Data on sociodemographic characteristics, awareness, knowledge, and risk factors were collected using a pretested structured questionnaire. Blood samples were collected and tested for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis C virus antibodies using rapid diagnostic test kits. Data were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics with descriptive and inferential statistical methods.
analysis.main_results: Of the 145 participants, 72.4% were aged 21-30 years, and 96.6% were married. Awareness of hepatitis B was 75.2%, while that of hepatitis C was 58.6%. Only 13.1% of participants had received hepatitis B vaccination. Screening results showed 2.8% tested positive for hepatitis B, with none positive for hepatitis C.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that while awareness of hepatitis B was relatively high, the low vaccination uptake remains a major concern, highlighting the need for improved health education and preventive measures.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform targeted health education programs during antenatal visits and emphasize the importance of regular screening and vaccination to reduce the burden of hepatitis B infections among pregnant women.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design and small sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study evaluated awareness, risk factors, and prevalence of viral hepatitis B and C among 145 pregnant women at Federal Medical Centre, Asaba, from June to October 2025. Awareness of hepatitis B was relatively high at 75.2%, while that of hepatitis C was lower at 58.6%. Only 13.1% of participants had received hepatitis B vaccination, despite acknowledging its importance. Screening results showed 2.8% tested positive for hepatitis B, with none positive for hepatitis C. The authors interpreted these findings as highlighting the need for stronger health education and preventive measures during antenatal visits. The study's moderate evidence strength is due to its cross-sectional design and limited sample size, which may affect generalizability.

papers.title_zh: 阿萨巴联邦医疗中心产前参加者对乙型和丙型病毒性肝炎的认识、危险因素和 患病率:一项横断面研究
papers.source_body_en: Aim: To evaluate the level of awareness, risk factors, and prevalence of viral hepatitis B and C among antenatal attendees at Federal Medical Centre, Asaba. Place and Duration of Study: Federal Medical Centre, Asaba, Delta State, from June to October 2025. Methodology: This hospital-based descriptive cross-sectional study involved 145 pregnant women attending the antenatal clinic at Federal Medical Centre, Asaba, from June to October 2025. Ethical approval was obtained before the commencement of the study, and informed consent was secured from all participants prior to enrolment. Data on participants’ sociodemographic characteristics, level of awareness, knowledge, and possible risk factors associated with hepatitis B and C infection were collected using a pretested structured questionnaire. Approximately 3 mL of venous blood was collected aseptically from each participant and analysed for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis C virus antibodies using standard rapid diagnostic test kits. The data obtained were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics, with both descriptive and inferential statistical methods applied. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Results: Of the 145 pregnant women who attended the antenatal clinic, most were between 21 and 30 years old (72.4%), and almost all were married (96.6%). Awareness of hepatitis B was relatively high, with about three-quarters of participants having heard of it (75.2%), while awareness of hepatitis C was lower (58.6%). Overall, participants demonstrated a moderate understanding of how these infections are transmitted (52.4%). Healthcare professionals were the most commonly reported source of information on viral hepatitis (46.9%). Although a large proportion of the women acknowledged the importance of hepatitis B vaccination (77.9%), only a small number had received the vaccine (13.1%). Screening results showed that 2.8% of the participants tested positive for hepatitis B, while none tested positive for hepatitis C. Conclusion: The findings indicate that although awareness of viral hepatitis among pregnant women was fairly encouraging, the low uptake of hepatitis B vaccination remains a major concern. This highlights the need for stronger health education during antenatal visits, regular screening, and improved preventive measures to reduce the burden of hepatitis infections among pregnant women.
papers.abstract_zh: 目的:评估 Asaba 联邦医疗中心的产前参加者对乙型和丙型病毒性肝炎的认识水平、危险因素和 患病率。研究地点和持续时间:三角洲州阿萨巴联邦医疗中心,2025 年 6 月至 10 月。方法:这项基于医院的描述性横断面研究涉及 2025 年 6 月至 10 月在阿萨巴联邦医疗中心产前诊所就诊的 145 名孕妇。研究开始前获得了伦理批准,并在入组前获得了所有参与者的知情同意。使用预先测试的结构化问卷收集了参与者的社会人口学特征、意识水平、知识以及与乙型肝炎和丙型肝炎感染相关的可能危险因素的数据。从每位参与者身上无菌采集约 3 mL 静脉血,并使用标准快速诊断检测试剂盒分析乙型肝炎表面抗原 (HBsAg) 和丙型肝炎病毒抗体。使用 IBM SPSS Statistics 并应用描述性和推论性统计方法对获得的数据进行分析。统计显着性设定为 p ≤ 0.05。结果:到产前门诊就诊的145名孕妇中,大多数年龄在21岁至30岁之间(72.4%),几乎全部已婚(96.6%)。对乙型肝炎的认知度较高,约四分之三的参与者听说过它(75.2%),而对丙型肝炎的认知度较低(58.6%)。总体而言,参与者对这些感染的传播方式有一定的了解(52.4%)。医疗保健专业人员是最常报告的病毒性肝炎信息来源(46.9%)。尽管大部分女性承认乙型肝炎 疫苗接种 的重要性(77.9%),但只有少数女性接受过 疫苗(13.1%)。筛查结果显示,2.8% 的参与者乙型肝炎检测呈阳性,而没有人丙型肝炎检测呈阳性。结论:研究结果表明,尽管孕妇对病毒性肝炎的认识相当令人鼓舞,但乙型肝炎 疫苗接种 的低摄取率仍然是一个主要问题。这凸显了加强产前检查、定期筛查和改进预防措施以减轻孕妇肝炎感染负担的必要性。

papers.title: Successful treatment of recurrent anal fistula in a patient with hepatitis B using Kshar Sutra: a case report
papers.abstract: The ideal treatment for fistula‐in‐ano remains elusive, despite several treatments being described. The treatment of fistula‐in‐ano is a tightrope walk between preserving continence and preventing recurrence. A 49-year-old male patient was suffering from fistula‐in‐ano for 9 years. The patient was positive for HBsAg (Australia antigen). Kshara Sutra thread was used for the treatment. No internal medication was given for wound healing or infection control. There were no complications such as infection, severe pain, severe bleeding, and incontinence after the procedure. The patient was completely cured and is disease-free for 33 months. Kshara Sutra is an effective treatment with no complications and complete healing.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore an alternative treatment for recurrent anal fistula in a patient with hepatitis B virus infection, as the ideal treatment for fistula-in-ano remains elusive.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This case report describes the treatment of a 49-year-old male patient with a history of fistula-in-ano for 9 years and HBsAg positivity, indicating chronic hepatitis B virus infection.
analysis.methods: The treatment involved the use of Kshara Sutra thread, with no internal medication provided for wound healing or infection control.
analysis.main_results: The patient achieved complete healing with no complications such as infection, severe pain, severe bleeding, or incontinence, and remained disease-free for 33 months.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors suggest that Kshara Sutra is an effective treatment for recurrent anal fistula in patients with hepatitis B virus infection, with no complications and complete healing observed.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform the development of alternative treatment strategies for patients with hepatitis B virus-associated anal fistula, particularly in settings where conventional treatments may be limited.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single case report, which may not be generalizable, and the evidence is based solely on the patient's clinical outcome.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes the successful treatment of recurrent anal fistula in a 49-year-old male patient with chronic hepatitis B virus infection using Kshara Sutra thread. The patient was disease-free for 33 months following the procedure, with no complications observed. The study highlights the potential of Kshara Sutra as an effective treatment option for such cases. However, the findings are based on a single case and may not be generalizable. The evidence is limited to clinical outcomes and does not include broader statistical or mechanistic data.

elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single case report, which may not be generalizable, and the evidence is based solely on the patient's clinical outcome.

The treatment of fistula‐in‐ano is a tightrope walk between preserving continence and preventing recurrence. A 49-year-old male patient was suffering from fistula‐in‐ano for 9 years. The patient was positive for HBsAg (Australia antigen). Kshara Sutra thread was used for the treatment. No internal medication was given for wound healing or infection control. There were no complications such as infection, severe pain, severe bleeding, and incontinence after the procedure. The patient was completely cured and is disease-free for 33 months. Kshara Sutra is an effective treatment with no complications and complete healing.

papers.title: Pegylated interferon α-2b add-on to nucleos(t)ide analogues reduces hepatocellular carcinoma and decompensation in advanced fibrotic chronic hepatitis B
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND The current therapeutic strategy of adding pegylated interferon (Peg-IFN) α-2b to nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) is primarily aimed at achieving functional cure. However, its value in improving prognosis and the suitable candidates for this combination strategy in patients with hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related advanced fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis remain to be further explored. AIM To evaluate the long-term prognosis benefit of add-on Peg-IFNα-2b therapy in patients with HBV-related advanced fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis. METHODS This retrospective cohort study enrolled patients diagnosed with HBV-related advanced fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis. Participants were divided into two groups: (1) Those receiving combination therapy (Peg-IFNα-2b add-on to ongoing NA treatment); and (2) Those receiving NA monotherapy. A 1:1 propensity score matching approach was applied to balance baseline characteristics between groups. In survival analysis, the outcomes of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and decompensated cirrhosis were stratified by baseline clinical features and established HCC risk scores. RESULTS The analysis included 302 matched pairs, with a median follow-up duration of 220 weeks. Combination therapy was associated with a significantly lower risk of developing HCC (hazard ratio = 0.22; 95%CI: 0.11-0.48) and decompensated cirrhosis (hazard ratio = 0.39; 95%CI: 0.20-0.77) than NA monotherapy. These benefits were particularly pronounced among patients classified as intermediate-to-high risk by validated HCC prediction models and in those with persistent biochemical abnormalities lasting > 12 months. CONCLUSION Add-on therapy with Peg-IFNα-2b to NAs is significantly associated with reduced HCC and decompensation in high-risk patients with HBV-related advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, supporting its use in this population.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估附加 Peg-IFNα-2b 治疗对 HBV 相关晚期纤维化或代偿性肝硬化患者的长期预后益处。当前在核苷(酸)类似物(NA)中添加聚乙二醇化干扰素(Peg-IFN)α-2b的治疗策略主要旨在实现功能性治愈。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项回顾性 队列研究 研究纳入了诊断患有 HBV 相关晚期纤维化或代偿性肝硬化的患者。参与者被分为两组:(1)接受联合治疗(Peg-IFNα-2b 附加到正在进行的 NA 治疗);(2) 接受 NA 单一疗法的患者。
elements_zh.methods: 采用 1:1 倾向评分匹配方法来平衡各组之间的基线特征。在生存分析中,肝细胞癌 (HCC) 和失代偿性肝硬化的结果根据基线临床特征和既定的 HCC 风险评分进行分层。
elements_zh.main_results: 该分析包括 302 对配对,中位随访时间为 220 周。与 NA 单一疗法相比,联合治疗与发生 HCC(风险比 = 0.22;95% CI:0.11-0.48)和失代偿性肝硬化(风险比 = 0.39;95% CI:0.20-0.77)的风险显着降低相关。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些益处在经验证的 HCC 预测模型分类为中高风险的患者以及持续生化异常持续 > 12 个月的患者中尤其明显。Peg-IFNα-2b 与 NA 的附加治疗与患有 HBV 相关晚期纤维化或肝硬化的高危患者的 HCC 减少和代偿失调显着相关,支持其在该人群中的使用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,Peg-IFNα-2b 联合治疗可能为减少高危 HBV 患者的 HCC 和失代偿带来重要益处。这可以为未来 治疗 治疗 慢性乙型肝炎 晚期纤维化和肝硬化的策略提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究是一项回顾性队列研究研究,可能会引入偏倚和混杂因素。证据是中等的,因为它依赖于倾向评分匹配和分层生存分析。

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the clinical characteristics, transmission routes, and outcomes of children with chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and compare patients born before and after the national vaccination program. The rationale is grounded in the need to understand the impact of vaccination on HBV epidemiology in children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted involving 387 children aged 0–18 years diagnosed with chronic HBV infection between 2006 and 2025. Patients were categorized into pre-vaccination (born ≤1997) and post-vaccination (born ≥1998) groups based on their birth years.
analysis.methods: Demographic, clinical, and serological data were analyzed to assess the differences between the pre-vaccination and post-vaccination groups. The study design included a retrospective cohort analysis of diagnosed cases over a defined time period.
analysis.main_results: The number of diagnosed cases of chronic HBV declined markedly over time, with 375 cases identified between 2006–2015 compared with 12 cases between 2016–2025 (p < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the decline in diagnosed cases as evidence of the effectiveness of the national vaccination program in reducing HBV infection in children. This finding highlights the program's impact on HBV epidemiology.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide important insights into the success of the national vaccination program in preventing HBV infection in children, which can inform future public health strategies and surveillance efforts.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design, which may introduce biases and confounding factors. However, the evidence is strong given the clear decline in cases and the statistical significance of the results.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the clinical characteristics, transmission routes, and outcomes of children with chronic hepatitis B (HBV) before and after the national vaccination program. A retrospective cohort study included 387 children aged 0–18 years diagnosed with HBV between 2006 and 2025, divided into pre-vaccination (born ≤1997) and post-vaccination (born ≥1998) groups. The results showed a marked decline in diagnosed cases, with 375 cases between 2006–2015 and 12 cases between 2016–2025 (p < 0.001). The authors interpreted this decline as evidence of the program's effectiveness in reducing HBV infection. The findings have significant implications for public health, demonstrating the impact of vaccination on HBV epidemiology in children. The study's retrospective design may introduce biases, but the evidence is strong due to the statistical significance of the results.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估 传播 (HBV) 儿童的临床特征、传播 途径和结局,并比较国家 传播 计划之前和之后出生的患者。其基本原理是需要了解 疫苗接种 对儿童 HBV 流行病学 的影响。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 一项回顾性队列研究研究纳入了2006年至2025年间诊断为慢性乙型肝炎的387名0-18岁儿童。根据出生年份将患者分为疫苗接种前(≤1997年出生)和疫苗接种后(≥1998年出生)组。
elements_zh.methods: 分析人口统计学、临床和血清学数据,以评估 疫苗接种 治疗前和 疫苗接种 治疗后组之间的差异。研究设计包括对指定时间段内诊断病例进行回顾性 队列研究 分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 随着时间的推移,慢性乙肝确诊病例数显着下降,2006 年至 2015 年期间确诊为 375 例,而 2016 年至 2025 年期间为 12 例(p < 0.001)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将诊断病例的下降解释为国家 疫苗接种 计划在减少儿童乙型肝炎病毒感染方面的有效性的证据。这一发现强调了该计划对 HBV 流行病学 的影响。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为国家 疫苗接种 计划在预防儿童 HBV 感染方面的成功提供了重要见解,可以为未来的公共卫生战略和 监测 工作提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性设计而受到限制,可能会引入偏差和混杂因素。然而,考虑到病例数的明显下降和结果的统计显着性,证据是强有力的。

analysis_zh.methods: 分析人口统计学、临床和血清学数据,以评估 疫苗接种 治疗前和 疫苗接种 治疗后组之间的差异。研究设计包括对指定时间段内诊断病例进行回顾性 队列研究 分析。
analysis_zh.main_results: 随着时间的推移,慢性乙肝确诊病例数显着下降,2006 年至 2015 年期间确诊为 375 例,而 2016 年至 2025 年期间为 12 例(p < 0.001)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将诊断病例的下降解释为国家 疫苗接种 计划在减少儿童乙型肝炎病毒感染方面的有效性的证据。这一发现强调了该计划对 HBV 流行病学 的影响。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为国家 疫苗接种 计划在预防儿童 HBV 感染方面的成功提供了重要见解,可以为未来的公共卫生战略和 监测 工作提供信息。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性设计而受到限制,可能会引入偏差和混杂因素。然而,考虑到病例数的明显下降和结果的统计显着性,证据是强有力的。

papers.title: Seroprevalence and Risk Factors of Hepatitis B and C Virus Infections among Pregnant Women in Kaduna State, Nigeria
papers.abstract: Background: Hepatitis is caused by Viruses that are all contagious and the infection can be transmitted from one person to another. Estimating the prevalence of hepatitis B and C viral infections among pregnant women will help reduce mortality and morbidity rates in these subjects. Methodology: A total of three hundred (300) blood samples were collected from three Hospitals in Saminaka, Lere and Gure based on the availability of samples. The sera samples were assayed using in-vitro diagnostic kit (dipsticks/strips) to detect the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and antibodies to hepatitis C virus (anti-HCV). Results: Test strip revealed that 18/330 (6.00%) of pregnant women tested positive for HBV and 15/300 (5.00%) were infected with HCV. The Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) kit confirmed 25/300 (8.33%) of HBV and 21/300 (7.00%) of HCV in the study population.. Conclusion: There is need for proper screening of blood before transfusion as most women that had blood transfusion once were found to be infected also there is need for proper sensitization about the disease as many participants were not aware of its capacity to spread and cause life threatening infection.
papers.journal: International Journal of Emerging Research in Applied Medical Sciences

papers.title: Distinct immune signatures define hepatitis D- versus hepatitis B-associated hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Hepatitis D is the most severe form of viral hepatitis. However, the clinical, virological, and systemic inflammatory characteristics of HDV-associated HCC remain insufficiently characterized. METHODS: In this single-center retrospective study, we identified 162 patients with HCC due to chronic hepatitis D (HDV-HCC; n=54) or chronic hepatitis B (HBV-HCC; n=108). Plasma levels of 92 soluble inflammatory mediators (SIMs) were quantified using proximity extension assay in HCC patients [HBV-HCC (n=50), HDV-HCC (n=30), and matched non-HCC controls (HBV=19, HDV=17)]. RESULTS: At the time of HCC diagnosis, patients with CHD were younger, had more impaired liver synthesis and detoxification function, and lower levels of AST, CRP, and leukocytes. HDV-HCCs presented with smaller tumors, less frequent portal vein infiltration, and more often fulfilled Milan criteria (all p<0.01). Systemic immune profiling revealed distinct inflammatory patterns between both etiologies. Compared with HBV-HCC, HDV-HCC was characterized by a comparatively stronger IL-10-associated immunoregulatory signature, whereas HBV-HCC exhibited a more pronounced pro-inflammatory profile involving IL-6- and phosphorylation- and proliferation-associated signaling. Despite these differences, event-free survival did not differ between groups. CONCLUSIONS: HBV-HCC more frequently presented with advanced tumor stage, whereas HDV-HCC was associated with more severe underlying liver disease but smaller tumors. Importantly, HBV-associated and HDV-associated HCC exhibit distinct systemic inflammatory signatures, potentially reflecting differences in systemic immune regulation between etiologies. These findings may have implications for biomarker development and future etiology-specific therapeutic strategies.

papers.title_zh: 不同的免疫特征定义了与乙型肝炎病毒相关和与丁型肝炎病毒相关的肝细胞癌。
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Hepatitis D is the most severe form of viral hepatitis. However, the clinical, virological, and systemic inflammatory characteristics of HDV-associated HCC remain insufficiently characterized. METHODS: In this single-center retrospective study, we identified 162 patients with HCC due to chronic hepatitis D (HDV-HCC; n=54) or chronic hepatitis B (HBV-HCC; n=108). Plasma levels of 92 soluble inflammatory mediators (SIMs) were quantified using proximity extension assay in HCC patients [HBV-HCC (n=50), HDV-HCC (n=30), and matched non-HCC controls (HBV=19, HDV=17)]. RESULTS: At the time of HCC diagnosis, patients with CHD were younger, had more impaired liver synthesis and detoxification function, and lower levels of AST, CRP, and leukocytes. HDV-HCCs presented with smaller tumors, less frequent portal vein infiltration, and more often fulfilled Milan criteria (all p<0.01). Systemic immune profiling revealed distinct inflammatory patterns between both etiologies. Compared with HBV-HCC, HDV-HCC was characterized by a comparatively stronger IL-10-associated immunoregulatory signature, whereas HBV-HCC exhibited a more pronounced pro-inflammatory profile involving IL-6- and phosphorylation- and proliferation-associated signaling. Despite these differences, event-free survival did not differ between groups. CONCLUSIONS: HBV-HCC more frequently presented with advanced tumor stage, whereas HDV-HCC was associated with more severe underlying liver disease but smaller tumors. Importantly, HBV-associated and HDV-associated HCC exhibit distinct systemic inflammatory signatures, potentially reflecting differences in systemic immune regulation between etiologies. These findings may have implications for biomarker development and future etiology-specific therapeutic strategies.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:肝细胞癌(HCC)是全球癌症相关死亡的主要原因之一。丁型肝炎病毒(HDV)是病毒性肝炎中最严重的形式。然而,与HDV相关的HCC的临床、病毒学和全身炎症特征仍不够明确。方法:本研究为单中心回顾性研究,纳入了162例因慢性乙型肝炎(HBV-HCC;n=108)或慢性丁型肝炎(HDV-HCC;n=54)导致的HCC患者。使用邻近扩展检测法(proximity extension assay)对HCC患者的血浆中92种可溶性炎症介质(SIMs)水平进行了定量分析,包括50例HBV-HCC、30例HDV-HCC以及匹配的非HCC对照组(HBV=19,HDV=17)。结果:在HCC诊断时,慢性乙型肝炎患者年龄较小,肝合成和解毒功能受损更严重,AST、CRP和白细胞水平较低。HDV-HCC肿瘤体积较小,门静脉浸润较少见,且更常符合米兰标准(所有p<0.01)。全身免疫特征分析显示两种病因的HCC具有不同的炎症模式。与HBV-HCC相比,HDV-HCC表现出更强的IL-10相关免疫调节特征,而HBV-HCC则表现出更显著的促炎特征,涉及IL-6和磷酸化及增殖相关信号。尽管存在这些差异,各组的无事件生存率没有显著差异。结论:HBV-HCC更常表现为晚期肿瘤阶段,而HDV-HCC则与更严重的潜在肝病但较小的肿瘤相关。重要的是,HBV相关和HDV相关的HCC表现出不同的全身炎症特征,这可能反映了两种病因之间系统性免疫调节的差异。这些发现可能对生物标志物的开发和未来针对病因的治疗策略具有重要意义。

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTBackgroundHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remain major public health challenges globally and in Ethiopia. Although policies, regulations, and strategies have been developed to support their control and elimination, translating these policy commitments into effective implementation remains challenging. Understanding stakeholder experiences and perspectives is important for identifying gaps in policy awareness, participation, implementation, and program coordination.ObjectiveThis study aimed to explore the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia.MethodsA facility‐ and institution‐based qualitative study was conducted among stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, research, and service delivery. Thirty‐four participants were purposively selected based on their professional roles, experience, knowledge, and involvement in relevant programs. Data were collected from April 17 to May 27, 2023, using qualitative interviews and focus group discussions, complemented by a review of relevant policy, strategy, guideline, and program documents and observations of selected service‐delivery and pharmaceutical settings. Data were transcribed, translated where necessary, and thematically analysed using MAXQDA Analytics Pro 2024. The analysis focused on policy awareness, stakeholder involvement, stakeholder roles, implementation status, opportunities, and challenges.ResultsParticipants had a mean work experience of 16.82 years (SD = 0.79), and 30 (88.2%) were male. Of the 34 participants, 12 (35.3%) clearly identified or described the existence and key features of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies, while 22 (64.7%) did not. Fifteen (44.1%) participants reported stakeholder involvement in policy and strategy development, whereas 19 (55.9%) did not report adequate opportunities for participation. Most participants, 32 (94.1%), demonstrated an understanding of stakeholder roles and responsibilities in policy development and implementation. However, only 8 (23.5%) participants reported a clear current implementation status or progress, while 26 (76.5%) reported no clear implementation status. Twenty‐nine (85.3%) participants reported limited or unclear opportunities for strengthening HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination. Nearly all participants, 32 (94.1%), identified challenges affecting policy and strategy implementation, including COVID‐19‐related disruptions and concerns regarding the translation of policies and strategies into practice.ConclusionThe findings indicate a substantial gap between recognition of stakeholder responsibilities and the practical awareness and implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. Strengthening policy dissemination, inclusive stakeholder engagement, implementation monitoring, coordination, and the translation of policy commitments into service‐delivery activities may support progress toward national and global elimination targets. Sustainable financing, strengthened health‐system capacity, stakeholder accountability, and reliable monitoring and evaluation systems are important considerations for improving implementation. 2Methods2.1Study Setting and PeriodThe study was conducted at selected national, regional, and subnational institutions in Ethiopia that are directly involved in the development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, and delivery of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination services. The study sites included the Ministry of Health (MoH), Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), Amhara Public Health Institute (APHI), regional health bureaus, zonal health offices, district health offices, University of Gondar Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, selected health centers, drug stores, and regional blood bank units.These institutions were selected because they represent key stakeholders involved in policy formulation, program coordination, disease surveillance, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, laboratory services, pharmaceutical supply, and implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination interventions. Their inclusion enabled the study to capture perspectives from different levels of the health system and to identify contextual factors influencing the development, implementation, and effectiveness of relevant policies, regulations, and strategies.Data collection was conducted from April 17, 2023, to May 27, 2023. The principal investigator conducted the qualitative data collection using semi‐structured interview and discussion guides developed in accordance with the study objectives. Key informant interviews, in‐depth interviews, and focus group discussions were conducted with relevant stakeholders and participants, while institutional visits and review of relevant policy, strategic, guideline, and regulatory documents were undertaken to complement the interview data.2.2Study DesignA facility‐ and institution‐based qualitative study was conducted to explore the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The study employed an interpretive qualitative approach to obtain in‐depth information from policymakers, program managers, researchers, healthcare professionals, laboratory personnel, pharmacists, and other relevant stakeholders involved in policy development, program implementation, regulation, and service delivery. Data were collected through qualitative interviews and focus group discussions, complemented by a review of relevant policies, strategies, guidelines, and other program documents, as well as observations from selected health‐service and pharmaceutical settings.2.3Study ParticipantThe study participants were purposively selected from key stakeholders involved in the development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, and delivery of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination programs in Ethiopia. Participants included policymakers and program managers from the Federal Ministry of Health (MoH), regional health bureaus, and zonal and district health offices; researchers and technical experts from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), Amhara Public Health Institute (APHI), and Ethiopian higher education institutions; healthcare professionals, including physicians, nurses, and other clinical practitioners; laboratory technologists from regional blood bank units and health facilities; pharmacists working in government and private institutions; and other relevant stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and pharmaceutical supply.In addition, individuals receiving HIV, HBV, or HCV‐related healthcare services were included to provide perspectives on service accessibility, utilization, experiences, and challenges encountered at the patient and community levels. Relevant policy, program, and strategic documents were also reviewed to complement the information obtained from participants.Participants were selected based on their knowledge, professional experience, or direct involvement in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy development, implementation, regulation, research, or service delivery. The selection was based on participants’ knowledge, professional experience, roles, and direct involvement in the development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, research, or delivery of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination programs in Ethiopia.A total of 34 participants were purposively selected from relevant stakeholder groups, including policymakers and program managers, researchers and technical experts, healthcare professionals, laboratory and blood‐bank personnel, pharmacists, and other stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination. The diversity of participants across national, regional, subnational, research, clinical, laboratory, pharmaceutical, and service‐delivery settings was intended to capture multiple perspectives on the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia.2.5Data Collection StrategyData were collected in three sequential phases using qualitative methods to explore the challenges and opportunities influencing the development, implementation, and effectiveness of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The qualitative data collection comprised in‐depth interviews (IDIs), key informant interviews (KIIs), and focus group discussions (FGDs), allowing the study to capture individual experiences, stakeholder perspectives, and shared experiences related to HIV, HBV, and HCV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and elimination. Phase 1: In‐Depth Interviews (IDIs) In‐depth interviews were conducted with individuals living with HIV, including those receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), to explore their experiences and perceptions regarding HIV, HBV, and HCV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and related health services. Particular attention was given to challenges related to access, affordability, availability of medicines and diagnostic services, stigma and discrimination, continuity of care, and opportunities for improving implementation. Phase 2: Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) Key informant interviews were conducted with policymakers, program managers, health‐system leaders, healthcare professionals, researchers, laboratory professionals, pharmacists, and other stakeholders involved in the planning, coordination, regulation, implementation, and monitoring of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination programs in Ethiopia.The KIIs explored participants’ perspectives on the development and implementation of national HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies; stakeholder roles and responsibilities; coordination mechanisms; availability of financial, human, pharmaceutical, laboratory, and other resources; and the current status of implementation. Participants were also asked to identify major barriers and enabling factors affecting policy implementation at national, regional, and service‐delivery levels.The interviews further explored opportunities for strengthening prevention, case identification, testing and diagnosis, linkage to care, treatment, viral suppression, monitoring, surveillance, and integration of HIV, HBV, and HCV services within the Ethiopian health system. Participants were encouraged to provide recommendations for addressing identified policy, regulatory, organizational, and implementation gaps. The FGDs facilitated discussion of shared experiences, perceptions, and contextual factors influencing the implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies.The discussions explored health‐system challenges, availability of medicines and diagnostic services, human‐resource capacity, provider knowledge and skills, referral and linkage systems, stigma and discrimination, financing, coordination among stakeholders, monitoring and evaluation, and the integration of HIV, HBV, and HCV services. Participants also discussed opportunities to improve implementation and accelerate progress toward national and global control and elimination targets.2.6Trustworthiness of the StudyTo ensure the trustworthiness and methodological rigor of the qualitative study, the principles of credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability were considered throughout the research process.Credibility was enhanced through the use of multiple qualitative data sources, including in‐depth interviews (IDIs), key informant interviews (KIIs), focus group discussions (FGDs), document review, and direct observation of relevant service and pharmacy settings. These complementary sources enabled triangulation of information and provided opportunities to compare perspectives across different participant groups and sources. The semi‐structured interview and discussion guides were developed based on the study objectives, reviewed by subject‐matter experts, and pre‐tested in a non‐study setting to improve their clarity, relevance, and applicability. Such contextual descriptions enable readers and researchers to assess the applicability of the findings to similar settings.Dependability was strengthened through the systematic application of standardized data‐collection procedures, researcher training, close supervision, and documentation of methodological decisions throughout the study. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTBackgroundHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remain major public health challenges globally and in Ethiopia. Although policies, regulations, and strategies have been developed to support their control and elimination, translating these policy commitments into effective implementation remains challenging. Understanding stakeholder experiences and perspectives is important for identifying gaps in policy awareness, participation, implementation, and program coordination.ObjectiveThis study aimed to explore the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia.MethodsA facility‐ and institution‐based qualitative study was conducted among stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, research, and service delivery. Thirty‐four participants were purposively selected based on their professional roles, experience, knowledge, and involvement in relevant programs. Data were collected from April 17 to May 27, 2023, using qualitative interviews and focus group discussions, complemented by a review of relevant policy, strategy, guideline, and program documents and observations of selected service‐delivery and pharmaceutical settings. Data were transcribed, translated where necessary, and thematically analysed using MAXQDA Analytics Pro 2024. The analysis focused on policy awareness, stakeholder involvement, stakeholder roles, implementation status, opportunities, and challenges.ResultsParticipants had a mean work experience of 16.82 years (SD = 0.79), and 30 (88.2%) were male. Of the 34 participants, 12 (35.3%) clearly identified or described the existence and key features of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies, while 22 (64.7%) did not. Fifteen (44.1%) participants reported stakeholder involvement in policy and strategy development, whereas 19 (55.9%) did not report adequate opportunities for participation. Most participants, 32 (94.1%), demonstrated an understanding of stakeholder roles and responsibilities in policy development and implementation. However, only 8 (23.5%) participants reported a clear current implementation status or progress, while 26 (76.5%) reported no clear implementation status. Twenty‐nine (85.3%) participants reported limited or unclear opportunities for strengthening HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination. Nearly all participants, 32 (94.1%), identified challenges affecting policy and strategy implementation, including COVID‐19‐related disruptions and concerns regarding the translation of policies and strategies into practice.ConclusionThe findings indicate a substantial gap between recognition of stakeholder responsibilities and the practical awareness and implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. Strengthening policy dissemination, inclusive stakeholder engagement, implementation monitoring, coordination, and the translation of policy commitments into service‐delivery activities may support progress toward national and global elimination targets. Sustainable financing, strengthened health‐system capacity, stakeholder accountability, and reliable monitoring and evaluation systems are important considerations for improving implementation.

The principal investigator conducted the qualitative data collection using semi‐structured interview and discussion guides developed in accordance with the study objectives. Key informant interviews, in‐depth interviews, and focus group discussions were conducted with relevant stakeholders and participants, while institutional visits and review of relevant policy, strategic, guideline, and regulatory documents were undertaken to complement the interview data.2.2Study DesignA facility‐ and institution‐based qualitative study was conducted to explore the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The study employed an interpretive qualitative approach to obtain in‐depth information from policymakers, program managers, researchers, healthcare professionals, laboratory personnel, pharmacists, and other relevant stakeholders involved in policy development, program implementation, regulation, and service delivery. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis study explored stakeholder perspectives on the development, implementation, opportunities, and challenges related to HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The findings demonstrate an important discrepancy between recognition of stakeholder responsibilities and the practical visibility and implementation of policies. Although 94.1% of participants demonstrated an understanding of stakeholder roles, only 35.3% clearly identified the existence and key features of relevant policies, 44.1% reported stakeholder involvement in policy and strategy development, and only 23.5% reported a clear current implementation status. Furthermore, 85.3% perceived limited opportunities for strengthening hepatitis elimination activities, while 94.1% identified challenges affecting implementation. Taken together, these findings suggest that the principal issue is not simply the absence of policy documents, but the extent to which policies are communicated, translated into operational activities, monitored, financed, and coordinated across different levels of the health system.4.1Awareness of HIV, HBV, and HCV Policies, Regulations, and StrategiesOnly 35.3% of participants in this study clearly identified or described the existence and key features of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies, whereas 64.7% did not clearly identify or describe them. This finding is consistent with earlier Ethiopian evidence showing that, although Ethiopia had begun developing hepatitis strategic plans and guidelines, the national response was characterized by limited coordination, inadequate dissemination of guidance, weak surveillance, and limited access to hepatitis services. In their qualitative assessment of Ethiopia's hepatitis response, Abera et al. reported that the country was developing strategic plans and guidelines but lacked sufficient partnerships and resource mobilization, while treatment and screening guidelines were not adequately available or implemented [5].The finding is also consistent with more recent evidence showing that knowledge and awareness do not necessarily translate into appropriate hepatitis‐related practices in Ethiopia. For example, a systematic review and meta‐analysis of 26 Ethiopian studies reported that only 47.45% of participants had a good level of knowledge concerning HBV prevention, while good preventive practices were reported in only 36.22% (2026). Although that evidence concerns individual‐level knowledge rather than awareness of national policies, it supports the broader observation that information and communication gaps remain relevant to hepatitis prevention and control in Ethiopia.Evidence from other settings similarly demonstrates that policy formulation does not automatically ensure effective policy awareness or implementation. A global assessment of 55 national viral hepatitis strategic action plans found substantial gaps in alignment with WHO recommendations: 35% of plans did not include HBV and HCV elimination goals, and only 38% included a national budget or financing plan for hepatitis activities [7]. More recent country profiles also show continuing weaknesses in national monitoring and service coverage despite the existence of formal policies. Among 33 countries assessed for HCV elimination, only 55% had systems tracking the number of people tested and treated, while only 30% had achieved the WHO 2025 diagnosis‐coverage target [7, 8].The Ethiopian finding should therefore be interpreted as an implementation‐system issue rather than simply an individual knowledge deficit. The WHO Global Health Sector Strategy 2022–2030 emphasizes that countries need effective strategic information systems capable of generating and analyzing data from service‐delivery and administrative levels to monitor progress toward elimination targets [1]. The low awareness observed in the present study may therefore reflect limited dissemination and operational communication of policy documents between national, regional, and service‐delivery levels.4.2Stakeholder Involvement in Policy and Strategy DevelopmentOnly 44.1% of participants reported involvement of relevant stakeholders in the development of HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies, while 55.9% did not report adequate opportunities for participation. This finding is important because WHO's 2022–2030 Global Health Sector Strategies explicitly emphasize leadership, partnerships, multisectoral action, community engagement, and collaboration with stakeholders as central components of the response to HIV and viral hepatitis [1]. The WHO strategy also describes its own development process as broadly consultative, involving Member States, experts, communities, partners, and other stakeholders.The relatively limited stakeholder involvement identified in this study is consistent with the earlier Ethiopian qualitative assessment by Abera et al., which identified inadequate partnerships and limited resource mobilization as important weaknesses in the country's hepatitis response [5]. It also corresponds with evidence from sub‐Saharan Africa showing that operationalizing hepatitis elimination requires coordinated involvement of governments, healthcare providers, technical organizations, professional groups, and development partners. African countries have faced difficulties translating HCV elimination objectives into operational programs because of diagnostic costs, medicine access, logistics, and limited program infrastructure [9].There are also examples demonstrating the potential value of coordinated national and continental approaches. The establishment of the Africa CDC viral hepatitis prevention and control program represents a continental mechanism intended to support countries in developing and strengthening hepatitis elimination program [10]. Similarly, Rwanda and Egypt are among countries that have demonstrated progress in operationalizing hepatitis elimination approaches, although their experiences occur within different health‐system and financing contexts and should not be directly equated with Ethiopia.The finding from this study is therefore relevant to WHO's emphasis on a whole‐of‐government and whole‐of‐society approach. The global strategy recognizes that effective implementation requires political and community leadership and partnerships extending beyond the health sector [1]. Limited participation of stakeholders outside central institutions may reduce opportunities for incorporating service‐delivery experience, research evidence, professional expertise, and community perspectives into policy development.4.3Understanding of Stakeholder RolesA particularly notable finding was that 94.1% of participants demonstrated an understanding of their roles and responsibilities in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy development and implementation. This relatively high recognition contrasts with the lower levels of policy awareness and implementation‐status awareness observed in the same study. Thus, participants appeared to understand what their responsibilities were, even when they had less certainty about which policies were currently being implemented and how much progress had been achieved.This distinction is important in interpreting the findings. The Ethiopian evidence indicates that healthcare professionals can possess substantial hepatitis‐related knowledge while important gaps remain in translating knowledge into practice. For example, a study among healthcare professionals at the University of Gondar Hospital found that 73.1% had good knowledge of HBV transmission, progression, and vaccination, but knowledge varied substantially by professional group [11]. full_text_sections.conclusion: 6ConclusionMost stakeholders have no information about the availability of hepatitis control and elimination policy, regulations, and strategies, but they effectively understand their role during preparations and implementations of hepatitis control and elimination policy, regulations, and strategies. The policy, regulations, and strategies were not prepared with full involvement of concerned bodies as a result, there is no enough implementations progress reports from the respondents. The existence of hepatitis different guidelines, policies, regulations, strategies, documents, and hepatitis elimination program incorporation to sustainable development goals and vaccine availability for healthcare providers and newborn babies are a good opportunity. Funding problem, lack of training, community culture and belief, COVID‐19, commitments of different stakeholders including government, shortage of medications, lack of awareness and mobilizations, and weak practices of monitoring and evaluations are the most common challenges. Although the COVID‐19 pandemic required immediate public health measures, its effects on hepatitis control initiatives underscore the necessity of comprehensive approaches that tackle both COVID‐19 and persistent viral hepatitis issues. Based on the finding we recommend to revised the existing policy, regulations and strategies with the full invitations of concerned bodies, collaborate with many donor organizations, accessing screening, testing and treatment of the patients, practical performing of monitoring and evaluations, increase the awareness and mobilizations of for patients, health care providers and other concerned bodies are important activities to control and eliminate hepatitis.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remain major public health challenges worldwide and continue to cause substantial morbidity, mortality, and health‐system burden. HBV and HCV can cause acute and chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, while HIV requires lifelong treatment and sustained healthcare services. These infections also share important prevention and health‐system priorities, including safe blood and injection practices, prevention of mother‐to‐child transmission, testing, treatment, monitoring, community engagement, and access to quality health services. Despite major advances in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, gaps remain in translating available interventions into effective population‐level program [1, 2]. In 2022, approximately 254 million people were living with chronic HBV infection and 50 million with HCV infection globally, and viral hepatitis B and C caused approximately 1.3 million deaths, mainly from cirrhosis and liver cancer [2].The burden of viral hepatitis is particularly important in low‐ and middle‐income countries and in the WHO African Region. Although effective prevention, diagnostic, and treatment interventions are available, access remains inadequate in many settings. WHO's Global Health Sector Strategies 2022–2030 established the goal of eliminating viral hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030 and emphasized people‐centered services, health‐system strengthening, strategic information, partnerships, community engagement, and integrated approaches to service delivery [1]. However, recent evidence demonstrates that the global response remains off track. The 2026 WHO Global Hepatitis Report estimated that approximately 1.3 million people died from HBV‐ and HCV‐related cirrhosis and liver cancer in 2024, while treatment coverage for chronic HBV remained below 5% despite the availability of effective antiviral therapy [3]. These findings indicate that the availability of effective interventions alone is insufficient without appropriate policies, financing, governance, stakeholder coordination, monitoring, and implementation systems.Ethiopia has a substantial burden of HBV and HCV and has progressively developed policy and strategic responses to address viral hepatitis. Earlier systematic evidence estimated the pooled prevalence of HBV infection in Ethiopia at 7.4% [3], while an updated systematic review reported a pooled prevalence of approximately 6% [4]. More recent evidence continues to demonstrate a considerable HBV burden, with a systematic review of studies conducted in Ethiopia reporting a pooled prevalence of 6.9%. Previous Ethiopian studies have also identified important gaps in prevention, diagnosis, treatment, surveillance, and health‐system capacity.Ethiopia has recognized viral hepatitis as an important public health problem and has developed policies, strategies, and program structures to address it. A landmark qualitative assessment examined the national response to HBV and HCV using interviews with key informants, policy and strategy document review, and observation of pharmaceutical premises [5]. The study found that Ethiopia was developing strategic plans and guidelines but faced limited partnerships and resource mobilization, inadequate community awareness, restricted availability of screening, insufficient treatment guidance, weak surveillance, and limited availability of effective medicines. The authors concluded that the national response was fragmented and recommended strengthening surveillance, screening, vaccination, treatment, policy guidance, partnerships, and access to affordable medicines. Subsequent research has identified additional opportunities for HCV elimination in Ethiopia, including phased micro‐elimination, task shifting, improved access to affordable diagnostics and direct‐acting antivirals, blood‐safety interventions, and multisectoral collaboration [6].Despite these developments, existing HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies are understood and experienced by stakeholders responsible for their development and implementation at different levels of the Ethiopian health system. In particular, limited recent evidence is available regarding stakeholders’ awareness of existing policies and strategies, their participation in policy development, understanding of roles and responsibilities, perceptions of current implementation status, available opportunities, and challenges affecting implementation. The 2016 Ethiopian policy assessment provided important baseline evidence regarding the national hepatitis response, but the policy and program environment has subsequently evolved, including the development of newer strategic frameworks. Therefore, there is a need for updated evidence examining whether policy commitments are visible and understood by stakeholders and how they are translated into implementation across national, regional, district, and service‐delivery levels.There is limited stakeholder‐level evidence linking the formal existence of HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies with their practical implementation, coordination, monitoring, and perceived effectiveness in Ethiopia. The existence of policy documents does not necessarily demonstrate that stakeholders are aware of them, participate in their development, understand their responsibilities, or have adequate resources and institutional mechanisms to implement them. This gap is particularly important because WHO identifies strategic information, accountability, partnerships, financing, community engagement, and integrated service delivery as essential components of achieving the 2030 HIV and viral hepatitis targets [1]. The continuing global shortfall in progress toward viral hepatitis elimination further demonstrates the importance of understanding implementation barriers at country level.To address this gap, the present study explored the challenges and opportunities of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The study examined perspectives from stakeholders involved in policy development, program management, research, regulation, laboratory and pharmaceutical services, healthcare delivery, and other relevant activities. Qualitative interviews and focus group discussions were complemented by review of relevant policies, strategies, guidelines, and program documents and observations of selected health‐service and pharmaceutical settings. Specifically, the study assessed stakeholders’ awareness of policy and strategy existence and features, involvement in policy development, understanding of roles and responsibilities, perceptions of current implementation status, available opportunities, and challenges affecting implementation. analysis.summary_en: This study explores the challenges and opportunities in the control and elimination of HIV, HBV, and HCV policies in Ethiopia. Conducted from April 17 to May 27, 2023, it involved 34 purposively selected stakeholders from key institutions. Data were gathered through interviews, focus groups, and document reviews. Results showed that only 35.3% of participants recognized the existence of HBV-related policies, while 94.1% understood stakeholder roles. However, only 23.5% reported clear implementation status. The authors interpret these findings as indicating a substantial gap between policy recognition and practical implementation, with challenges such as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and inadequate translation of policies into practice. The study's qualitative design and purposive sampling limit its generalizability, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.

papers.title: Clonorchis sinensis co-infection potentiates polymorphonuclear-myeloid-derived suppressor cells expansion and metabolic reprogramming in chronic hepatitis B patients
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Clonorchis sinensis (C. sinensis ) co-infection is known to accelerate disease progression and induce immune tolerance in patients with hepatitis B virus (HBV), particularly in regions where both infections are endemic. Metabolic reprogramming has emerged as a key driver of immunosuppression. These metabolic shifts are often orchestrated by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), which expand during chronic infections to promote immune tolerance. sinensis co-infection reprograms metabolism to favor MDSC-linked suppression and how this process relates to normal liver enzyme levels remains unclear. AIM To investigate whether C. sinensis co-infection induces MDSC- linked metabolic reprogramming in patients with HBV and normal liver enzyme levels. METHODS In this cross-sectional study, a total of 117 participants were enrolled and assigned to four groups: Healthy controls (n = 30), C. sinensis mono-infected participants (n = 29), HBV mono-infected participants (n = 28), and co-infected participants (n = 30). Serum cytokine profiles were measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay, amino acid metabolites using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and MDSC subsets using flow cytometry. Spearman correlation and mediation analyses were performed to explore the relationships among inflammation, metabolism, and immunity. RESULTS HBV mono-infected and co-infected patients showed no statistically significant differences in liver enzyme and HBV DNA levels. However, compared with the HBV mono-infected group, the co-infected group had higher levels of the inflammatory cytokine: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), accompanied by markedly lower interferon-γ (IFN-γ) levels. Flow cytometric assay revealed that polymorphonuclear MDSCs (PMN-MDSCs) showed the greatest expansion in the co-infected group, and their proportion correlated strongly with IL-6 and TNF-α levels. Metabolically, the co-infected group had a significantly higher ornithine-to-arginine ratio. Mediation analysis suggested that PMN-MDSCs accounted for approximately 45% of the total effect of IL-6 on IFN-γ suppression. sinensis co-infection was associated with immunosuppression through IL-6/TNF-α-linked PMN-MDSC expansion and elevated ornithine-to-arginine ratio, resulting in suppressed IFN-γ production despite normal liver enzyme levels.

papers.abstract_zh: 背景已知华支睾吸虫(C. sinensis)合并感染会加速乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)患者的疾病进展并诱导免疫耐受,特别是在两种感染流行的地区。代谢重编程已成为免疫抑制的关键驱动因素。这些代谢变化通常是由骨髓源性抑制细胞(MDSC)精心策划的,这些细胞在慢性感染期间会扩张以促进免疫耐受。中华丝虫合并感染会重新编程代谢以有利于 MDSC 相关的抑制,而这一过程与正常肝酶水平的关系仍不清楚。目的 探讨中华支原体合并感染是否会诱导肝酶水平正常的 HBV 患者发生 MDSC 相关的代谢重编程。方法 在这项横断面研究中,总共招募了 117 名参与者,并分为四组:健康对照(n = 30)、单一感染中华支原体的参与者(n = 29)、单一感染 HBV 的参与者(n = 28)和混合感染的参与者(n = 30)。使用化学发光免疫测定法测量血清细胞因子谱,使用液相色谱-串联质谱法测量氨基酸代谢物,并使用流式细胞术测量MDSC子集。进行 Spearman 相关性和中介分析来探讨炎症、代谢和免疫之间的关系。结果 HBV单一感染和合并感染患者的肝酶和HBV DNA水平无统计学差异。然而,与HBV单一感染组相比,合并感染组的炎症细胞因子白细胞介素6(IL-6)和肿瘤坏死因子-α(TNF-α)水平较高,同时干扰素-γ(IFN-γ)水平明显较低。流式细胞术检测显示,多形核MDSC(PMN-MDSC)在共感染组中表现出最大的扩增,并且其比例与IL-6和TNF-α水平密切相关。在代谢方面,共同感染组的鸟氨酸与精氨酸的比率显着较高。中介分析表明,PMN-MDSC 约占 IL-6 对 IFN-γ 抑制总效应的 45%。中华线虫合并感染通过 IL-6/TNF-α 连接的 PMN-MDSC 扩增和鸟氨酸与精氨酸比率升高与免疫抑制相关,导致尽管肝酶水平正常,但 IFN-γ 的产生受到抑制。
