papers.full_text: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden, with an estimated 254 million people living with chronic infection worldwide in 2022.1 Chronic HBV infection is a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for more than half of HCC cases globally.2 Despite vaccination and antiviral therapy, HBV-related HCC continues to contribute substantially to cancer-related mortality.3,4 Importantly, HBV infection confers a risk of HCC even in the absence of cirrhosis, suggesting direct virus-associated genomic mechanisms beyond inflammation and fibrosis.5 Although HBV lacks a viral oncogene, it can promote tumor development through genetic damage, chromosomal instability, and the expression of viral regulatory elements.3,6 HBV replicates through reverse transcription of pregenomic RNA, generating relaxed circular DNA, which is converted to covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) by host machinery.4,7 Some viral genomes form double-stranded linear DNA, which cannot produce infectious progeny but can integrate into host chromosomes.5 These linear molecules resemble cellular DNA breaks and enter host repair pathways, generating integration-competent viral DNA early in infection.7 HBV integration has been detected as early as 23–49 days after infection, indicating that integration is not merely a late consequence of chronic infection.6 Integrated HBV DNA can remain transcriptionally active and contribute to circulating hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels, thereby promoting immune exhaustion and viral persistence.4,7 HBV lacks an integrase and relies on host DNA repair. Double-stranded linear DNA molecules resemble cellular double-strand breaks and are incorporated into host chromosomes primarily through nonhomologous end joining and microhomology-mediated end joining. Because both pathways are error prone, HBV integration generates small insertions, deletions, and complex virus-host junctions that contribute to chromosomal instability.7,8 Although the initial sites of integration in the host genome are largely random, viral DNA linearization breakpoints occur at specific hotspots (Fig. 1).3 Hepatocytes harboring oncogenic integrations may undergo clonal expansion.8 HBV integrations are enriched in regions of high chromatin accessibility, active transcription, early replication, and genomic fragility, and the breakpoint pattern can influence which viral genes remain intact after integration.3 This commentary reviews the mechanisms of HBV integration, common HBV breakpoints, and their implications for HCC risk and clinical management. A well-supported mechanism of HBV-driven oncogenesis is enhancer-mediated cis-activation of adjacent host genes. HBV enhancer I (HBV-Enh I) and the X region are preferentially preserved in integrated viral sequences, suggesting positive clonal selection of hepatocytes harboring these integrations.8,9 HBV-Enh I can act in cis to drive the expression of nearby oncogenes, such as telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and the MYC proto-oncogene (MYC) (Fig. 2).10 Ectopic MYC overexpression driven by HBV-Enh I integration has been reported to promote HCC cell migration and invasion.10 A preferential breakpoint at the 3′ end of hepatitis B virus X protein (HBx) results in C-terminally truncated HBx variants with enhanced oncogenic potential.9 These 3′-deleted proteins lack regulatory domains involved in p53-dependent transcription, Sp1 binding, and growth suppression, thereby promoting cellular proliferation, transformation, and invasion.9 C-terminally truncated HBx was detected in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases and was associated with venous invasion, increased c-Jun activity, metalloproteinase expression, mitogen-activated protein kinase activation, and cell-cycle dysregulation—features of metastatic potential.9 The generation of C-terminally truncated HBx proteins is supported by experimental and clinical studies, although its relative contribution to human hepatocarcinogenesis remains under investigation. Nontumor liver tissue contains a greater diversity of unique HBV integration sites, which are generally low frequency and nonclonal. In contrast, tumor tissue contains fewer unique integration sites but shows substantially greater clonality, indicating the selective expansion of hepatocytes harboring oncogenic integrations.3,10 Although HBV integration occurs in only approximately 0.1% of infected hepatocytes, integrated HBV DNA has been detected in 85%–90% of HBV-related HCCs, indicating strong biological selection.10 Integrations in nontumor liver tissue are largely transcriptionally silent, whereas tumor-associated integrations occur near functionally relevant regions.3,8 HBV integration events can also promote hepatocarcinogenesis by inactivating tumor suppressor pathways. Tumor suppressor alterations, including mutations and deletions, were identified in up to 48% of HBV-related tumors, compared with 16% of non-HBV-related HCCs.10 Homozygous deletions of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A) occurred in 2%–12%, retinoblastoma 1 (RB1) alterations in 3%–8%, and p53 mutations in 41% of HBV-related HCCs.10 HBV integration-associated telomeric deletions increase the risk of biallelic inactivation of flanking tumor suppressor genes.11 Truncated HBx can suppress p53-dependent transcriptional activity. Loss of RB1 promotes uncontrolled S-phase entry and cellular proliferation, whereas CDKN2A loss impairs both RB1 and p53 tumor suppressor activity.9 Integrated HBV DNA frequently exists as concatemers that generate unstable virus-host junctions prone to recombination and breakage.11 These events can cause genomic restructuring, including nonhomologous chromosomal fusions, dicentric chromosomes, and megabase-scale deletions.10,11 In one genomic analysis, HBV-mediated telomeric deletion events were identified in 8% of HCCs; 40 structural rearrangements resulted in the deletion or inactivation of 244 tumor suppressor genes, including tumor protein p53 (TP53) and RB1.11 A 14.9-Mb telomeric deletion encompassing TP53, with mutation of the remaining allele, was reported, exemplifying HBV-driven biallelic inactivation.11 In HBV-associated HCC, p53 dysfunction is consistently associated with more aggressive tumor biology and a poorer prognosis.10,11 Nevertheless, current evidence suggests that direct disruption of tumor suppressor genes is less common than enhancer-mediated oncogene activation and integration-associated structural rearrangements. Genome-wide sequencing studies have identified recurrent integration hotspots in HCC involving TERT in 20%–50% of cases, lysine methyltransferase 2B/mixed-lineage leukemia 4 (KMT2B/MLL4) in 1%–10%, and cyclin E1 (CCNE1) in approximately 5%. These frequencies exceed those expected by chance and are associated with clonal expansion and altered gene expression (Table 1).12 | Host locus | Key effect | Mechanism | Frequency in HBV-related HCC | Cohort details | |---|---|---|---|---| | TERT | Telomerase activation through cis-regulatory enhancer hijacking | Strongest recurrent hotspot; supports early clonal advantage and telomere maintenance | 20%–50% | 18/88 (20.5%); 101/426 (23.7%); 39/153 (25.5%); 48/177 (27.1%) | | KMT2B/MLL4 | Histone methyltransferase activity, chromatin remodeling, and epigenetic dysregulation | Recurrent epigenetic driver; promotes tumorigenesis through enhancer/chromatin dysregulation | 2%–11% in large series; higher in some small cohorts | 9/88 (10.2%); 31/426 (7.3%); 16/153 (10.5%); 3/177 (1.7%); 6/27 (22.2%) | | CCNE1 | G1/S transition and replication stress | Supports unscheduled cell-cycle entry and genomic instability | 1%–5% | 4/88 (4.5%); 7/426 (1.6%); 4/177 (2.3%) | | CCNA2 | Cell-cycle progression | Less frequent but recurrent; suggests broader cell-cycle selection beyond CCNE1 | 2% in one major cohort | 8/426 (1.9%) | | MYC and PVT1 region | Oncogene amplification and cis-activation | Viral enhancer donation and structural amplification can activate MYC programs | Recurrent, but the frequency has not been consistently reported across cohorts | – | | TP53 | Structural disruption or deletion rather than hotspot integration | Tumor suppressor alteration associated with uncontrolled proliferation | Recurrent, but the frequency has not been consistently reported across cohorts | – | TERT is the most frequent HBV integration hotspot, with tumor-level frequencies reported as 35.8% (34/95),13 23.7% (101/426),3 and 29.8% (28/94).14TERT integration has been associated with more aggressive tumor behavior.13TERT promoter integrations were rare (3%) in nontumor liver tissue, indicating strong positive selection.13 Insertion of HBV-Enh I into the TERT promoter region increases TERT transcription through cis-activation by recruiting host transcription factors to the chimeric TERT promoter, thereby activating telomerase.13 HBV integration at TERT and TERT promoter mutations or other alterations are generally mutually exclusive, suggesting distinct but functionally redundant mechanisms of telomerase reactivation.15 KMT2B/MLL4 is the second most consistently reported recurrent hotspot. KMT2B and KMT2C encode histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferases involved in chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation.12 Disruption of these genes through HBV integration can lead to dysregulated transcription and aberrant chromatin states. Reported frequencies include 10.5% in a 153-case capture-sequencing series, 7.3% in a 426-case cohort, 10.2% in an 88-case dataset, and 1.7% in a 177-case cohort.12 CCNE1 regulates the G1/S cell-cycle transition, and its overexpression can drive uncontrolled cellular proliferation and genomic instability.12,15 Recurrent CCNE1 integrations were identified in 4 of 88 (4.5%), 7 of 426 (1.6%), and 4 of 177 (2.3%) HBV-related HCCs.12 Integration at CCNE1 can upregulate the gene through the insertion of viral enhancer elements or structural rearrangements; these events were tumor-specific and positively selected.12,14 MYC and plasmacytoma variant translocation 1 (PVT1) are less frequently recognized HBV integration targets.12,15 HBV integration can induce focal MYC amplification through structural rearrangements or enhancer-mediated activation, thereby promoting proliferation, clonal expansion, and chromosomal instability.10,15 Reported frequencies of HBV integration patterns vary substantially among cohorts because of differences in geographic region, HBV genotype, disease stage, viral replication level, and sequencing methodology. Genotype C has been associated with more HBV integration events, greater clonal expansion, and more frequent integration into cancer-associated genes.12,15 A meta-analysis of more than 10,000 patients found that HCC developed in 25% of patients with genotype C versus 13% of those with genotype B.16 Passenger HBV integrations, typically found in nontumor liver tissue, occur randomly at low clonal frequencies, whereas driver integrations can contribute to oncogenesis by activating proto-oncogenes, inactivating tumor suppressors, or inducing genomic instability, thereby conferring a proliferative advantage and promoting clonal expansion.3,8,12,17 Only 3%–5% of HBV integration sites overlap between tumor and adjacent nontumor tissue within the same patient, indicating clonal selection.3,17 Oncogenic integration events may arise early, including in preneoplastic dysplastic nodules, and expand during tumor progression.6,8 HBV acts primarily as a regulatory mutagen by donating enhancer activity that activates adjacent oncogenes and as a structural mutagen by inducing chromosomal instability, telomeric deletions, and copy-number alterations.10,11 Truncated HBx further amplifies oncogenic signaling by suppressing p53-dependent transcription, activating mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and dysregulating the cell cycle.9 Together, these mechanisms may help explain the persistent risk of HCC despite viral suppression and in the absence of cirrhosis. HBV integration occurs early in infection, including in patients with minimal liver injury, particularly during high-level viral replication.6,7 The 2025 American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases/Infectious Diseases Society of America guideline suggests antiviral therapy for patients in the immune-tolerant phase who are older than 40 years or have significant hepatic inflammation or fibrosis; for younger patients interested in earlier treatment, it recommends shared decision-making.18 Because evidence that treatment of otherwise low-risk patients in the immune-tolerant phase reduces HCC risk remains uncertain, the possibility that suppression of high-level HBV replication could reduce insertional mutagenesis and HCC risk warrants prospective evaluation. Another emerging area of investigation is the interaction between HBV integration and the tumor immune microenvironment. Integrated HBV DNA can remain transcriptionally active and produce viral transcripts and proteins, particularly HBsAg and HBx, even when viral replication is suppressed.5,17 These persistently expressed viral antigens may influence local hepatic immune responses, with potential downstream effects on antitumor immunity and responses to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy.17 This hypothesis warrants evaluation in controlled studies. Although early studies suggested that circulating chimeric HBV-host DNA might enable earlier detection of residual or recurrent disease, clinical implementation remains limited by the need for highly specialized detection methods, methodological heterogeneity, and the lack of standardized assays.17,19 Commercial clinical laboratories currently offer serum HBV DNA quantification and related viral biomarkers but do not offer validated integration-site mapping as a standard-of-care assay.17,19 Detection of recurrent driver integrations involving TERT, KMT2B, or CCNE1 may help distinguish random background integrations from tumor-specific events and clarify whether a lesion is linked to an HBV-driven oncogenic pathway.12,17 Patient-specific HBV-host junction sequences may serve as molecular fingerprints for monitoring recurrence.12,19 However, integration profiling has not been validated for routine prognostic decision-making or for guiding surveillance, resectability, or systemic therapy. HBV integration is an early and intrinsic mechanism of hepatocarcinogenesis that can operate independently of cirrhosis. Although most integrations remain silent, a subset may undergo clonal selection through enhancer-mediated oncogene activation, tumor suppressor disruption, chromosomal instability, and the production of truncated HBx proteins. Thus, integrated HBV DNA can act as both a regulatory and a structural mutagen, potentially helping to explain the persistent risk of HCC in HBV infection despite viral suppression. The mechanisms of HBV integration provide an additional rationale for early and sustained suppression of viral replication. Although currently available nucleos(t)ide analogues do not eliminate preexisting integrations or cccDNA, antiviral therapy may reduce the formation of new integration events by suppressing viral replication and decreasing the generation of integration-competent double-stranded linear DNA intermediates. Observational data show that antiviral therapy is associated with a lower HCC incidence in broader populations with chronic hepatitis B, but whether treatment during the immune-tolerant phase reduces HCC risk remains uncertain.18,20 Large, multicenter, long-term controlled studies are needed to test this hypothesis. Prospective multicenter cohorts are needed to validate associations of specific integration sites—such as TERT, KMT2B, CCNE1, and MYC/PVT1—and tumor suppressor-disrupting structural events with prognosis, recurrence risk, and vascular invasion. Standardized integration assays are also needed to determine whether serial monitoring of circulating HBV-host junction DNA can reliably identify minimal residual disease or early recurrence and whether integration-site analysis improves risk stratification. papers.title_original: Hepatitis B Virus Insertional Mutagenesis and Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Mechanisms and Clinical Significance

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the mechanisms by which hepatitis B virus (HBV) insertional mutagenesis contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and its clinical significance. The background highlights the role of HBV integration in oncogenesis and the need to understand its impact on tumor biology.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed HBV integration patterns in both nontumor and tumor liver tissues, focusing on the clonality and diversity of integration sites. It examined patients with HBV-related HCC and compared them with non-HBV-related HCC cases to assess the association between integration events and tumor suppressor gene alterations.
analysis.methods: Genome-wide sequencing was used to identify recurrent integration hotspots in HCC, including TERT, KMT2B/MLL4, and CCNE1. The study also evaluated the frequency and impact of HBV integration on tumor suppressor pathways through analysis of breakpoints and truncation of HBx proteins.
analysis.main_results: C-terminally truncated HBx proteins were detected in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases and were linked to features of metastatic potential. Tumor suppressor alterations, including mutations and deletions, were found in up to 48% of HBV-related tumors, compared with 16% of non-HBV-related HCCs. HBV integration events were associated with the deletion or inactivation of 244 tumor suppressor genes, including TP53 and RB1.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that HBV integration contributes to hepatocarcinogenesis through both direct disruption of tumor suppressor genes and enhancer-mediated oncogene activation. The study highlights the importance of integration-associated structural rearrangements in promoting aggressive tumor biology.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results have implications for improving the detection and monitoring of HBV-driven oncogenic pathways in HCC. They also emphasize the need for integration-site analysis to better understand the mechanisms of HBV-related hepatocarcinogenesis and guide clinical decision-making.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on observational data and does not establish causality. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on genomic analysis and clinical observations without experimental validation of the causal relationship between HBV integration and HCC progression.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the mechanisms of hepatitis B virus (HBV) insertional mutagenesis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), emphasizing its role in oncogenesis. It identifies C-terminally truncated HBx proteins in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases, linked to metastatic features. The research also highlights the impact of HBV integration on tumor suppressor genes, such as TP53 and RB1, through structural rearrangements. These findings suggest that integration events are critical in HBV-related HCC progression, though the evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and lack of experimental validation. The study underscores the need for standardized integration assays to improve risk stratification and monitoring of HBV-driven oncogenic pathways in HCC.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)插入突变导致肝细胞癌(HCC)的机制及其临床意义。这一背景强调了 HBV 整合在肿瘤发生中的作用以及了解其对肿瘤生物学影响的必要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究分析了非肿瘤和肿瘤肝组织中的 HBV 整合模式,重点关注整合位点的克隆性和多样性。它检查了 HBV 相关 HCC 患者,并将其与非 HBV 相关 HCC 病例进行比较,以评估整合事件与肿瘤抑制基因改变之间的关联。
elements_zh.methods: 基因组 全测序用于识别 HCC 中的复发性整合热点,包括 TERT、KMT2B/MLL4 和 CCNE1。该研究还通过分析 HBx 蛋白的断点和截短,评估了 HBV 整合对肿瘤抑制途径的频率和影响。
elements_zh.main_results: 在高达 79.3% 的 HBV 相关 HCC 病例中检测到 C 端截短的 HBx 蛋白,并且与转移潜力的特征相关。在高达 48% 的 HBV 相关肿瘤中发现了肿瘤抑制基因的改变,包括 突变 和缺失,而在非 HBV 相关的 HCC 中这一比例为 16%。HBV 整合事件与 244 个肿瘤抑制基因的缺失或失活相关,其中包括 TP53 和 RB1。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,HBV 整合通过直接破坏肿瘤抑制基因和增强子介导的癌基因激活而导致肝癌发生。该研究强调了整合相关的结构重排在促进侵袭性肿瘤生物学方面的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果对于改善 HCC 中 HBV 驱动的致癌途径的检测和监测具有重要意义。他们还强调需要进行整合位点分析,以更好地了解 HBV 相关肝癌发生的机制并指导临床决策。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于观察数据,并未建立因果关系。证据是中等的,因为它基于基因组分析和临床观察,没有对 HBV 整合与 HCC 进展之间的因果关系进行实验验证。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the mechanisms by which hepatitis B virus (HBV) insertional mutagenesis contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and its clinical significance. The background highlights the role of HBV integration in oncogenesis and the need to understand its impact on tumor biology.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed HBV integration patterns in both nontumor and tumor liver tissues, focusing on the clonality and diversity of integration sites. It examined patients with HBV-related HCC and compared them with non-HBV-related HCC cases to assess the association between integration events and tumor suppressor gene alterations.
analysis_en.methods: Genome-wide sequencing was used to identify recurrent integration hotspots in HCC, including TERT, KMT2B/MLL4, and CCNE1. The study also evaluated the frequency and impact of HBV integration on tumor suppressor pathways through analysis of breakpoints and truncation of HBx proteins.
analysis_en.main_results: C-terminally truncated HBx proteins were detected in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases and were linked to features of metastatic potential. Tumor suppressor alterations, including mutations and deletions, were found in up to 48% of HBV-related tumors, compared with 16% of non-HBV-related HCCs. HBV integration events were associated with the deletion or inactivation of 244 tumor suppressor genes, including TP53 and RB1.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that HBV integration contributes to hepatocarcinogenesis through both direct disruption of tumor suppressor genes and enhancer-mediated oncogene activation. The study highlights the importance of integration-associated structural rearrangements in promoting aggressive tumor biology.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results have implications for improving the detection and monitoring of HBV-driven oncogenic pathways in HCC. They also emphasize the need for integration-site analysis to better understand the mechanisms of HBV-related hepatocarcinogenesis and guide clinical decision-making.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on observational data and does not establish causality. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on genomic analysis and clinical observations without experimental validation of the causal relationship between HBV integration and HCC progression.

papers.source_body_en: 2).10 Ectopic MYC overexpression driven by HBV-Enh I integration has been reported to promote HCC cell migration and invasion.10 A preferential breakpoint at the 3′ end of hepatitis B virus X protein (HBx) results in C-terminally truncated HBx variants with enhanced oncogenic potential.9 These 3′-deleted proteins lack regulatory domains involved in p53-dependent transcription, Sp1 binding, and growth suppression, thereby promoting cellular proliferation, transformation, and invasion.9 C-terminally truncated HBx was detected in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases and was associated with venous invasion, increased c-Jun activity, metalloproteinase expression, mitogen-activated protein kinase activation, and cell-cycle dysregulation—features of metastatic potential.9 The generation of C-terminally truncated HBx proteins is supported by experimental and clinical studies, although its relative contribution to human hepatocarcinogenesis remains under investigation. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden, with an estimated 254 million people living with chronic infection worldwide in 2022.1 Chronic HBV infection is a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for more than half of HCC cases globally.2 Despite vaccination and antiviral therapy, HBV-related HCC continues to contribute substantially to cancer-related mortality.3,4 Importantly, HBV infection confers a risk of HCC even in the absence of cirrhosis, suggesting direct virus-associated genomic mechanisms beyond inflammation and fibrosis.5 Although HBV lacks a viral oncogene, it can promote tumor development through genetic damage, chromosomal instability, and the expression of viral regulatory elements.3,6 HBV replicates through reverse transcription o...

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)插入突变导致肝细胞癌(HCC)的机制及其临床意义。这一背景强调了 HBV 整合在肿瘤发生中的作用以及了解其对肿瘤生物学影响的必要性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究分析了非肿瘤和肿瘤肝组织中的 HBV 整合模式,重点关注整合位点的克隆性和多样性。它检查了 HBV 相关 HCC 患者,并将其与非 HBV 相关 HCC 病例进行比较,以评估整合事件与肿瘤抑制基因改变之间的关联。
analysis_zh.methods: 基因组 全测序用于识别 HCC 中的复发性整合热点,包括 TERT、KMT2B/MLL4 和 CCNE1。该研究还通过分析 HBx 蛋白的断点和截短,评估了 HBV 整合对肿瘤抑制途径的频率和影响。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在高达 79.3% 的 HBV 相关 HCC 病例中检测到 C 端截短的 HBx 蛋白,并且与转移潜力的特征相关。在高达 48% 的 HBV 相关肿瘤中发现了肿瘤抑制基因的改变,包括 突变 和缺失,而在非 HBV 相关的 HCC 中这一比例为 16%。HBV 整合事件与 244 个肿瘤抑制基因的缺失或失活相关,其中包括 TP53 和 RB1。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,HBV 整合通过直接破坏肿瘤抑制基因和增强子介导的癌基因激活而导致肝癌发生。该研究强调了整合相关的结构重排在促进侵袭性肿瘤生物学方面的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果对于改善 HCC 中 HBV 驱动的致癌途径的检测和监测具有重要意义。他们还强调需要进行整合位点分析,以更好地了解 HBV 相关肝癌发生的机制并指导临床决策。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于观察数据,并未建立因果关系。证据是中等的,因为它基于基因组分析和临床观察,没有对 HBV 整合与 HCC 进展之间的因果关系进行实验验证。

news.content_title: Global Burden and Elimination Progress of Viral Hepatitis B and C Toward the 2030 WHO Targets: A Structured Review of Epidemiology, Inequities, and Service Delivery Gaps
news.content: Abstract Viral hepatitis B and C remain leading infectious causes of cirrhosis, liver cancer, and premature death worldwide, and the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for both infections to be eliminated as public health threats within this decade. This single-reviewer, selectively sourced structured narrative review provides a non-exhaustive overview of progress toward that goal, with attention to long-term burden trends, inequities between and within countries, model-based projections of elimination timelines, and gaps in service delivery. It is not a systematic review and makes no claim to be comprehensive. Evidence was identified through a small number of general web queries and full-text files held by the author; bibliographic database search strings were drafted but not executed, so relevant evidence may have been missed or misclassified. One reviewer performed screening, extraction, and appraisal, and a PRISMA-style flow diagram is provided for transparency only. Eligible records were global, regional, or multinational analyses and WHO reports addressing disease burden, service coverage, elimination progress, or prevention. Reporting completeness, risk of bias, and funding and conflict-of-interest declarations were appraised as separate dimensions. In the sources reviewed, age-standardized rates of infection have declined over recent decades, a pattern consistent with the effects of vaccination and improved treatment, although the analyses cannot establish causation. However, population growth, aging, and infections acquired before vaccination have kept the absolute burden high. Modeled estimates suggest that low-resource settings and people who inject drugs bear a disproportionate share of that burden, and the projections and program data reviewed indicate that most countries are not on course to meet the elimination targets. The main obstacles appear to lie in diagnosis, treatment access, timely birth-dose vaccination, antenatal testing, and harm reduction rather than in a lack of effective tools. Falling age-standardized rates should therefore not be mistaken for sufficient progress. These findings are hypothesis-generating and should be confirmed by a prospectively registered, database-complete systematic review. Introduction & Background Infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains one of the most common infectious routes to cirrhosis and liver cancer. In 2022, the two viruses accounted for an estimated 1.3 million deaths, about 3,500 a day, and the global reservoir comprised 254 million people with chronic HBV and 50 million with chronic HCV [1]. Controlling them requires different tools. A vaccine protects against HBV, yet infection acquired in the first year of life becomes chronic in 80-90% of cases, compared with roughly 5% of infected adults, and available treatment suppresses the virus without clearing it [2,3]. Vaccination cannot prevent HCV, but direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) now cure it [4]. HBV is transmitted from mother to child around the time of birth, through percutaneous or mucosal exposure to infected blood or body fluids, and sexually. HCV is transmitted mainly through blood-borne exposure, including injecting drug use, unsafe medical procedures, and unscreened blood products, with vertical and sexual transmission being less common. Over years to decades, chronic infection with either virus can progress to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [2,4]. The burden is unevenly distributed: prevalence and mortality are highest, and gaps in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment are widest in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [1]. Two terms need to be distinguished. In WHO usage, "elimination as a public health threat" means achieving defined, measurable reductions in new infections and deaths against a fixed baseline, whereas "eradication" means the permanent worldwide absence of the pathogen, a status achieved for only one human disease (smallpox). Neither HBV nor HCV is currently considered eradicable: HBV persists in chronic carriers, and treatment suppresses rather than clears it, and HCV, although curable, has no vaccine and can be re-acquired after cure. The Global Health Sector Strategy frames elimination as a 90% reduction in incidence and a 65% reduction in mortality by 2030 relative to a 2015 baseline, supported by 90% diagnosis and 80% treatment coverage [5]. The incidence target refers to new chronic HBV infections and new HCV infections, and the mortality target to deaths from HBV- and HCV-related liver disease, including cirrhosis and HCC. The diagnosis target is expressed against all people living with chronic infection, and the treatment target against those eligible for treatment [1]. The programmatic routes differ by virus: HBV targets center on childhood immunization, including a timely birth dose, and on prevention of mother-to-child transmission, whereas HCV targets center on harm-reduction services for people who inject drugs, blood and injection safety, and access to DAA treatment [1]. Two ways of expressing burden are also used throughout this review. An age-standardized rate (per 100,000 population) re-weights observed rates to a common reference age structure so that places and years can be compared independently of differences in age composition, and it approximates individual-level risk. Absolute burden, expressed as counts of cases, deaths, or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), reflects the number of people affected and rises with population growth and aging even when individual risk falls. Rates and counts can therefore move in opposite directions. Several recent publications have examined individual elements of this agenda, namely, chronic HBV [3], total HCV burden [4], the timing of HCV elimination in high-income countries [5], acute HBV in women of childbearing age [6], HCV incidence in people who inject drugs [7], and national policy performance [8,9]. As their data sources and endpoints differ, these reports are seldom interpreted together. This review therefore offers a selectively sourced, single-reviewer narrative overview that brings evidence on burden trends, inequities, elimination trajectories, and delivery gaps into one structured account and that seeks to separate apparent progress from improvement that exists only in standardized rates. It is not comprehensive or database-complete, and it does not pool data. Review Design and reporting This was a single-reviewer structured narrative review of selectively sourced evidence. It is not a systematic review: it was not registered in advance, bibliographic database searches were not executed, and one reviewer carried out all screening, extraction, and appraisal without independent verification. A PRISMA 2020-style flow diagram [10] is used solely to document how records were handled and does not imply that systematic-review methods were followed (Figure 1). The single-reviewer design carries a risk of missed or misclassified evidence, extraction error, and subjective appraisal judgments, which are addressed under Limitations. Information sources Searching was limited to general web queries and to author-held files. On 4 October 2026, three queries were submitted to Google Search and Google Scholar. The first (Table 1, Q1) was exploratory, and the second and third were targeted title lookups used to confirm the bibliographic details of records surfaced by the first. The queries returned 28 records in total (Q1: 18 records; Q2: six records; Q3: four records), and every item returned was counted. Search strings were drafted for PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library (Table 1), but these databases were not queried, and no database records are reported; the strings are provided solely to allow future replication. Eleven full-text files already in the authors' possession were added as records from other methods. Eligibility criteria Eligible records were peer-reviewed articles and WHO reports from 2020 to 2026, available in English as an abstract or full text, that offered quantitative or systematic evidence at a global, regional, or multinational scale on HBV or HCV burden, service coverage, elimination progress, or prevention. We included narrative overviews only if they provided quantitative service-coverage data or explicit guideline-gap data. We excluded editorials and commentaries, narrative overviews that did not meet this condition, book chapters, conference posters, earlier versions superseded by updates, single-country or local studies, and analyses that did not separate viral etiologies. Selection and level of text access The flow of records (Figure 1) began with 39 identifications: 28 from web queries and 11 from author-supplied files. After 10 duplicates were removed, 29 records were screened by title and abstract, 14 reports were sought, 13 were assessed in full, and 11 studies were included. One reviewer screened and assessed records and extracted the design, data source, scope, key figures, and limitations. Text access varied by source and is stated for each study in Table 2. Eight studies were evaluated from the full text. Three were assessed at abstract or summary level only: the Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology Commission update (abstract) [8], the 33-country hepatitis C elimination profiles (summary) [9], and the WHO 2025 report [1], which was available as a slide presentation. Findings and appraisal ratings for these sources are correspondingly less detailed and should be read with more caution. The included studies were ecological burden analyses, mathematical models, policy indices, and evidence syntheses. Critical appraisal Design-specific instruments for trials or cohort studies, such as Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) [13], Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) [14], or the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale [15], did not apply to these diverse designs, and no single validated instrument fits all of them. To make each source's strengths and weaknesses transparent, we applied an informal, domain-based appraisal adapted from elements of the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER) statement [16] for health estimates, Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards (CHEERS) 2022 [17] and International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research-Society for Medical Decision Making (ISPOR-SMDM) good-practice guidance [18] for modeling studies, and the domain-based logic of ROBIS [19] and A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews (AMSTAR 2) [20] for evidence syntheses. The framework is not validated, yields no numerical score, and relies on a single reviewer's judgment. Three distinct dimensions were assessed, and they are reported separately rather than combined: (1) Reporting completeness: Were data sources, methods, assumptions, uncertainty intervals, and limitations described sufficiently for a reader to understand and reproduce the estimates? This dimension concerns reporting transparency, not the likelihood of bias, and was rated as complete, partial, or limited. (2) Risk of bias: Were input-data selection and coverage, reliance on imputation or covariate-driven modeling, trend-extrapolation assumptions, and the testing of alternative scenarios likely to distort the main conclusions? This dimension was rated as low, moderate, high, or unclear. (3) Funding and conflict-of-interest (COI) declarations: What funding sources and COI were declared? This dimension is documented descriptively (declared non-commercial source, declared commercial source, or unclear). We classified declarations that were not checked as unclear. Commercial funding was recorded as context for the reader and did not automatically raise the risk-of-bias rating, and an academic affiliation was not taken as evidence that no conflict existed. Each rating carries a one-sentence justification (Table 3). Ratings were assigned from full text where it was accessible and from abstracts or summaries otherwise, and the level of access is shown in Table 3. No rule-based algorithm was used to derive an overall judgment; the final column of Table 3 records the reviewer's overall level of concern for interpretation, informed by all three dimensions. Appraisal ratings were not used to exclude studies. As we synthesized the evidence narratively without pooling, we used the ratings to weight the interpretation of findings and flag conclusions that rest on higher-risk sources. Four Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analyses [2-4,6] use a shared modeling framework [21] and were not regarded as independent replications. Excluded editorials and reports are cited for context only. Where available in the accessed text, 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) are reported alongside principal estimates; where none is shown, none was reported in or extracted from the accessible text. Study selection and characteristics The three web queries yielded 28 records, and the authors' own files added 11, for a total of 39 identifications (Figure 1). After removing 10 duplicates (nine mirrored copies of the same articles in the web results and one repeated file), 29 records remained for screening. Fifteen of these were excluded at title and abstract level: five editorials or commentaries, two narrative overviews, one book chapter, one superseded conference poster, one non-peer-reviewed institutional web page, one trial protocol, one modeling study published before 2020, and three single-country or regional analyses of people who inject drugs. Fourteen reports were then sought. One, a 2025 national HBV policy report, could not be assessed because only its listing was accessible. Of the 13 reports assessed in full, two were excluded: a GBD 2021 liver cancer analysis that did not distinguish etiology [22] and a WHO methods annex with no outcome data [23]. The 11 remaining studies (Table 2) comprised four GBD analyses, one HCV elimination model, one global incidence analysis in people who inject drugs, one policy-index commission update, one report based on country profiles, one narrative review of research gaps, one qualitative systematic review, and one WHO program dataset. Reading the estimates: Sources, definitions, and reference years Estimates in the included studies differ in source, case definition, and reference year, and they are therefore not interchangeable. The reference year or period is stated for each principal statistic below. The four GBD analyses [2-4,6] share a common modeling infrastructure [21]; their consistent findings therefore constitute one body of evidence, not independent replications. GBD and WHO figures should not be compared directly. The GBD 2019 estimate of 555,000 deaths in 2019 refers to HBV-related disease, which includes deaths from cirrhosis and liver cancer attributed to HBV [2]. The WHO figure of 1.3 million deaths in 2022 combines HBV and HCV, includes cirrhosis and HCC, and derives from country-validated data supplemented by partner models [1,23]. The scope of the death counts in the GBD 2021 chronic HBV analysis [3] was not detailed in the accessible text, so those counts are not compared with the 2019 or WHO figures. For HCV, the incident cases reported by GBD 2021 [4] and the new infections attributed to injecting drug use [7] use different case definitions: the latter distinguishes all new infections, including re-infections, from primary infections only, whereas the accessible text of the GBD analysis did not state whether re-infections are counted. news.content_original: Abstract Viral hepatitis B and C remain leading infectious causes of cirrhosis, liver cancer, and premature death worldwide, and the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for both infections to be eliminated as public health threats within this decade. This single-reviewer, selectively sourced structured narrative review provides a non-exhaustive overview of progress toward that goal, with attention to long-term burden trends, inequities between and within countries, model-based projections of elimination timelines, and gaps in service delivery. It is not a systematic review and makes no claim to be comprehensive. Evidence was identified through a small number of general web queries and full-text files held by the author; bibliographic database search strings were drafted but not executed, so relevant evidence may have been missed or misclassified. One reviewer performed screening, extraction, and appraisal, and a PRISMA-style flow diagram is provided for transparency only. Eligible records were global, regional, or multinational analyses and WHO reports addressing disease burden, service coverage, elimination progress, or prevention. Reporting completeness, risk of bias, and funding and conflict-of-interest declarations were appraised as separate dimensions. In the sources reviewed, age-standardized rates of infection have declined over recent decades, a pattern consistent with the effects of vaccination and improved treatment, although the analyses cannot establish causation. However, population growth, aging, and infections acquired before vaccination have kept the absolute burden high. Modeled estimates suggest that low-resource settings and people who inject drugs bear a disproportionate share of that burden, and the projections and program data reviewed indicate that most countries are not on course to meet the elimination targets. The main obstacles appear to lie in diagnosis, treatment access, timely birth-dose vaccination, antenatal testing, and harm reduction rather than in a lack of effective tools. Falling age-standardized rates should therefore not be mistaken for sufficient progress. These findings are hypothesis-generating and should be confirmed by a prospectively registered, database-complete systematic review. Introduction & Background Infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains one of the most common infectious routes to cirrhosis and liver cancer. In 2022, the two viruses accounted for an estimated 1.3 million deaths, about 3,500 a day, and the global reservoir comprised 254 million people with chronic HBV and 50 million with chronic HCV [1]. Controlling them requires different tools. A vaccine protects against HBV, yet infection acquired in the first year of life becomes chronic in 80-90% of cases, compared with roughly 5% of infected adults, and available treatment suppresses the virus without clearing it [2,3]. Vaccination cannot prevent HCV, but direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) now cure it [4]. HBV is transmitted from mother to child around the time of birth, through percutaneous or mucosal exposure to infected blood or body fluids, and sexually. HCV is transmitted mainly through blood-borne exposure, including injecting drug use, unsafe medical procedures, and unscreened blood products, with vertical and sexual transmission being less common. Over years to decades, chronic infection with either virus can progress to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [2,4]. The burden is unevenly distributed: prevalence and mortality are highest, and gaps in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment are widest in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [1]. Two terms need to be distinguished. In WHO usage, "elimination as a public health threat" means achieving defined, measurable reductions in new infections and deaths against a fixed baseline, whereas "eradication" means the permanent worldwide absence of the pathogen, a status achieved for only one human disease (smallpox). Neither HBV nor HCV is currently considered eradicable: HBV persists in chronic carriers, and treatment suppresses rather than clears it, and HCV, although curable, has no vaccine and can be re-acquired after cure. The Global Health Sector Strategy frames elimination as a 90% reduction in incidence and a 65% reduction in mortality by 2030 relative to a 2015 baseline, supported by 90% diagnosis and 80% treatment coverage [5]. The incidence target refers to new chronic HBV infections and new HCV infections, and the mortality target to deaths from HBV- and HCV-related liver disease, including cirrhosis and HCC. The diagnosis target is expressed against all people living with chronic infection, and the treatment target against those eligible for treatment [1]. The programmatic routes differ by virus: HBV targets center on childhood immunization, including a timely birth dose, and on prevention of mother-to-child transmission, whereas HCV targets center on harm-reduction services for people who inject drugs, blood and injection safety, and access to DAA treatment [1]. Two ways of expressing burden are also used throughout this review. An age-standardized rate (per 100,000 population) re-weights observed rates to a common reference age structure so that places and years can be compared independently of differences in age composition, and it approximates individual-level risk. Absolute burden, expressed as counts of cases, deaths, or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), reflects the number of people affected and rises with population growth and aging even when individual risk falls. Rates and counts can therefore move in opposite directions. Several recent publications have examined individual elements of this agenda, namely, chronic HBV [3], total HCV burden [4], the timing of HCV elimination in high-income countries [5], acute HBV in women of childbearing age [6], HCV incidence in people who inject drugs [7], and national policy performance [8,9]. As their data sources and endpoints differ, these reports are seldom interpreted together. This review therefore offers a selectively sourced, single-reviewer narrative overview that brings evidence on burden trends, inequities, elimination trajectories, and delivery gaps into one structured account and that seeks to separate apparent progress from improvement that exists only in standardized rates. It is not comprehensive or database-complete, and it does not pool data. Review Design and reporting This was a single-reviewer structured narrative review of selectively sourced evidence. It is not a systematic review: it was not registered in advance, bibliographic database searches were not executed, and one reviewer carried out all screening, extraction, and appraisal without independent verification. A PRISMA 2020-style flow diagram [10] is used solely to document how records were handled and does not imply that systematic-review methods were followed (Figure 1). The single-reviewer design carries a risk of missed or misclassified evidence, extraction error, and subjective appraisal judgments, which are addressed under Limitations. Information sources Searching was limited to general web queries and to author-held files. On 4 October 2026, three queries were submitted to Google Search and Google Scholar. The first (Table 1, Q1) was exploratory, and the second and third were targeted title lookups used to confirm the bibliographic details of records surfaced by the first. The queries returned 28 records in total (Q1: 18 records; Q2: six records; Q3: four records), and every item returned was counted. Search strings were drafted for PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library (Table 1), but these databases were not queried, and no database records are reported; the strings are provided solely to allow future replication. Eleven full-text files already in the authors' possession were added as records from other methods. Eligibility criteria Eligible records were peer-reviewed articles and WHO reports from 2020 to 2026, available in English as an abstract or full text, that offered quantitative or systematic evidence at a global, regional, or multinational scale on HBV or HCV burden, service coverage, elimination progress, or prevention. We included narrative overviews only if they provided quantitative service-coverage data or explicit guideline-gap data. We excluded editorials and commentaries, narrative overviews that did not meet this condition, book chapters, conference posters, earlier versions superseded by updates, single-country or local studies, and analyses that did not separate viral etiologies. Selection and level of text access The flow of records (Figure 1) began with 39 identifications: 28 from web queries and 11 from author-supplied files. After 10 duplicates were removed, 29 records were screened by title and abstract, 14 reports were sought, 13 were assessed in full, and 11 studies were included. One reviewer screened and assessed records and extracted the design, data source, scope, key figures, and limitations. Text access varied by source and is stated for each study in Table 2. Eight studies were evaluated from the full text. Three were assessed at abstract or summary level only: the Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology Commission update (abstract) [8], the 33-country hepatitis C elimination profiles (summary) [9], and the WHO 2025 report [1], which was available as a slide presentation. Findings and appraisal ratings for these sources are correspondingly less detailed and should be read with more caution. The included studies were ecological burden analyses, mathematical models, policy indices, and evidence syntheses. Critical appraisal Design-specific instruments for trials or cohort studies, such as Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) [13], Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) [14], or the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale [15], did not apply to these diverse designs, and no single validated instrument fits all of them. Three distinct dimensions were assessed, and they are reported separately rather than combined: (1) Reporting completeness: Were data sources, methods, assumptions, uncertainty intervals, and limitations described sufficiently for a reader to understand and reproduce the estimates? This dimension concerns reporting transparency, not the likelihood of bias, and was rated as complete, partial, or limited. (2) Risk of bias: Were input-data selection and coverage, reliance on imputation or covariate-driven modeling, trend-extrapolation assumptions, and the testing of alternative scenarios likely to distort the main conclusions? This dimension was rated as low, moderate, high, or unclear. (3) Funding and conflict-of-interest (COI) declarations: What funding sources and COI were declared? This dimension is documented descriptively (declared non-commercial source, declared commercial source, or unclear). We classified declarations that were not checked as unclear. Commercial funding was recorded as context for the reader and did not automatically raise the risk-of-bias rating, and an academic affiliation was not taken as evidence that no conflict existed. Each rating carries a one-sentence justification (Table 3). Ratings were assigned from full text where it was accessible and from abstracts or summaries otherwise, and the level of access is shown in Table 3. No rule-based algorithm was used to derive an overall judgment; the final column of Table 3 records the reviewer's overall level of concern for interpretation, informed by all three dimensions. Appraisal ratings were not used to exclude studies. Of the 13 reports assessed in full, two were excluded: a GBD 2021 liver cancer analysis that did not distinguish etiology [22] and a WHO methods annex with no outcome data [23]. The 11 remaining studies (Table 2) comprised four GBD analyses, one HCV elimination model, one global incidence analysis in people who inject drugs, one policy-index commission update, one report based on country profiles, one narrative review of research gaps, one qualitative systematic review, and one WHO program dataset. Home/ Research Areas/ Regulatory & Industry News FDA approves GSK's functional cure for hepatitis B Clinical trial updates, regulatory approvals, and more led the news this week. Brought to you byDDN editorial team Oct 23, 2026| 5 min read Catch up on this week’s top stories from the editors. Credit: Kristyn Reid Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 5:00 Welcome to the Weekly Rundown where the DDN editors cover this week’s top biotech and pharma news. FDA approves GSK’s functional cure for hepatitis B Tuesday brought good news for many patients with chronic hepatitis B. GSK’s antisense oligonucleotide Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection received the green light from the FDA, effectively offering a chance for some people with chronic hepatitis B to stop taking their antivirals entirely. The approval was based on two Phase 3 B-WELL trials, which demonstrated that 24 percent of patients who received the Hibsago treatment qualified to stop taking their medications — compared to zero percent taking the placebo. After 24 weeks without antivirals, Hibsago led to a functional cure in 19 percent of patients who no longer had detectable viral proteins in their blood. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease,” said Wendy Carter, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, in the press release. The approval marks the first to reach the finish line in a competitive landscape, with therapeutic options for hepatitis B from companies like Brii Biosciences now lagging behind. – Allison Whitten New trial aims to speed up the search for Alzheimer’s treatments A UK clinical trial is testing whether two existing medicines, metformin and atomoxetine, could help treat Alzheimer’s disease, using a platform design intended to speed up the search for effective therapies. The AD-SMART trial will recruit around 1,200 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s across more than 30 UK sites to assess metformin, commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Researchers believe both medicines could influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's, potentially helping patients remain independent for longer. The multi-arm, multi-stage design allows researchers to test several treatments alongside standard care and a shared placebo group, drop candidates that show insufficient benefit, and introduce new ones without restarting the trial. Over 18 months, researchers will assess whether each drug safely improves cognitive symptoms, daily functioning, or neuropsychiatric symptoms, while blood tests and MRI scans will help track biological changes associated with disease progression. The first treatments are expected to complete evaluation in 2030, with additional candidates potentially added in the meantime. The drugs were selected by an international panel drawing on earlier laboratory and clinical evidence, alongside input from people with lived experience of Alzheimer’s. – Bree Foster Inhaled exosome therapy shows promise for ARDS in Phase 2b trial Nano24 announced positive results from their Phase 2b trial testing EXO-CD24, an inhaled therapy that delivers the immune checkpoint CD24 via exosomes, to treat patients with the life-threatening condition acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). “Exosomes offer a promising foundation for drug delivery because their surfaces and internal cargo can be engineered to perform complementary functions,” said Robert Langer, Head of Nano24’s Scientific Advisory Board, in the press release. Based on data from 90 patients, the trial showed that EXO-CD24 led to 85 percent of patients being free of respiratory failure compared with just 33.3 percent of placebo, and a 72 percent reduced risk of death. The treatment also reduced the mean number of days in the hospital from 14.4 days down to 6.5. With current treatment options only focusing on supportive care, Nano24’s therapy could offer a very welcome change for patients and physicians alike. The company said in the statement that they now plan to move forward with an international Phase 3 trial to confirm efficacy and safety in ARDS. “The findings on the proportion of patients free of respiratory failure at Day 7 and on all-cause mortality are encouraging in this deadly condition. I look forward to taking part in the upcoming Phase 3 study,” said Matthew Baldwin, Associate Professor of Medicine at Columbia University, in the press release. – Allison Whitten Pfizer and Valneva present full Phase 3 data for Lyme vaccine candidate Pfizer and Valneva presented Phase 3 VALOR results for their six-valent Lyme disease vaccine candidate, PF-07307405 (LB6V), at the IDWeek congress in Washington, DC, with Amsterdam UMC’s Joppe Hovius presenting efficacy and safety data in healthy participants aged five and older living in Lyme disease-endemic regions of North America and Europe. The presentation builds on March’s topline readout, which showed efficacy of roughly 73 to 75 percent but missed the first prespecified statistical criterion because fewer Lyme disease cases accrued than expected. The European Medicines Agency began reviewing the marketing application in August, and Pfizer has said the findings support the vaccine’s potential to provide clinically meaningful antibody-associated protection. If approved, LB6V would be the first Lyme disease vaccine on the market in decades. – Andrea Corona Jemperli approval opens a new treatment path for some rectal cancer patients The FDA has granted accelerated approval to GSK’s Jemperli (dostarlimab) as the first and only immunotherapy for adults with previously untreated stage 2 or 3 locally advanced rectal cancer whose tumors are microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR). Jemperli is a PD-1-blocking antibody that is designed to help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. The approval, based on the Phase 2 AZUR-1 trial, could allow eligible patients to avoid chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery, which can cause lasting effects on bowel, urinary, and reproductive function. In the trial, 68 percent of evaluable patients achieved a clinical complete response sustained for at least 12 months, while an exploratory analysis found no evidence of cancer one year or more after treatment in 76 percent of patients. No disease recurrences have been reported among responders after a median follow-up of more than two years. The safety profile was consistent with previous experience, although serious adverse reactions occurred in 20 percent of patients and three percent discontinued treatment because of adverse reactions. Longer follow-up will be needed to establish how durable these responses are, but the results suggest that immunotherapy could offer some patients a way to avoid the lasting effects of conventional treatment. – Bree Foster FDA launches neuroscience program, starting with Alzheimer’s prevention The FDA launched the Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus (NAIN), a program that will bring together experts from its drug, biologics, and device centers to coordinate how it regulates products for conditions of the brain and nervous system. The scope covers neurologic and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders, and pain. NAIN’s first initiative, the Alzheimer’s Prevention Accelerator, will explore how to run clinical trials aimed at preventing or delaying Alzheimer’s disease, with a focus on trial populations, stage-appropriate endpoints, and the kind of evidence needed to show that cognitive decline was delayed or prevented. The agency said the difficulty of demonstrating clinical benefit in conditions that develop over many years is a core challenge, and pointed to biomarkers and digital health tools as opportunities to address it. Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said the program will help regulatory science keep pace with advances in neuroscience, and the launch is tied to the federal government’s national Alzheimer’s plan. For developers, the accelerator signals that the agency may be open to new endpoint and evidence standards for prevention trials, though no specific policy changes have been announced. – Andrea Corona Download PDF Add Drug Discovery News as a preferred Google source to see more of our trusted coverage. Written byAndrea Corona Aug 12, 2026| 4 min read BTK degradation is proving relevant far beyond oncology — and the Nurix and Roche partnership on bexobrutideg shows just how far. istock.com/alexkich Download PDF Highlights in this article What degrading BTK actually means Why BTK matters beyond oncology Translating degraders into autoimmune disease Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors have transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies over the past decade. Ibrutinib's approval in 2013 validated BTK as a drug target, and a succession of second-generation inhibitors — acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib, pirtobrutinib — have extended that validation with improved selectivity and tolerability. More recently, BTK inhibition has moved into autoimmune disease: The FDA approved remibrutinib and rilzabrutinib in 2025 for chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) and immune thrombocytopenia, respectively, and multiple Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials in multiple sclerosis (MS) are underway. Against that backdrop, Nurix Therapeutics and Roche announced a global collaboration to co-develop and co-commercialize bexobrutideg, an oral BTK degrader, across B-cell malignancies, MS, and CSU. The deal includes a $700 million upfront payment to Nurix and up to $2.3 billion in potential total payments. The partnership's scope reflects something broader than a single drug program: It is a bet that degrading BTK, rather than inhibiting it, is meaningfully different — and that the difference matters clinically across a range of conditions where BTK biology is central. Gwenn Hansen, Chief Scientific Officer at Nurix, responded to DDN's questions on that distinction. Their answers trace the mechanistic logic from molecular biology through clinical translation. What degrading BTK actually means The fundamental difference between a BTK inhibitor and a BTK degrader is occupancy versus elimination. Inhibitors bind BTK and block its kinase activity while the protein remains present in the cell. Bexobrutideg recruits BTK to an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which marks the protein for destruction by the proteasome — removing BTK from the cell rather than simply occupying its active site. Continue reading below... Application NoteRevealing cell-cell interactions in immuno-oncology Imaging-enabled flow cytometry helps distinguish biologically relevant cell-cell interactions from coincident events to support immunotherapy research. Read More "Unlike a traditional inhibitor, which typically blocks a single target protein while it remains bound, a degrader acts catalytically," Hansen said. "One degrader molecule can trigger the degradation of thousands of BTK proteins over time because it is recycled to engage additional target proteins after each binding event." In preclinical systems, a single bexobrutideg molecule has been shown to drive the elimination of up to 10,000 BTK molecules per hour — a catalytic efficiency that no stoichiometric inhibitor can match. That catalytic mechanism has several practical implications. First, it means therapeutic effect can be achieved at substantially lower drug concentrations than inhibition-based approaches, because the degrader is not consumed in the process. Lower systemic exposure is a meaningful advantage for a drug intended for chronic administration across a range of patients. Second, and perhaps more importantly for the longer arc of the field, it means the protein's scaffolding function is disrupted alongside its kinase activity. BTK is not only an enzyme — it participates in signaling complexes independent of its catalytic role. "By removing BTK rather than simply blocking its active site, a degrader has the potential to suppress both kinase-dependent and kinase-independent BTK functions," Hansen said. The resistance question follows directly from that, asacquired mutations that alter BTK's kinase domain can limit the effectiveness of inhibitors by reducing drug binding. A degrader that eliminates the protein rather than occupying its active site is less susceptible to resistance mutations that emerge at the binding interface. Nurix has reported early clinical activity in CLL patients with acquired resistance mutations to current BTK inhibitors — a population where available therapeutic options are limited. To date, six BTK inhibitors have been approved by the FDA, with most approved drugs used in B-cell malignancies, leaving a significant gap in the treatment of patients who progress on those therapies. Bexobrutideg's clinical development program is designed in part to address that gap. Why BTK matters beyond oncology The rationale for moving into autoimmune disease begins with where BTK is expressed and what it does there. BTK, expressed in B cells and myeloid-derived cells including microglia, serves as a shared intracellular signaling node linking adaptive and innate immune pathways.That expression pattern is what makes BTK relevant across disease categories that appear clinically distinct. In MS, the biology is particularly compelling. Although high-efficacy disease-modifying therapies have been effective in suppressing relapses in MS patients, they fail to effectively target chronic microglial activation and smoldering lesions. Most existing therapies act on peripheral immune infiltration; they do not reach the compartmentalized inflammation behind the blood-brain barrier that drives progressive disability. A brain-penetrant BTK-directed therapy could modulate immune activity in both the periphery and the central nervous system simultaneously — targeting both the B-cell axis and the microglial axis of MS pathology. Continue reading below... ArticlesMiniaturizing patient-derived organoid screening for precision oncology By combining organoid biology with precision automation, researchers developed a miniaturized organoid screening platform that could help speed personalized cancer treatment testing. Read More "In multiple sclerosis, the biology is compelling because both B cells and central nervous system-resident myeloid cells, including microglia, are thought to contribute to inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease processes," Hansen said. Bexobrutideg has demonstrated CNS penetration and pharmacologically relevant concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid — a prerequisite for any agent intended to act on brain-resident immune cells. In CSU, the mechanism differs but the BTK rationale is similarly grounded. Mast cell and basophil activation are central to CSU pathology, driving the histamine and inflammatory mediator release that produces wheals, angioedema, and itch. BTK sits upstream of that activation cascade. Nurix has demonstrated complete BTK degradation in the skin of healthy volunteers following systemic administration, providing direct evidence that the approach can achieve target degradation in peripheral tissues relevant to immune-mediated disease. Translating degraders into autoimmune disease Targeted protein degradation has accumulated its most compelling clinical evidence in oncology. Translating degrader programs into autoimmune disease raises a different set of challenges — and Nurix is direct about what those challenges are. "In cancer, the therapeutic goal is often to eliminate malignant cells or disable oncogenic signaling. In autoimmune disease, the objective is more nuanced: modulate pathogenic immune signaling while preserving normal immune function," Hansen noted. That distinction places a premium on selectivity, pharmacokinetics, and dose optimization in ways that oncology programs can sometimes accommodate more bluntly. For BTK degradation specifically, the desired therapeutic profile may differ substantially across indications. The degree and duration of BTK degradation needed to achieve benefit in CLL is not necessarily the same as what is required in MS or CSU — and in autoimmune settings, chronic administration introduces safety and tolerability considerations that acute oncology use cases can avoid. Hepatic safety has emerged as an important consideration in the development of BTK inhibitors for MS…

Longer follow-up will be needed to establish how durable these responses are, but the results suggest that immunotherapy could offer some patients a way to avoid the lasting effects of conventional treatment. – Bree Foster FDA launches neuroscience program, starting with Alzheimer’s prevention The FDA launched the Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus (NAIN), a program that will bring together experts from its drug, biologics, and device centers to coordinate how it regulates products for conditions of the brain and nervous system. The scope covers neurologic and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders, and pain. NAIN’s first initiative, the Alzheimer’s Prevention Accelerator, will explore how to run clinical trials aimed at preventing or delaying Alzheimer’s disease, with a focus on trial populations, stage-appropriate endpoints, and the kind of evidence needed to show that cognitive decline was delayed or prevented. The agency said the difficulty of demonstrating clinical benefit in conditions that develop over many years is a core challenge, and pointed to biomarkers and digital health tools as opportunities to address it. Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said the program will help regulatory science keep pace with advances in neuroscience, and the launch is tied to the federal government’s national Alzheimer’s plan. For developers, the accelerator signals that the agency may be open to new endpoint and evidence standards for prevention trials, though no specific policy changes have been announced. – Andrea Corona Download PDF Add Drug Discovery News as a preferred Google source to see more of our trusted coverage.
