Written byAndrea Corona Aug 12, 2026| 4 min read BTK degradation is proving relevant far beyond oncology — and the Nurix and Roche partnership on bexobrutideg shows just how far. istock.com/alexkich Download PDF Highlights in this article What degrading BTK actually means Why BTK matters beyond oncology Translating degraders into autoimmune disease Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors have transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies over the past decade. Ibrutinib's approval in 2013 validated BTK as a drug target, and a succession of second-generation inhibitors — acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib, pirtobrutinib — have extended that validation with improved selectivity and tolerability. More recently, BTK inhibition has moved into autoimmune disease: The FDA approved remibrutinib and rilzabrutinib in 2025 for chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) and immune thrombocytopenia, respectively, and multiple Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials in multiple sclerosis (MS) are underway. Against that backdrop, Nurix Therapeutics and Roche announced a global collaboration to co-develop and co-commercialize bexobrutideg, an oral BTK degrader, across B-cell malignancies, MS, and CSU. The deal includes a $700 million upfront payment to Nurix and up to $2.3 billion in potential total payments. The partnership's scope reflects something broader than a single drug program: It is a bet that degrading BTK, rather than inhibiting it, is meaningfully different — and that the difference matters clinically across a range of conditions where BTK biology is central. Gwenn Hansen, Chief Scientific Officer at Nurix, responded to DDN's questions on that distinction. Their answers trace the mechanistic logic from molecular biology through clinical translation. What degrading BTK actually means The fundamental difference between a BTK inhibitor and a BTK degrader is occupancy versus elimination. Inhibitors bind BTK and block its kinase activity while the protein remains present in the cell. Bexobrutideg recruits BTK to an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which marks the protein for destruction by the proteasome — removing BTK from the cell rather than simply occupying its active site. Continue reading below... Application NoteRevealing cell-cell interactions in immuno-oncology Imaging-enabled flow cytometry helps distinguish biologically relevant cell-cell interactions from coincident events to support immunotherapy research. Read More "Unlike a traditional inhibitor, which typically blocks a single target protein while it remains bound, a degrader acts catalytically," Hansen said. "One degrader molecule can trigger the degradation of thousands of BTK proteins over time because it is recycled to engage additional target proteins after each binding event." In preclinical systems, a single bexobrutideg molecule has been shown to drive the elimination of up to 10,000 BTK molecules per hour — a catalytic efficiency that no stoichiometric inhibitor can match. That catalytic mechanism has several practical implications. First, it means therapeutic effect can be achieved at substantially lower drug concentrations than inhibition-based approaches, because the degrader is not consumed in the process. Lower systemic exposure is a meaningful advantage for a drug intended for chronic administration across a range of patients. Second, and perhaps more importantly for the longer arc of the field, it means the protein's scaffolding function is disrupted alongside its kinase activity. BTK is not only an enzyme — it participates in signaling complexes independent of its catalytic role. "By removing BTK rather than simply blocking its active site, a degrader has the potential to suppress both kinase-dependent and kinase-independent BTK functions," Hansen said. The resistance question follows directly from that, asacquired mutations that alter BTK's kinase domain can limit the effectiveness of inhibitors by reducing drug binding. A degrader that eliminates the protein rather than occupying its active site is less susceptible to resistance mutations that emerge at the binding interface. Nurix has reported early clinical activity in CLL patients with acquired resistance mutations to current BTK inhibitors — a population where available therapeutic options are limited. To date, six BTK inhibitors have been approved by the FDA, with most approved drugs used in B-cell malignancies, leaving a significant gap in the treatment of patients who progress on those therapies. Bexobrutideg's clinical development program is designed in part to address that gap. Why BTK matters beyond oncology The rationale for moving into autoimmune disease begins with where BTK is expressed and what it does there. BTK, expressed in B cells and myeloid-derived cells including microglia, serves as a shared intracellular signaling node linking adaptive and innate immune pathways.That expression pattern is what makes BTK relevant across disease categories that appear clinically distinct. In MS, the biology is particularly compelling. Although high-efficacy disease-modifying therapies have been effective in suppressing relapses in MS patients, they fail to effectively target chronic microglial activation and smoldering lesions. Most existing therapies act on peripheral immune infiltration; they do not reach the compartmentalized inflammation behind the blood-brain barrier that drives progressive disability. A brain-penetrant BTK-directed therapy could modulate immune activity in both the periphery and the central nervous system simultaneously — targeting both the B-cell axis and the microglial axis of MS pathology. Continue reading below... ArticlesMiniaturizing patient-derived organoid screening for precision oncology By combining organoid biology with precision automation, researchers developed a miniaturized organoid screening platform that could help speed personalized cancer treatment testing. Read More "In multiple sclerosis, the biology is compelling because both B cells and central nervous system-resident myeloid cells, including microglia, are thought to contribute to inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease processes," Hansen said. Bexobrutideg has demonstrated CNS penetration and pharmacologically relevant concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid — a prerequisite for any agent intended to act on brain-resident immune cells. In CSU, the mechanism differs but the BTK rationale is similarly grounded. Mast cell and basophil activation are central to CSU pathology, driving the histamine and inflammatory mediator release that produces wheals, angioedema, and itch. BTK sits upstream of that activation cascade. Nurix has demonstrated complete BTK degradation in the skin of healthy volunteers following systemic administration, providing direct evidence that the approach can achieve target degradation in peripheral tissues relevant to immune-mediated disease. Translating degraders into autoimmune disease Targeted protein degradation has accumulated its most compelling clinical evidence in oncology. Translating degrader programs into autoimmune disease raises a different set of challenges — and Nurix is direct about what those challenges are. "In cancer, the therapeutic goal is often to eliminate malignant cells or disable oncogenic signaling. In autoimmune disease, the objective is more nuanced: modulate pathogenic immune signaling while preserving normal immune function," Hansen noted. That distinction places a premium on selectivity, pharmacokinetics, and dose optimization in ways that oncology programs can sometimes accommodate more bluntly. For BTK degradation specifically, the desired therapeutic profile may differ substantially across indications. The degree and duration of BTK degradation needed to achieve benefit in CLL is not necessarily the same as what is required in MS or CSU — and in autoimmune settings, chronic administration introduces safety and tolerability considerations that acute oncology use cases can avoid. analysis.time: The FDA approval was announced on October 23, 2026, with the publication date being October 29, 2026. The trials were conducted over 24 weeks.
analysis.location_and_population: The approval is relevant to patients with chronic hepatitis B globally, particularly those in the United States and other regions where the FDA regulates pharmaceuticals.
analysis.event: The FDA approved GSK's antisense oligonucleotide Hibsago (bepirovirsen) as a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B, based on results from two Phase 3 B-WELL trials.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The trials showed that 24 percent of patients who received Hibsago qualified to stop taking their antivirals entirely, with 19 percent achieving a functional cure after 24 weeks without antivirals. No specific death counts or exposure numbers were reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The approval is confirmed by the FDA. The trials demonstrated efficacy, and the treatment is now available for patients with chronic hepatitis B. No unresolved information was mentioned in the supplied evidence.

analysis.brief_en: The FDA has approved GSK's antisense oligonucleotide Hibsago (bepirovirsen) as a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B, based on results from two Phase 3 B-WELL trials. The trials showed that 24 percent of patients who received Hibsago qualified to stop taking their antivirals entirely, with 19 percent achieving a functional cure after 24 weeks without antivirals. This approval marks a significant advancement in treating chronic hepatitis B, offering patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after discontinuing medication. The treatment was developed through rigorous clinical trials and is now available for use in the United States and other regions where the FDA regulates pharmaceuticals. The approval also highlights the competitive landscape in hepatitis B therapy, with other companies like Brii Biosciences still in development. No specific death counts or exposure numbers were reported in the supplied evidence, but the findings are grounded in target-specific methods and results.

Send Close Hepatitis Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print OCTOBER 23, 2026 IDWeek 2026 Many Children Exposed to Hepatitis B at Home Are Unvaccinated, Study Finds By Brian Dunleavy More than 6% of newborns living in households with hepatitis B (HBV)-positive contacts are not vaccinated against the virus within seven days of birth, placing them at potential risk for infection, according to a study presented during IDWeek 2026, in Washington, D.C. (abstract 83). Source: Adobe. Although based on a subset of the population in northern California, this figure could represent a potential gap in national vaccine coverage, given planned revisions to current vaccination guidelines that emphasize maternal exposure, according to the authors. Related Content Starting HPV Vaccine at Age 9 or 10 Raises Series Completion by 13 Starting the HPV vaccine series younger substantially increased the share of children who began and finished the ... PIDS Chair Angela Campbell, MD, MPH, on IDWeek 2026 So Far Angela Campbell, MD, MPH, tells us about the best things she’s seen so far at the conference, and what she's ... RSV-B Lineage Emerges as Standout in Severe Pediatric Disease Young children infected with certain respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) subgroup B lineages experienced greater ... Historically, at least until recently, transmission of HBV to infants via non-maternal exposure in the United States has been relatively rare, due to high vaccination rates nationally. However, that could change if vaccination rates among infants born to uninfected mothers decline, the authors cautioned. “Infants can acquire [HBV] from their mother through perinatal infection, but young children can also become infected through close interpersonal contacts, such as between household members,” Karen B. Jacobson, MD, MPH, a research scientist with the Vaccine Study Center at the Kaiser Permanente Northern California Division of Research, told reporters during a press conference on Oct. 15. “Vaccination at birth substantially reduces risk of mother-to-child transmission around the time of delivery and also protects infants after birth from other sources of exposure.” Dr. Jacobson and her colleagues performed a retrospective cohort study of Kaiser Permanente Northern California members aged 5 years and younger as of June 16, 2023, who were linked through electronic medical records (EMR) to their birth mother and shared a household, defined by street address, with at least one other member of the health plan. They extracted laboratory results and vaccinations from the EMR through March 26, 2026, for children and through June 16, 2023, for their household contacts. The analysis included 158,169 children living in 131,800 households, 1,689 of which had a person with active HBV (or positive B antigen or DNA with no subsequent positive surface antibody). In all, 1.3% (n=2,024) of the children included in the study lived in a household with a person with active HBV. Of these, 846 (41.8%) were birth-exposed and 1,178 (58.2%) were household-exposed. Although all of the birth-exposed children were vaccinated against the virus within seven days of their birth, just 93.5% of those who HBV-positive household contacts received the shot. Of the unexposed children included in the analysis, only 86.7% were vaccinated against HBV, the research showed. “Vaccination coverage was very high overall, with 97% eventually receiving at least one vaccine dose,” Dr. Jacobson noted. However, while 95% of birth-exposed children were tested in the study population were tested for HBV at birth, only 3.6% of the household-exposed children were tested, revealing a “potential gap in care for children with a known household contact,” she added. It is unclear how many of the HBV-exposed children were ultimately infected. The researchers also noted that the 1.3% estimate of household-exposed children is likely an underestimate, as the researchers had no way of knowing whether households also included any non-members of Kaiser Permanente Northern California with HBV. The apparent discrepancy in vaccination and testing among children with household contacts is significant, given that, in 2025, the U.S. Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices revised its long-standing recommendation for universal HBV vaccination for newborns. Under the revised guidelines, which are still being finalized, vaccination is recommended only for infants born to mothers with known HBV or unknown HBV status. For all other children 2 months of age and younger, vaccination is essentially optional, with the decision left up to parents in consultation with their pediatricians. The new recommendation “does not take into account the risk for potential for exposure from non-maternal contacts,” Dr. Jacobson noted. Many public health experts are concerned that, under the new guidance, some children will fall through the cracks and not be vaccinated against HBV. “Even if it is possible to accurately identify every single maternal exposure, this would not account for potential exposure to an infected father, grandparent, or other person living in the house,” she said. “Our study highlights the importance of being very comprehensive about how we identify exposures and not focusing only on that perinatal period.” The sources reported no relevant financial disclosures. Although based on a subset of the population in northern California, this figure could represent a potential gap in national vaccine coverage, given planned revisions to current vaccination guidelines that emphasize maternal exposure, according to the authors. Historically, at least until recently, transmission of HBV to infants via non-maternal exposure in the United States has been relatively rare, due to high vaccination rates nationally. However, that could change if vaccination rates among infants born to uninfected mothers decline, the authors cautioned. “Infants can acquire [HBV] from their mother through perinatal infection, but young children can also become infected through close interpersonal contacts, such as between household members,” Karen B. Jacobson, MD, MPH, a research scientist with the Vaccine Study Center at the Kaiser Permanente Northern California Division of Research, told reporters during a press conference on Oct. 15. “Vaccination at birth substantially reduces risk of mother-to-child transmission around the time of delivery and also protects infants after birth from other sources of exposure.” Dr. Jacobson and her colleagues performed a retrospective cohort study of Kaiser Permanente Northern California members aged 5 years and younger as of June 16, 2023, who were linked through electronic medical records (EMR) to their birth mother and shared a household, defined by street address, with at least one other member of the health plan. They extracted laboratory results and vaccinations from the EMR through March 26, 2026, for children and through June 16, 2023, for their household contacts. The analysis included 158,169 children living in 131,800 households, 1,689 of which had a person with active HBV (or positive B antigen or DNA with no subsequent positive surface antibody). In all, 1.3% (n=2,024) of the children included in the study lived in a household with a person with active HBV. Of these, 846 (41.8%) were birth-exposed and 1,178 (58.2%) were household-exposed. Although all of the birth-exposed children were vaccinated against the virus within seven days of their birth, just 93.5% of those who HBV-positive household contacts received the shot. Of the unexposed children included in the analysis, only 86.7% were vaccinated against HBV, the research showed. “Vaccination coverage was very high overall, with 97% eventually receiving at least one vaccine dose,” Dr. Jacobson noted. However, while 95% of birth-exposed children were tested in the study population were tested for HBV at birth, only 3.6% of the household-exposed children were tested, revealing a “potential gap in care for children with a known household contact,” she added. It is unclear how many of the HBV-exposed children were ultimately infected. The researchers also noted that the 1.3% estimate of household-exposed children is likely an underestimate, as the researchers had no way of knowing whether households also included any non-members of Kaiser Permanente Northern California with HBV. The apparent discrepancy in vaccination and testing among children with household contacts is significant, given that, in 2025, the U.S. Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices revised its long-standing recommendation for universal HBV vaccination for newborns. Under the revised guidelines, which are still being finalized, vaccination is recommended only for infants born to mothers with known HBV or unknown HBV status. For all other children 2 months of age and younger, vaccination is essentially optional, with the decision left up to parents in consultation with their pediatricians. The new recommendation “does not take into account the risk for potential for exposure from non-maternal contacts,” Dr. Jacobson noted. Many public health experts are concerned that, under the new guidance, some children will fall through the cracks and not be vaccinated against HBV. “Even if it is possible to accurately identify every single maternal exposure, this would not account for potential exposure to an infected father, grandparent, or other person living in the house,” she said. “Our study highlights the importance of being very comprehensive about how we identify exposures and not focusing only on that perinatal period.” The sources reported no relevant financial disclosures. news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 23 日在华盛顿特区举行的 IDWeek 2026 上发表的一项研究发现,有乙型肝炎 (HBV) 阳性接触者的家庭中超过 6% 的新生儿在出生后 7 天内未接种疫苗,使他们面临潜在的感染风险。这项研究由北加州 Kaiser Permanente 的 Karen B. Jacobson 博士和她的同事进行,分析了居住在 131,800 个家庭中的 158,169 名 5 岁及以下儿童。其中,1.3%(n=2,024)通过家庭接触接触过乙肝病毒,只有 3.6% 的人接受了病毒检测。该研究强调了对家庭成员中有乙肝病毒暴露儿童的护理存在潜在差距,因为仍在最终确定的美国新 疫苗接种 指南规定,非乙肝病毒阳性母亲所生的婴儿可以选择接受乙肝病毒 疫苗接种 治疗。研究人员警告说,这可能会导致一些儿童被忽视,无法获得针对乙肝病毒的必要保护,尤其是来自父亲或祖父母等非母源的保护。

The event is centered on the U.S. and involves the human hepatitis B virus, specifically chronic hepatitis B. analysis.brief_en: The article 'Do the New Hepatitis B Birth Dose Guidelines Miss Horizontal Transmission?' published on Contagion Live on October 25, 2026, discusses concerns about the new Hepatitis B birth dose guidelines potentially overlooking horizontal transmission. The piece highlights the importance of addressing this transmission route, especially in young children, as household contacts are identified as a significant source of Hepatitis B exposure. While the guidelines focus on vertical transmission, the article questions whether they adequately account for horizontal spread. The piece does not provide confirmed cases or specific data on the impact of this oversight but raises the issue for further investigation. The analysis suggests that the topic is under review, and the findings are not yet definitive. This discussion is part of broader conversations about vaccine strategies and their effectiveness in preventing Hepatitis B in different transmission contexts.

news.content_zh: 文章“新乙型肝炎出生剂量指南是否未达到水平 传播?”于 2026 年 10 月 25 日在 Contagion Live 上发表,讨论了对新乙型肝炎出生剂量指南可能忽视水平 传播 的担忧。这篇文章强调了解决这一 传播 途径的重要性,特别是对于幼儿,因为家庭接触者被认为是乙型肝炎暴露的重要来源。虽然指南重点关注垂直 传播,但本文质疑它们是否充分考虑了水平传播。这篇文章没有提供有关这一疏忽影响的确诊病例或具体数据,但提出了需要进一步调查的问题。分析表明该主题正在接受审查,调查结果尚未确定。本讨论是有关 疫苗 策略及其在不同 传播 背景下预防乙型肝炎的有效性的更广泛对话的一部分。

The FDA’s recent approval of bepirovirsen (Hibsago; GSK), the first antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, marks a step beyond lifelong viral suppression toward functional cure.1 Reaching a functional cure matters because current therapy, although very effective, must be taken for a long time and, for many people, for life, Jordan Feld, MD, MPH, professor of medicine at the University of Toronto and section head of hepatology at University Health Network, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® at IDWeek 2026, held October 21-24 in Washington, DC. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up Functional cure lowers the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer, even compared with long-term suppressive therapy, and lets patients come off all of their therapy, Feld said. Patients also lose the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) marker in their blood, which many find stigmatizing. “In some countries, it can actually lead to people losing their jobs or having problems in their family,” he said. “So being surface antigen negative, which is really the definition of a functional cure, for many people is sort of giving them their freedom back to be living free of hep B instead of living with hep B with it controlled.” Because some people clear HBV on their own, the search for a cure has focused on therapies that stimulate the immune system, Feld explained. Even antisense oligonucleotides, which directly target viral replication, appear to have an immunostimulatory effect that “might be the more important mechanism that’s driving functional cure,” he said. To prepare, Feld said clinicians, patients, and payers should keep 2 points in mind. Patients will need to be restratified using quantitative HBsAg, which has not historically been measured routinely, and broader use of suppressive nucleos(t)ide analogue (NUC) therapy will be important, because most novel treatments are being studied in patients already on NUCs. “Are you a good candidate for these new treatments, yes or no? And if you are, are you on a NUC? And if the answer is no, then we need to get you on a NUC first, suppress viral replication, and now you’re ready for that new therapy,” Feld said. Bepirovirsen’s label also requires intensive monitoring, including platelet counts and renal function, and clinics will need the capacity “to be able to safely deliver these therapies,” he said. References 1. McCormick B. Bepirovirsen approval offers new option for chronic HBV treatment. AJMC. October 21, 2026. The FDA recently approved bepirovirsen (Hibsago; GSK), the first antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B.1 Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up The approval made waves at IDWeek 2026, held October 21 to 24, 2026, in Washington, DC. Bepirovirsen is administered by subcutaneous injection and is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have taken hepatitis B virus (HBV) antiviral therapy for at least 6 months, have suppressed HBV levels in their blood, and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less.1 In the 2 trials supporting the approval, 19% of patients who received bepirovirsen still had undetectable HBsAg 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment.1 It is the first therapy approved with a primary endpoint of functional cure in the hepatitis B space, and a significant proportion of patients achieved a functional cure after 6 months of treatment, something that hasn't been seen with previous therapy, Jordan Feld, MD, MPH, professor of medicine at the University of Toronto and section head of hepatology at University Health Network, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care®. “This is a very exciting time to be able to have this option available. But the whole field is exciting because it's not just antisense oligonucleotides like bepirovirsen that look promising. There's a whole host of therapies,” he said. More advanced capsid assembly modulators, which inhibit replication, are also in development. These investigational therapies are expected to be more potent than nucleoside or nucleotide analogues, or “nukes,” as Feld referred to them, and are taken as oral once-daily tablets. Other therapies directly target covalently closed circular DNA, the reservoir of hepatitis B in the liver. “By targeting that directly, that's taking away the source of hep[atitis] B,” he explained. “And there are a few therapies now with gene editing or gene silencing that look really exciting. Still early days, but the idea of those therapies is that you could actually get to a true cure.” References 1. FDA approves first-of-its-kind chronic hepatitis B treatment. FDA. October 20, 2026. The FDA recently approved bepirovirsen (Hibsago; GSK), the first antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B.1 Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up The approval made waves at IDWeek 2026, held October 21 to 24, 2026, in Washington, DC. Bepirovirsen is administered by subcutaneous injection and is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have taken hepatitis B virus (HBV) antiviral therapy for at least 6 months, have suppressed HBV levels in their blood, and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less.1 In the 2 trials supporting the approval, 19% of patients who received bepirovirsen still had undetectable HBsAg 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment.1 It is the first therapy approved with a primary endpoint of functional cure in the hepatitis B space, and a significant proportion of patients achieved a functional cure after 6 months of treatment, something that hasn't been seen with previous therapy, Jordan Feld, MD, MPH, professor of medicine at the University of Toronto and section head of hepatology at University Health Network, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care®. “This is a very exciting time to be able to have this option available. But the whole field is exciting because it's not just antisense oligonucleotides like bepirovirsen that look promising. There's a whole host of therapies,” he said. More advanced capsid assembly modulators, which inhibit replication, are also in development. These investigational therapies are expected to be more potent than nucleoside or nucleotide analogues, or “nukes,” as Feld referred to them, and are taken as oral once-daily tablets. Other therapies directly target covalently closed circular DNA, the reservoir of hepatitis B in the liver. “By targeting that directly, that's taking away the source of hep[atitis] B,” he explained. “And there are a few therapies now with gene editing or gene silencing that look really exciting. Still early days, but the idea of those therapies is that you could actually get to a true cure.” References 1. FDA approves first-of-its-kind chronic hepatitis B treatment. FDA. October 20, 2026. news.content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Coalition of 16 Attorneys General Widens Lawsuit Over CDC’s Hepatitis B Change as a Model Projects a Sharp Rise in Childhood Infections By Avery Porter Published: Oct 29 2026, 12:26 PM EDT Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail ADEK BERRY | AFP via Getty Images The legal fight over the federal government's decision to drop a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose at birth is widening. Vermont joined a multistate lawsuit this month, bringing the coalition to 16 state attorneys general plus Pennsylvania's governor, after the states filed an amended complaint on Oct. 2, according to the Vermont attorney general's office. The case arrives alongside new evidence. A study published Oct. 19 in Annals of Internal Medicine projected that moving the first dose from birth to a family decision could raise chronic hepatitis B infections in children by 83% by age 20, according to a release from the American College of Physicians. Under that scenario, more than half of children could enter adulthood without protection. For parents of newborns, the practical question is simpler than the legal one. Because a federal court has paused the change, the CDC's website still says all infants should receive the hepatitis B vaccine, ABC News reported. The American Academy of Pediatrics continues to recommend a first dose within 24 hours of birth. Two Court Fights, One Policy In December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices voted to end the universal birth-dose recommendation in place since 1991. The CDC then adopted shared clinical decision-making for babies whose mothers test negative, meaning parents and providers decide together whether to give the dose at birth or start no earlier than 2 months, according to the Department of Health and Human Services. A January 2026 CDC memo went further, removing the universal recommendation for seven childhood vaccines, including hepatitis B. The states argue in federal court in Northern California that these changes violate the Administrative Procedure Act and that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s replacement of all 17 voting committee members in June 2025 was unlawful. Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark said the changes "run afoul of decades of scientific evidence." A separate case brought by the American Academy of Pediatrics produced the ruling now in effect. On March 16, U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy in Massachusetts stayed the January memo, the new committee appointments and the committee's votes, including the hepatitis B decision. The Justice Department appealed on April 29, STAT reported, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit heard arguments on Oct. 6. As of Oct. 29, no appellate ruling had been reported. The Administration's Case for Choice HHS has defended the change as a matter of informed consent for low-risk families. Babies born to mothers who test positive or whose status is unknown are still recommended to receive the birth dose with immunoglobulin. When the policy was adopted, then-acting CDC Director Jim O'Neill said those newborns whose mothers test negative "face little risk of contracting hepatitis B." Asked about the new study, HHS pointed ABC News to a post by Kennedy. "I reject the idea that respecting parents' choices means abandoning children's health," he wrote. HHS has also said insurance coverage for the vaccine remains in place across federal programs, including Vaccines for Children and Medicaid. What the Model Projects Researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School followed a simulated birth cohort of 3.6 million U.S. infants through age 20. They compared three approaches for babies of mothers who test negative: a universal birth dose, a first dose delayed to 2 months, and shared decision-making for that first dose. Delaying the first dose raised projected chronic infections by 19%, while shared decision-making raised them by 83%. The number of children still vulnerable to infection at age 20 rose from about 232,000 under the universal birth dose to about 1.8 million under shared decision-making, according to ABC News. If high-risk babies were also vaccinated less reliably, infections passed from mother to child could double or triple. Corresponding author Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious-disease physician at Mass General Brigham, said the team aimed to add evidence to a debate already playing out in courts and professional societies. He called for restoring the universal birth-dose recommendation. Limits of a Projection The study is a peer-reviewed computer model, not a count of real infections. Its results depend on assumptions about vaccine uptake, maternal screening, exposure in households and missed follow-up doses, and the release did not report absolute numbers of new chronic infections. It also modeled a single year of births, so the authors' warning that effects would add up over many years is an extrapolation. What is not in dispute is the stakes of infection — and how early they begin. Most babies infected at birth or in infancy develop lifelong chronic hepatitis B, which has no cure and raises the risk of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer decades later. The vaccine is up to 90% effective at preventing mother-to-child infection when given within 24 hours of birth, the Vermont Attorney General's Office noted. For expectant parents, the most useful step now is to ask about prenatal hepatitis B testing and discuss the birth dose with their obstetrician or pediatrician before delivery. Families who skipped the birth dose can ask their pediatrician about starting the series. The hepatitis B vaccine remains covered for children through Vaccines for Children and most insurance plans. The First Circuit ruling is the next major event, and it will decide whether the March stay remains in place while the cases continue. The bottom line is that the universal birth dose is still the recommendation in effect today — but its future depends on appeals judges, and new modeling suggests the policy choice could shape liver health for millions of children decades from now. The legal and policy changes were made in 2025, with the January 2026 CDC memo removing the universal recommendation for seven childhood vaccines, including hepatitis B. The states argue that these changes could lead to a significant increase in the risk of lifelong chronic hepatitis B, which raises the risk of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer decades later. The CDC's decision has been paused by a federal court, and the Justice Department has appealed the ruling. The hepatitis B vaccine remains covered for children through Vaccines for Children and most insurance plans.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hepatitis B found in nearly one in five suspected hepatitis patients in Northwest Ethiopia by October 28, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Hepatitis B found in nearly one in five suspected hepatitis patients in Northwest Ethiopia Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Eighteen percent of patients who came to a large referral hospital in Bahir Dar, Northwest Ethiopia, with symptoms suggesting viral hepatitis tested positive for hepatitis B surface antigen, according to a cross-sectional study conducted at Felege Hiwot Comprehensive Specialized Hospital between October and December 2025. The figure, 36 positive results among 204 participants, carries a 95 percent confidence interval of 12.4 to 22.9 percent, and places the tested group in what the World Health Organization would classify as a high-endemicity setting, where surface antigen prevalence exceeds 8 percent. The study, published in the Springer Nature journal Discover Viruses, enrolled adults who presented to the hospital’s outpatient department with at least one clinical feature suggestive of viral hepatitis, such as jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, right upper quadrant pain, or hepatomegaly. All 204 eligible participants consented and completed the study, with no exclusions after enrollment. Because the investigators used consecutive sampling, every clinically suspected patient who arrived during the study window was recruited until the required sample size was met, a design the authors acknowledge may introduce selection bias and limit how far the findings generalize beyond this single referral center. Laboratory testing relied on the SNIBE Maglumi chemiluminescence immunoassay analyzer, which captures hepatitis B surface antigen from serum using magnetic microbeads coated with specific antibodies. After unbound components are removed by magnetic separation, an enzyme-labeled detection antibody is added, and the instrument measures light emitted when the enzyme reacts with a chemiluminescent substrate. The signal is proportional to the antigen concentration in the sample. Results were classified as positive when a cutoff index reached 1.0 or above, and borderline or equivocal readings flagged by the instrument were retested, with repeatedly reactive samples counted as positive. Daily internal and external quality controls were run, reagents were checked for expiration and storage conditions, and the analyzer was calibrated regularly. Discover more Check Symptoms Book Care Services Read Med Journals Compare Clinics Donate to Research Sample size was calculated in advance using a single population proportion formula, assuming a 95 percent confidence level, a 5 percent margin of error, and an expected prevalence of 14 percent drawn from a 2024 study at Guhalla Primary Hospital in Northwest Ethiopia. The initial calculation of 185 participants was inflated by 10 percent for anticipated non-response, yielding a final target of 204. Data collectors administered a structured questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, behaviors such as alcohol use and sharing of sharp instruments, and medical exposures including blood transfusion, surgery, dental procedures, tattooing, and vaccination status. Venous blood samples of 3 to 5 milliliters were drawn aseptically with single-use needles and tubes. The participant group was evenly split by sex, with 101 men and 103 women. Nearly half, 98 people or 48 percent, were aged 25 to 34 years, while 58 participants, 28 percent, were 35 or older and 48, or 24 percent, were under 25. Clinically, 40 percent reported jaundice, 45 percent reported dark urine or pale stools, 48 percent reported fatigue or weakness, 43 percent reported right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and 32 percent reported nausea or vomiting. Behaviorally, 62 percent reported alcohol consumption within the past year, 45 percent reported sharing sharp materials such as razors, blades, or nail clippers, and 59 percent reported a previous sexually transmitted infection diagnosis or treatment. In bivariable analysis, three factors stood out. Participants aged over 35 had roughly three times the odds of surface antigen positivity compared with those under 25, with a crude odds ratio of 3.15 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.14 to 8.74. Jaundice showed the strongest crude association, with an odds ratio of 5.2 and a confidence interval of 2.34 to 11.54. Sharing sharp materials doubled the odds, with a crude odds ratio of 2.2 and a confidence interval of 1.05 to 4.60. After adjustment in a multivariable logistic regression model, four factors remained independently associated with positivity. Age of 35 years or older carried an adjusted odds ratio of 2.85, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.08 to 7.55 and a p value of 0.035, meaning these participants were roughly 2.9 times more likely to test positive than the youngest age group. Those aged 25 to 34 did not differ significantly from the reference group, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.90. Alcohol consumption was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.52, a confidence interval of 1.13 to 5.63, and a p value of 0.037. A self-reported history of blood transfusion was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.45, a confidence interval of 1.04 to 2.94, and a p value of 0.040, while sharing sharp materials yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 1.72, a confidence interval of 1.01 to 2.93, and a p value of 0.046. Discover more Explore Data Study Biology Get Health Tips Health health The authors are explicit that these associations should not be read as causal. The cross-sectional design cannot establish whether the measured exposures preceded infection, and with only 36 positive outcomes relative to the number of candidate predictors, the risk of model overfitting, unstable coefficients, and inflated effect estimates cannot be excluded. The transfusion finding in particular is treated cautiously: the study did not record when transfusions occurred, how many units were given, or how donor blood was screened, so the association cannot demonstrate that hepatitis B was acquired through transfusion. Alcohol consumption may likewise serve as a marker for unmeasured behavioral or socioeconomic factors, and residual confounding remains possible. Model diagnostics were nonetheless reassuring within their limits. Variance inflation factors peaked at 2.34 and tolerance values ranged from 0.43 to 0.89, indicating no substantial multicollinearity. The Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test produced a chi-square statistic of 8.14 with 8 degrees of freedom and a p value of 0.42, consistent with adequate calibration. No observation showed excessive influence, with Cook’s distance values below 1.0. The final model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.78, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.71 to 0.85, correctly classifying 75.0 percent of participants at the selected threshold, with 69.4 percent sensitivity and 76.2 percent specificity. A sensitivity analysis treating age as a continuous variable was reported in supplementary material. The 18 percent prevalence sits within a broader landscape of hepatitis B burden in the region. It is comparable to the 14 percent reported among clinically suspected patients at Guhalla Primary Hospital, to a 21.2 percent figure from Northern Uganda, and to a 17.6 percent estimate from Ethiopia, but lower than rates of 22.3 percent among chronic hepatitis patients and 28 percent among patients with chronic liver disease in prior studies. It is higher than community-based estimates, including 5.4 percent in a general Ethiopian sample and 9.0 percent among adults in another study, a gap the authors attribute partly to the symptomatic, hospital-recruited population studied here. Globally, an estimated 254 million people were living with chronic hepatitis B surface antigen positivity in 2022, with about 1.2 million new infections and roughly 1.1 million deaths. In Ethiopia, where surface antigen prevalence ranges from 6 to 12 percent and the infant hepatitis B vaccine was added to the routine immunization schedule in 2007, the authors call for strengthened screening, vaccination coverage, blood safety, and infection-prevention measures, and note that longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal and causal relationships suggested by their cross-sectional findings. (2026). Prevalence and factors associated with HBsAg positivity among clinically suspected viral hepatitis patients in Northwest Ethiopia. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hepatitis B prevalence reaches 41.9% in Ethiopian chronic liver disease patients by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Hepatitis B prevalence reaches 41.9% in Ethiopian chronic liver disease patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A facility-based cross-sectional study found hepatitis B virus infection in 41.9% of patients with chronic liver disease treated at three public referral hospitals in Bahir Dar, Northwest Ethiopia. Researchers assessed 320 patients from October 2023 through January 2024, combining structured questionnaires, physical examinations and medical-chart reviews. HBsAg positivity, indicating the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen, was identified in 134 participants, giving a prevalence of 41.9% with a 95% confidence interval of 36.5% to 47.5%. The hospital-based design establishes the burden among people already receiving care for chronic liver disease, but it does not show whether hepatitis B caused their underlying liver disease or how common infection is in the wider regional population. The study focused on patients with established chronic liver disease, a group described in the research as vulnerable to acute or superimposed hepatitis B infection. The authors noted that such infections can trigger rapid hepatic decompensation, accelerate progression toward cirrhosis and increase the lifetime risk of neoplastic transformation. Its primary result was the prevalence of HBsAg positivity and the statistical associations between this status and reported or recorded characteristics. Multivariable binary logistic regression identified several characteristics associated with positive HBsAg status. HIV-positive participants had three times the adjusted odds of positivity compared with HIV-negative patients, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.00 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.40 to 6.80. Discover more Study Biology Find Treatments Read Med Journals Soothe Digestion Check Symptoms A family history of liver disease was associated with 4.70 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.90 to 11.00, while a history of dental procedures was associated with 4.50 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.00 to 10.00. Contact with a person who had jaundice was also associated with higher odds of positivity, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.40 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 4.80. These are associations in the sampled population, not evidence that any listed exposure transmitted the virus. Because hepatitis B prevalence was high in the study population, the investigators also applied a modified Poisson regression model with robust variance to complement the odds-ratio estimates with adjusted prevalence ratios. In that model, HIV-positive status was associated with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.68, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 2.35. Family history of liver disease was associated with a ratio of 1.76, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.29 to 2.40. Contact with a jaundiced person had an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.48, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.14 to 1.92, and a history of dental procedures had a ratio of 1.62, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.21 to 2.17. The logistic and modified Poisson analyses pointed in the same direction for these four predictors. Post-hoc power calculations indicated greater than 85% statistical power for the primary multivariable predictors. That calculation was performed after model fitting and does not eliminate uncertainties associated with the sample size, model specification, confounding or the cross-sectional design. In particular, the study cannot establish the timing or route of infection, determine whether identified characteristics preceded HBsAg positivity, or measure changes in prevalence over time. The referral-hospital setting also limits generalization: the participants were patients attending selected public facilities in Bahir Dar, rather than a population-based sample representing all people with chronic liver disease in Northwest Ethiopia. Discover more View Census Data Get Health Tips Book Care Services infection infections Within those limits, the 41.9% estimate documents a substantial hepatitis B burden among the chronically ill patients attending the three hospitals during the study period. The hospital sample included patients with chronic liver disease, so the result should not be presented as a regional prevalence estimate for the general population. Nor does the cross-sectional analysis demonstrate that HIV, family history, dental procedures or contact with a jaundiced person caused infection. The adjusted estimates identify groups with higher observed prevalence in this clinical setting, while their confidence intervals show the degree of precision around each association. The authors proposed that the results may inform regional planning for hepatitis B screening within liver clinics, evaluation of targeted adult vaccination strategies and stronger use of standard infection-control measures in health facilities. The immediate research contribution is instead a cross-sectional measurement of HBsAg prevalence and its reported correlates among 320 chronic liver disease patients in a defined Ethiopian hospital network. For interpreting the results, the study type and population are central. It was a facility-based, cross-sectional assessment conducted from October 2023 to January 2024, not a longitudinal study or a clinical trial. Its strongest supported conclusion is that hepatitis B infection was common among the sampled chronic liver disease patients, with HIV positivity, family history of liver disease, dental-procedure history and contact with a jaundiced person each associated with higher adjusted prevalence or odds of HBsAg positivity. Healthy Living Hepatitis B Model Projects 83% More Chronic Childhood Infections if Newborn Birth Dose Becomes a Family Choice Published Oct 24, 2026 10:34 PM EDT By Elena Vega JEAN-SEBASTIEN EVRARD | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on WhatsApp Chronic hepatitis B infections among U.S. children could rise 83% over 20 years if the newborn vaccine dose shifts from a routine shot to a decision parents make with their doctor, according to a computer model published in Annals of Internal Medicine. The figure is a projection based on stated assumptions, not a count of actual infections. Researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School built the model. The team followed a hypothetical group of 3.6 million babies born in the U.S. in 2026 through age 20, ABC News reported. Delaying the first dose until 2 months raised projected chronic infections by 19%. A shared decision-making approach raised them by 83% and left about 1.8 million young adults unprotected at age 20, compared with about 474,000 under a delayed dose and about 232,000 under a universal birth dose. For families expecting a baby, the finding lands on a real decision. Federal advice on the birth dose has shifted over the past year, and the guidance parents hear may depend on which hospital, pediatrician, or website they consult. Model Projections and Their Limits The study, described in a journal news release, used a Markov state transition model, a standard tool that moves simulated people through health states over time. It compared three approaches for babies whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B during pregnancy: a universal birth dose, a first dose at 2 months, and shared clinical decision-making. Results depend heavily on how many families end up vaccinating. In a scenario in which only about 26% of infants were vaccinated at 2 months, chronic cases rose 225%, TIME reported. The model also projected that perinatal infections could double or triple if babies of mothers who test positive, or whose status is unknown, became less likely to get the vaccine. The study does not prove that infections will rise by these amounts. It modeled a single year of births and relied on assumptions about vaccine uptake and infection rates. The researchers stressed that the numbers are simulation estimates, and real-world vaccination and infection data will be the true test. Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious disease researcher at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital and an author of the study, told TIME that the team "wanted to add some evidence to the conversation" about the possible impact of the changes. Two other recent modeling studies examined the issue. One found that delaying the first dose by 2 months would add about $16.4 million in health care spending on new infections, even if every child eventually received the vaccine. Vaccination Data Already Show a Decline Vaccination data suggest the shift is not only theoretical. U.S. newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates fell from 83.5% to 73.2% between 2023 and 2025, according to an electronic health record analysis of 12 million infants. That decline began before the federal change took effect. Infancy is when the virus does the most lasting damage. About 90% of babies infected around the time of birth develop chronic hepatitis B, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. Untreated infection early in life carries a lifetime liver cancer risk of about 1 in 4, TIME reported, and many people do not learn they are infected until liver damage appears years later. Families Weighing the Newborn Shot In December 2025, the CDC dropped its universal birth-dose recommendation for babies of mothers who test negative and adopted shared clinical decision-making instead. In March, a federal judge in Massachusetts stayed the votes of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee, including the one behind that change, and the CDC website now states that all infants should receive the hepatitis B vaccine, ABC reported. The American Academy of Pediatrics continues to recommend a first dose within 24 hours of birth. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said his department puts informed consent, individual medical circumstances, and conversations between parents and doctors at the center of health decisions. Physicians worry that softer language changes behavior. Stanford pediatrician Dr. Alok Patel told ABC News, "When a recommendation shifts from 'every baby' to 'Let's discuss it,' a lot of families hear 'optional' or 'Maybe it was never that important.'" Babies born to mothers who test positive, or whose status is unknown, face the highest risk and should still get the vaccine within 12 hours of birth, according to the CDC fact sheet. But a negative maternal test does not eliminate risk, since babies can be exposed through infected caregivers or household members who may not know their status. Physicians also warn that delaying the first dose can make it harder for some children to complete the full vaccine series. Expectant parents can ask the hospital before delivery whether it offers the birth dose, confirm the result of the prenatal hepatitis B test, and keep a record of every dose. The vaccine is available through the Vaccines for Children program for eligible uninsured and underinsured children. Many infected infants show no symptoms, but yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or poor feeding should prompt a call to a pediatrician. Lawsuits over the vaccine schedule are ongoing, including one filed by 15 states. Court rulings, future advisory committee meetings, and new vaccination data will show whether the model's warnings are playing out. Read more The FDA Approves the First-Ever Hepatitis Delta Treatment: Here's Why Hepatitis B Patients Should Get Tested If You Have Chronic Hepatitis B, a New FDA Approval Means You Should Ask About This Dangerous Co-Infection Hepatitis Delta Is the Deadliest Form of Viral Hepatitis — and the U.S. Just Got Its First Treatment for It Key Questions Answered What did the new study find? A computer model projected that chronic hepatitis B infections in U.S. children could rise 83% over 20 years under shared decision-making, and 19% if the first dose were delayed to 2 months. Are these real infections? No. The figures are projections from a simulation of 3.6 million babies, not measured cases. What is the current federal recommendation? The CDC dropped the universal birth dose in December 2025, but a federal judge stayed the related advisory committee votes in March, and the CDC website now says all infants should receive the vaccine. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a first dose within 24 hours of birth. Why is infection in infancy so serious? About 90% of babies infected around birth develop chronic hepatitis B, which can lead to liver damage and liver cancer years later. Which babies face the greatest risk? Babies of mothers who test positive or have unknown status, as well as babies exposed to infected caregivers or household members. Is the vaccine available for families who cannot afford it? Yes. It is available through the Vaccines for Children program for eligible uninsured and underinsured children. supplementary_news.content_title: 500 babies received ‘improperly stored' hepatitis B vaccines at Albany Med
supplementary_news.content: ALBANY - An estimated 500 newborns received doses of the hepatitis B vaccine that had been improperly stored at Albany Medical Center in recent weeks, state and hospital officials said. State Department of Health workers discovered the error while reviewing refrigeration logs in preparation for a site visit to the hospital, agency spokesperson Marissa Crary told the Times Union on Thursday. The logs showed the doses had been stored below the manufacturer's recommended temperature range and may not have fully protected the babies who received them, Crary added. The improperly stored doses do not pose a health threat to the babies who received them, but their effectiveness may have been compromised. The concern is that the infants may not have developed the intended protection against hepatitis B, making repeat vaccinations necessary to ensure they are fully protected. Newborns typically receive their first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth, often before leaving the hospital. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends they receive a second dose within two months. Albany Medical Center sent a letter to affected parents and doctors informing them "that a repeat dose may be needed to ensure children remain fully protected," a hospital spokesperson said. It was unclear Thursday how many parents had brought their children back for a repeat vaccination. "We apologize for this situation and have implemented additional safeguards to help prevent it from happening again," the spokesperson said. State health officials will continue to oversee the hospital's "corrective actions," Crary said. The hospital is required to submit documentation showing it has remedied its vaccine tracking and temperature monitoring system. A Hepatitis B virus infection can cause serious liver conditions. School-aged children are required to receive three doses of the preventive vaccine. About 90% of New York children complete the three-dose series before the age of 3, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation. "New York state maintains vigilant programmatic oversight to protect patients and ensure hospitals provide safe, quality care," Crary said. There's more to Albany with the Times Union. Hepatitis Cases Author(s)Skylar Jeremias Fact checked by: Ashley Gallagher, MA https://doi.org/10.1111/jgh.70533 Key Takeaways About half of patients with chronic hepatitis B or C also had MASLD, which tracked with worse fatigue and quality of life. HBV patients with MASLD had more advanced fibrosis; HCV patients with MASLD were younger and more often female. MASLD independently predicted worse quality-of-life scores, a case for metabolic screening alongside antiviral care. SHOW MORE Nearly half of patients with chronic HBV or HCV also had MASLD, tied to worse fatigue and quality of life. Advertisement Roughly half of patients with chronic hepatitis B or C also have metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and those carrying both diagnoses reported significantly worse fatigue, systemic symptoms, and quality of life than patients with viral hepatitis alone, according to a cross-sectional analysis of the Global Liver Registry published in the Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology.1 MASLD Adds to a Persistent Global Hepatitis Burden Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remain among the world's most common liver diseases. An estimated 287 million people were living with chronic HBV or HCV infection in 2024, and the 2 viruses together caused roughly 1.3 million deaths that year, according to the World Health Organization's most recent global hepatitis report. Fewer than 5% of the 240 million people living with chronic HBV were receiving treatment.2 MASLD, driven by obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other cardiometabolic risk factors, has grown more common worldwide and increasingly coexists with viral hepatitis in the same patient. How that overlap affects day-to-day symptoms and quality of life, rather than liver histology alone, had not been systematically examined across a large, multinational cohort. A Global Registry Compares MASLD in Chronic Hepatitis The researchers analyzed cross-sectional clinical and patient-reported outcome (PRO) data from the Global Liver Registry, an international database of patients with chronic liver disease. MASLD was defined as a Hepatic Steatosis Index of 36 or higher plus at least 1 cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia). PROs were captured with the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) scale, the Chronic Liver Disease Questionnaire (CLDQ), and the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire. The analysis included 4649 patients: 2063 with HBV (mean age, 48 years; 57% male; 11% with advanced fibrosis) and 2586 with HCV (mean age, 56 years; 47% male; 18% with advanced fibrosis). MASLD was present in 49% of the HBV group and 47% of the HCV group, underscoring how common the metabolic-viral overlap had become in this population. MASLD Worsens Fibrosis and Fatigue in HBV Patients with HBV and MASLD were similar in age, sex, and nonmetabolic comorbidities to those with HBV alone (all P > .05), but they had significantly more advanced fibrosis (P < .01). They also scored significantly lower on the FACIT-F Physical Well-Being and Fatigue domains and on every CLDQ domain (all P < .01), with the largest gap in the Fatigue domain, a 6% reduction across the scale's full range. That pattern suggests MASLD adds a distinct symptom burden on top of HBV itself, rather than simply reflecting older or sicker patients accumulating a second diagnosis. Because the Global Liver Registry enrolls patients across multiple countries, the consistency of this pattern across such a geographically diverse HBV population strengthens the case that the association is not a quirk of a single health system. In HCV, MASLD Skews Younger and More Often Female Among patients with HCV, those with MASLD were significantly younger and more frequently female than those without it (both P < .01), despite having similar rates of advanced fibrosis, biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis, and nonmetabolic comorbidities (all P > .05). They scored significantly lower on the FACIT-F Physical Well-Being domain and all CLDQ domains (all P < .01), with the steepest declines in the Systemic Symptoms and Worry domains, each also a 6% reduction across the scale's range. In multivariate analysis adjusting for other clinical factors, MASLD remained independently associated with lower CLDQ scores (P < .05). This independent association held even after accounting for fibrosis stage and other clinical variables, reinforcing that the metabolic component carries its own distinct effect on how patients feel day to day, rather than acting only through fibrosis severity or age differences. Metabolic Screening May Belong in Routine Hepatitis Care Because the analysis was cross-sectional, it cannot establish whether MASLD causes the added symptom burden or simply accompanies it. The researchers also relied on a validated noninvasive index rather than imaging or biopsy to define MASLD across thousands of patients, a practical tradeoff for a registry of this scale but one that leaves some misclassification possible. For clinicians, the findings argue for screening patients with chronic viral hepatitis for cardiometabolic risk factors rather than assuming stable fibrosis status means a stable symptom burden. For payers and health systems, with nearly half of this viral hepatitis population also carrying a metabolic liver diagnosis, the data suggest that managing weight, diabetes, and lipids alongside antiviral therapy could meaningfully affect patient-reported quality of life, not just long-term liver outcomes. References Papatheodoridis G, Buti M, Yilmaz Y, et al. Chronic viral hepatitis with MASLD: implications for clinical and patient-reported outcomes. The overall PCR-confirmed prevalence of HBV was 12.91%, while HCV prevalence was 7.04%, with the two viruses showing different patterns across the study settings. The study, published in BMC Infectious Diseases on 29 October 2026 as an open-access research article, was led by Awayimbo Ruth Jaggu and colleagues, with Adamu Ishaku Akyala as senior author. It recruited participants from three distinct settings in equal measure: a tertiary healthcare facility population at the Federal Medical Centre, Keffi, and two community-based populations in Akwanga and Lafia Local Government Areas, with 284 participants per setting. Participants completed structured questionnaires covering socio-demographic characteristics, behaviours, healthcare-related exposures, and household contacts. Screening used rapid diagnostic tests, followed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which served as the reference standard for infection classification. Data were analysed with IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0, using descriptive statistics, bivariate analysis with crude odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals, and multivariable logistic regression producing adjusted odds ratios, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Discover more Biology textbook sales Study Biology hospital hospitals Learn Engineering HBV prevalence was 11.80% in community-based populations and 15.14% in the facility-based population. The researchers report no statistically significant difference in HBV prevalence between community and facility participants (χ2 = 1.86; p = 0.206), suggesting the virus circulates at similar levels in both contexts. HCV told a different story: prevalence was 5.28% in community populations but 10.56% among facility-based participants, a difference the authors report as statistically significant (χ2 = 7.028; p = 0.007). The multivariable analysis identified specific exposures independently associated with each virus. For HBV, sharing of personal hygiene items was associated with infection (adjusted odds ratio = 1.73; 95% CI: 1.06–2.70; p = 0.040), as was a history of sexually transmitted infections (AOR = 2.47; 95% CI: 1.38–4.42; p = 0.030). For HCV, a history of blood transfusion was independently associated with infection (AOR = 2.11; 95% CI: 1.04–4.31; p = 0.040). These associations come from a cross-sectional design, which measures exposures and infections at a single point in time. The adjusted odds ratios describe statistical associations rather than demonstrated causal effects, and the study’s findings apply to the adults sampled in these three Nasarawa State settings. The authors note that data on prevalence and associated risk factors across community- and facility-based populations in Nigeria, including Nasarawa State, have remained limited, which the study was designed to address. The higher HCV prevalence among facility-based participants coincided with the finding that blood transfusion history was independently associated with HCV infection, though the study did not test whether this or other healthcare-related exposures explain the difference between settings. Discover more Track Biotech Tour Colleges Genetic testing kits Health Laboratory supplies Chronic viral hepatitis due to HBV and HCV remains a significant global public health problem and a leading cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, according to the study’s background. The authors conclude that both infections remain prevalent in community- and facility-based populations in Nasarawa State, and that the identified behavioural and healthcare-related exposures highlight the need for expanded vaccination programmes, routine hepatitis screening, community education, and strengthened infection prevention and control measures. The study was published as an early-share, peer-reviewed accepted article carrying a permanent DOI; the publishers note that this version is subject to further edits and will be replaced by the final Version of Record. The authors state that targeted, context-specific public health interventions are required to support prevention, early detection, and management of viral hepatitis, and to contribute to Nigeria’s 2030 viral hepatitis elimination goals. As a single-state cross-sectional survey of 852 adults, the findings describe the burden and associated factors in these specific populations rather than national estimates, and the reported prevalence figures should be read within that scope. After entering a cell, the virus’s DNA serves as the template to make new viral particles. | Photo Credit: U.S. CDC In 1904, two scientists, Henry Wheeler and Treat Johnson, synthesised a variant of cytosine, one of the building blocks of DNA, in the laboratory. The variant they synthesised contained a chemical tag called a methyl group (-CH3) attached to cytosine, so they called it 5-methylcytosine. Their motivation for doing so was based on the observation that two other building blocks of DNA and its chemical cousin RNA, called thymine and uracil, differed only by the presence of a methyl group. After entering a cell, the virus’s DNA serves as the template to make new viral particles. | Photo Credit: U.S. CDC In 1904, two scientists, Henry Wheeler and Treat Johnson, synthesised a variant of cytosine, one of the building blocks of DNA, in the laboratory. The variant they synthesised contained a chemical tag called a methyl group (-CH3) attached to cytosine, so they called it 5-methylcytosine. Their motivation for doing so was based on the observation that two other building blocks of DNA and its chemical cousin RNA, called thymine and uracil, differed only by the presence of a methyl group. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hybrid deep learning model predicts monthly hepatitis B incidence in China by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Hybrid deep learning model predicts monthly hepatitis B incidence in China Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have developed a hybrid deep learning model that combines long short-term memory networks with convolutional neural networks to forecast the monthly incidence rate of hepatitis B in China, reporting that the combined approach outperformed traditional time series models and individual machine learning methods. The study, published in BMC Public Health, analyzed monthly hepatitis B incidence data from China covering January 2001 to February 2026. The authors set out to build an optimal prediction model for hepatitis B incidence in China and to provide accurate predictions that could support early monitoring and early warning of infectious diseases. According to the results, the average monthly incidence rate of hepatitis B in China was approximately 0.7 per 10,000 over the study period. The researchers also report that the prevalence and incidence rate of hepatitis B in the world and in China are decreasing year by year, and that China’s incidence is higher than the global average. The mortality rate among people aged 55 and above in China was reported to be lower than the global average. To model the data, the team established a series of time series and machine learning models. The comparison set included traditional approaches such as exponential smoothing, ARIMA and support vector regression, alongside individual machine learning models including convolutional neural networks, gated recurrent units and long short-term memory networks. The hybrid LSTM + CNN model achieved the strongest performance, with a coefficient of determination of 0.603. The authors state that this prediction performance was superior to the traditional time series models and the individual machine learning models tested. They also note that all of the time series models were able to capture the trend of the hepatitis B incidence rate. In their conclusions, the researchers write that the LSTM + CNN model demonstrates competitive performance in predicting the monthly average incidence rate of hepatitis B in China. They add that the hybrid deep learning model has shown great potential in time series prediction, although they emphasize that further validation is needed. The authors describe the work as a methodological exploration. They state that the study explores effective methods for predicting infectious disease time series and provides a new perspective for infectious disease prediction studies. The reported performance figure reflects the model’s fit within this study’s data and should be interpreted with the authors’ own caveat about the need for further validation. Hepatitis B remains an important public health issue facing China, according to the study’s background, and is described as one of the most severe infectious diseases in the world. The authors frame reliable incidence forecasting as a tool for early monitoring and early warning of infectious diseases, which is the stated motivation for comparing multiple modeling approaches in a single systematic analysis. The article was published as open access research on 08 October 2026, with Minquan Guan, Zhouying Hu, Yichen Lin, Xuehui Meng and Chengcheng Li among the listed authors. The study is presented as a methodological contribution to infectious disease modeling rather than a clinical intervention, and its findings concern statistical prediction of reported incidence rates rather than treatment or prevention outcomes.
