supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hepatitis B Burden Runs High Among Displaced Populations, Review Finds by October 27, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Hepatitis B Burden Runs High Among Displaced Populations, Review Finds Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Displaced people worldwide carry a substantially heavier burden of hepatitis B than the general population, according to a systematic review and meta-analysis published in BMC Public Health. Pooling data from 117 studies identified through searches of eight academic databases covering 2016 to 2026, researchers led by Efosa Ekhator and colleagues estimated that 3.86 percent of internally displaced persons, refugees and asylum seekers are living with the viral infection, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 3.45 to 4.29 percent. The analysis followed the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline and was registered as CRD420261361168. The pooled figure masks considerable variation across groups. Prevalence was markedly higher among men, at 5.98 percent (95 percent CI: 4.61 to 7.50 percent), than among women, at 3.82 percent (95 percent CI: 2.96 to 4.78 percent). Displaced people from Eastern Asia recorded the highest pooled prevalence, 11.62 percent (95 percent CI: 7.61 to 16.32 percent), followed by those from South-eastern Asia at 7.18 percent (95 percent CI: 5.70 to 8.80 percent) and Sub-Saharan Africa at 6.62 percent (95 percent CI: 5.44 to 7.90 percent). Displacement status itself appeared to matter. Internally displaced persons showed a pooled prevalence of 9.99 percent (95 percent CI: 6.82 to 13.67 percent), significantly higher than other subgroups at the p ≤ 0.05 threshold. People hosted in African countries had a pooled prevalence of 7.74 percent (95 percent CI: 5.02 to 10.97 percent), and those living in displacement camps recorded 7.19 percent (95 percent CI: 5.47 to 9.11 percent). Discover more Check Symptoms Explore Data Read Med Journals View Census Data Get Health Tips The authors suggest that governments and non-governmental organisations should prioritise displaced populations in hepatitis B control efforts on the basis of these findings. Methodologically, the review screened 4,673 records and extracted data from each included study, assessing methodological quality with the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. That heterogeneity proved substantial. Even after subgroup analyses, considerable variability remained across the included studies, and multivariate meta-regression linked it to several study-level characteristics: displacement status, the percentage of male participants, the temporal design of the studies and the settings in which they were conducted. This means the pooled estimates should be read as averages across widely differing populations, sampling strategies and screening approaches rather than as a single uniform prevalence figure applicable everywhere. The authors took several steps to probe the reliability of their results. A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, which re-estimates the pooled prevalence while excluding each study in turn, demonstrated the robustness of the findings, indicating that no single study was driving the overall result. Publication bias, the tendency for smaller or less striking results to go unpublished, was assessed with Egger's regression test and funnel plot visualisation. The authors note that their estimates are subject to the limitations inherent in meta-analysis of observational prevalence studies, including the residual heterogeneity and the small-study effect detected by Egger's test. Even so, the consistency of the elevated burden across sensitivity analyses supports the paper's central conclusion that displaced populations represent a group with a high prevalence of hepatitis B and a corresponding claim on public health resources. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hepatitis B prevalence reaches 41.9% in Ethiopian chronic liver disease patients by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Hepatitis B prevalence reaches 41.9% in Ethiopian chronic liver disease patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A facility-based cross-sectional study found hepatitis B virus infection in 41.9% of patients with chronic liver disease treated at three public referral hospitals in Bahir Dar, Northwest Ethiopia. Researchers assessed 320 patients from October 2023 through January 2024, combining structured questionnaires, physical examinations and medical-chart reviews. HBsAg positivity, indicating the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen, was identified in 134 participants, giving a prevalence of 41.9% with a 95% confidence interval of 36.5% to 47.5%. The hospital-based design establishes the burden among people already receiving care for chronic liver disease, but it does not show whether hepatitis B caused their underlying liver disease or how common infection is in the wider regional population. The study focused on patients with established chronic liver disease, a group described in the research as vulnerable to acute or superimposed hepatitis B infection. The authors noted that such infections can trigger rapid hepatic decompensation, accelerate progression toward cirrhosis and increase the lifetime risk of neoplastic transformation. Its primary result was the prevalence of HBsAg positivity and the statistical associations between this status and reported or recorded characteristics. Multivariable binary logistic regression identified several characteristics associated with positive HBsAg status. HIV-positive participants had three times the adjusted odds of positivity compared with HIV-negative patients, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.00 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.40 to 6.80. A family history of liver disease was associated with 4.70 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.90 to 11.00, while a history of dental procedures was associated with 4.50 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.00 to 10.00. Contact with a person who had jaundice was also associated with higher odds of positivity, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.40 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 4.80. These are associations in the sampled population, not evidence that any listed exposure transmitted the virus. Because hepatitis B prevalence was high in the study population, the investigators also applied a modified Poisson regression model with robust variance to complement the odds-ratio estimates with adjusted prevalence ratios. In that model, HIV-positive status was associated with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.68, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 2.35. Family history of liver disease was associated with a ratio of 1.76, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.29 to 2.40. Contact with a jaundiced person had an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.48, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.14 to 1.92, and a history of dental procedures had a ratio of 1.62, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.21 to 2.17. The logistic and modified Poisson analyses pointed in the same direction for these four predictors. Post-hoc power calculations indicated greater than 85% statistical power for the primary multivariable predictors. That calculation was performed after model fitting and does not eliminate uncertainties associated with the sample size, model specification, confounding or the cross-sectional design. In particular, the study cannot establish the timing or route of infection, determine whether identified characteristics preceded HBsAg positivity, or measure changes in prevalence over time. The referral-hospital setting also limits generalization: the participants were patients attending selected public facilities in Bahir Dar, rather than a population-based sample representing all people with chronic liver disease in Northwest Ethiopia. Within those limits, the 41.9% estimate documents a substantial hepatitis B burden among the chronically ill patients attending the three hospitals during the study period. The hospital sample included patients with chronic liver disease, so the result should not be presented as a regional prevalence estimate for the general population. Nor does the cross-sectional analysis demonstrate that HIV, family history, dental procedures or contact with a jaundiced person caused infection. The adjusted estimates identify groups with higher observed prevalence in this clinical setting, while their confidence intervals show the degree of precision around each association. The authors proposed that the results may inform regional planning for hepatitis B screening within liver clinics, evaluation of targeted adult vaccination strategies and stronger use of standard infection-control measures in health facilities. The immediate research contribution is instead a cross-sectional measurement of HBsAg prevalence and its reported correlates among 320 chronic liver disease patients in a defined Ethiopian hospital network. For interpreting the results, the study type and population are central. It was a facility-based, cross-sectional assessment conducted from October 2023 to January 2024, not a longitudinal study or a clinical trial. Its strongest supported conclusion is that hepatitis B infection was common among the sampled chronic liver disease patients, with HIV positivity, family history of liver disease, dental-procedure history and contact with a jaundiced person each associated with higher adjusted prevalence or odds of HBsAg positivity. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Cross-sectional study finds suboptimal quality in Chinese hepatitis B videos by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Cross-sectional study finds suboptimal quality in Chinese hepatitis B videos Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A cross-sectional study of 174 short videos about hepatitis B virus (HBV) on the Chinese platforms Bilibili and Douyin found that the sampled content was generally of suboptimal quality. Douyin videos received substantially more user engagement, but popularity was not consistently associated with higher quality, according to the analysis published in BMC Infectious Diseases. The researchers searched both platforms on March 10, 2026, using the Chinese translation of “hepatitis B Virus.” After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, the final sample contained 174 videos, including 87 from each platform. The investigators extracted video characteristics such as duration, age, engagement metrics and uploader identity before evaluating the information presented in each video. Content quality and reliability were assessed with five instruments: the Global Quality Scale (GQS), the modified Decision-making Information Support Criteria for Evaluating the Reliability of Non-randomized Studies (mDISCERN), JAMA benchmark criteria, a Content Completeness Score (CCS) and the Video Information and Quality Index (VIQI). The statistical analysis included Mann–Whitney U tests, Kruskal–Wallis tests, Spearman correlation and multivariable regression, conducted in R version 4.3.2. Douyin videos attracted substantially greater engagement than Bilibili videos even after adjustment for video age. However, the study did not find a consistent relationship between engagement and superior content quality, indicating that user interaction could not serve as a dependable proxy for the quality of HBV-related videos. Bilibili videos were longer and scored significantly higher on three of the five assessment instruments: GQS, mDISCERN and VIQI. Discover more Check Symptoms Donate to Research Explore Data Study Biology Read Economics The reported P values for these differences were 0.027, 0.046 and below 0.001, respectively. These cross-sectional findings describe the selected videos and do not show that either platform inherently produces better material or that watching content from a particular platform improves viewers’ understanding of HBV. Multivariable analyses indicated that longer duration was independently associated with higher scores on all five quality measures, with all P values below 0.05. Platform was not independently associated with any quality measure after the other variables included in the models were considered. Video length was therefore the characteristic most consistently associated with higher assessed quality in this sample, rather than platform identity. The videos also differed in the clinical topics they addressed. Treatment was the most common subject, appearing in 59.8% of the sampled videos, followed by diagnosis in 52.9% and prevention in 48.3%. Symptoms were covered least frequently, appearing in 22.4%. The analysis therefore identified gaps in topic coverage as well as differences in the measured quality and reliability of the selected HBV content. Uploader identity showed no uniformly favorable pattern. Videos made by professionals received higher GQS scores but lower mDISCERN, JAMA and VIQI scores than videos from other uploader categories. Professional participation alone thus did not correspond to stronger results across the full assessment framework. Discover more Compare TVs Binge Hit Series health Health Get Health Tips The study was limited by its single-day search, the selected sample of 87 videos per platform and the variables included in the models; it does not represent all HBV material available on either service or establish effects on clinical decisions and health behavior. supplementary_news.content_title: Over Half of the Young Children Exposed to Household Hepatitis B Had an Infected Contact Other Than Their Mother
supplementary_news.content: Your Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More Video Events Specialties Topics RegisterLog In Ask AI Search Medscape Medical NewsConference News Over Half of the Young Children Exposed to Household Hepatitis B Had an Infected Contact Other Than Their Mother Tara Haelle October 26, 2026 WASHINGTON — More than 1% of infants and young children lived in a household with someone who had an active hepatitis B infection, and over half of those infected household contacts were not their birth mother, according to a retrospective cohort study presented at IDWeek in Washington, DC, on October 22. “Maternal hepatitis B screening would not identify these exposures,” Karen B. Jacobson, MD, MPH, an infectious disease physician and research scientist with the Vaccine Study Center at the Kaiser Permanente Northern California (KPNC) Division of Research in Oakland, told attendees. “Some household-exposed infants did not receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth and remained at risk for hepatitis B infection in the first months of life,” Jacobson said. “While most US children currently receive hepatitis B vaccine at birth, changes to vaccine policy may leave children at risk of hepatitis B transmission and chronic infection. Even if it is possible to accurately identify every single maternal infection, this would not account for potential exposure to an infected father, grandparent, or another person living in the household and, of course, anyone that they might come into close contact with outside the household.” A birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine protects infants before every possible exposure can be identified, she said, and avoids relying on whether close contacts or household members have been diagnosed with hepatitis B or are known to the family. “The key takeaway is that you can get hepatitis B from a source other than your mother in the first few years of life, at a time when you are most vulnerable,” Paul Offit, MD, an infectious disease pediatrician and director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia who was not involved in the study, said. “If you get hepatitis B in those first few years, you have a high rate of going on to develop cirrhosis or liver cancer later in life and limiting your lifespan. That makes it all the more important to get the hepatitis B vaccine.” An estimated 1-2 million people in the US have chronic hepatitis B infection, and infants can acquire hepatitis B via vertical transmission from their mothers during birth or from close interpersonal contact after birth, particularly from household contacts. Approximately 90% of infants who contract hepatitis B develop a chronic infection, but a birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine reduces risk for transmission by 85-95%. For that reason, the CDC has recommended vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B since 2005, an update from the 1991 recommendation to vaccinate infants at birth or within their first 2 months. But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), newly reconstituted by the US Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr, after he dismissed all the previous members, voted to change the recommendation. They recommended vaccinating newborns at birth only if their mothers had an active hepatitis B infection or unknown infection status and then offering the vaccine, with shared decision-making, to babies aged 2 months if their mothers were negative for hepatitis B. “This [recommendation] change sparked a lot of debate,” Jacobson said. “Many public health professionals and organizations voiced concerns that delayed vaccination would allow infants to fall through the cracks due to missed maternal infections or loss to follow-up. And furthermore, it does not take into account the risk of potential exposure from nonmaternal sources or close contacts of the infant.” The recommended change has currently been stayed by a federal judge due to an ongoing lawsuit between the American Academy of Pediatrics and Kennedy, but national discussion has continued over the risk of hepatitis B to unvaccinated infants in their first months of life. “Therefore, we sought to characterize household exposure to individuals with active hepatitis B infection among young children, including exposure through individuals who are not the birth mother,” Jacobson said. “In other words, is this a problem? Are there infants that could potentially be exposed either from the mother or from someone in their household during the weeks after birth, before most children go to daycare or school?” The researchers used data from the KPNC healthcare system, into which approximately 40,000 infants are delivered each year. The study population included all children younger than 5 years on June 16, 2023, whose record was linked to their birth mother and who lived with at least one household contact who used the KPNC. The researchers then tracked active hepatitis B infections among household contacts through March 26, 2026. Among 131,800 households, there were 158,169 children younger than 5 years and 363,070 household contacts with an average age of 31 years. The majority (98.7%) of children lived in homes without hepatitis B exposure, meaning neither their mothers nor any of their household contacts had an active infection. Only 0.5% of the households had an active hepatitis B infection. Among the 2024 (1.3%) children living in a household with an active hepatitis B exposure, 41.8% were exposed at birth to a mother with hepatitis B and the remaining 58.2% had been exposed to another household member with hepatitis B. “This demonstrates that potential household exposure to hepatitis B is not limited to just maternal infection,” Jacobson said. “So when you have RFK Jr’s fake ACIP saying that you should vaccinate high-risk children, which are the children who are passing through birth canal where there’s hepatitis B, but there is no no-risk child,” Offit said. “Everybody’s at some risk because you don’t know the infection status of everyone who comes in contact with your child. So why take the chance?” All the infants exposed to hepatitis B at birth had been vaccinated within 1 week of birth, but 4.2% of children exposed to hepatitis B in the household remained unvaccinated for more than 1 month after birth, and two household-exposed children were never vaccinated. Meanwhile, 86.7% of unexposed infants were vaccinated before they were 7 days old. “We also found that household-exposed children were more likely than unexposed children to be vaccinated, and this suggests that some families or healthcare providers did recognize the potential risk associated with household exposure,” Jacobson said. “However, there again were some of those household-exposed infants that did not receive any vaccination at birth or even ever, despite that potential exposure.” The researchers also looked at how many children were tested for hepatitis B, and although 95% of those exposed at birth had undergone testing, only 3.6% of household-exposed children were ever tested. “This is a potential gap in care for children who have a known household contact,” Jacobson said. Further, the exposure risk may be underestimated because this analysis did not capture household contacts with an undiagnosed infection, non-KPNC members, and close contacts outside the household. “Transmission of hepatitis B to children from nonmaternal sources is currently quite rare in the United States due to the high vaccination rates, but if rates decrease, more infants could be at risk,” Jacobson said. The research was funded by KPNC. Jacobson reported receiving research support from Pfizer unrelated to this presentation, and two of her co-authors reported receiving unrelated research support from Sanofi, Moderna, AstraZeneca, GSK, Pfizer, CSL Seqirus, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, and Merck. Offit reported having no disclosures. Tara Haelle has been an independent science/health journalist for over 15 years, with her work appearing in over two dozen trade and consumer publications. She is the author of Vaccination Investigation: The History and Science of Vaccines and The Informed Parent: A Science-Based Resource for Your Child’s First Four Years. Tara is the Public Health Beat Leader for the Association of Health Care Journalists, where she develops resources to help other journalists report on medical studies and public health. She is based in Dallas. Comments Commenting is limited to medical professionals. To comment please . Comments on Medscape are moderated and should be professional in tone and on topic. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Immune cell shifts track hepatitis B treatment response by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Immune cell shifts track hepatitis B treatment response Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Patients with chronic hepatitis B who lose the hepatitis B surface antigen, or HBsAg, while on combination therapy show a distinctive pattern of immune change, according to a new study published in BMC Immunology. The research tracked natural killer cell subsets and circulating cytokines in 27 patients treated with pegylated interferon-alpha together with nucleos(t)ide analogs, and found that those who achieved on-treatment HBsAg loss by week 48 differed measurably from those who did not. The study set out to characterize how NK cell phenotypes, receptor expression and cytokine profiles change during this combination regimen and how those changes relate to clinical outcomes. HBsAg loss remains a major challenge in chronic hepatitis B, and identifying immune signatures associated with treatment response could help clarify the mechanisms behind successful therapy. The 27 participants were stratified into two groups at week 48: an on-treatment HBsAg loss group, defined as HBsAg below 0.05 IU/mL, comprising 10 patients, and a non-HBsAg loss group of 17 patients. Flow cytometry was used to assess NK cell subsets, distinguishing CD56bright from CD56dim cells, and to measure expression of the receptors NKG2D, NKp30, NKp46, KIR, NKG2A and TIM3. Serum levels of the cytokines IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6 and IL-10 were measured by ELISA, and the researchers analyzed correlations between virological markers and NK cell subsets, receptors or cytokines. Discover more Check Symptoms Book Lab Tests Study Biology Get Health Tips Across both groups, the combination therapy expanded CD56bright NK cells while reducing CD56dim subsets. The groups diverged in receptor expression. In the on-treatment HBsAg loss group, the researchers observed persistent upregulation of KIR, the killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, on CD56bright NK cells. At the same time, CD56dim NK cells in that group maintained elevated expression of NKG2A, a receptor that modulates NK cell activity. Cytokine patterns also separated the two groups. Patients in the on-treatment HBsAg loss group showed significantly lower serum levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-2, while maintaining higher levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10. This combination of dampened inflammatory signaling and preserved anti-inflammatory activity characterized the group that achieved HBsAg loss. Correlation analysis added another layer. In the on-treatment HBsAg loss group, HBsAg levels showed significant inverse correlations with the proportion of CD56bright NK cells and with receptor expression. In the same group, HBsAg correlated positively with CD56dim NK cell frequency. In both treatment groups, HBsAg was positively correlated with pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, linking viral antigen burden to inflammatory cytokine output. The authors conclude that PEG-IFNα and NAs combination therapy is associated with on-treatment HBsAg loss at week 48, potentially through optimizing cytokine responses, regulating the CD56bright to CD56dim NK cell balance and modulating the related receptors. The study notes limitations including its single-center design and moderate sample size, and the findings are observational associations rather than proof of causation. The work was registered in a national medical research registry under the title Prediction of clinical curative effect of pegylated interferon a individualized intermittent treatment of nucleoside (acid) in patients with hepatitis B, with registration number MR-53-26-076931, dated 31 August 2026. The study was published as open access on 12 October 2026, and the article version shared at publication is citable and carries a permanent DOI, subject to further edits before the final version of record appears. It is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which attacks and injures the liver and is transmitted through blood and infected bodily fluids, including direct contact with blood, illegal drugs, and unsterilized or contaminated needles. Most hepatitis B infections clear up within 1-2 months without treatment. When the infection lasts more than 6 months, it can develop into chronic hepatitis B, leading to chronic inflammation of the liver, cirrhosis, liver cancer, and/or liver failure. The risk of chronic infection is directly related to the age at first exposure: nearly 90% of infected newborns and babies, up to 50% of infected children (1-5 years), and about 5-10% of infected adults develop chronic hepatitis B infection. Symptoms include fatigue, poor appetite, stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, darker urine, and jaundice. Screening involves a simple, low-cost blood test to detect HBsAg and anti-HBs in serum. A patient who tests positive for HBsAg has an active HBV infection, and further testing, including serum ALT and HBV DNA levels, HBeAg, and anti-HBe, is needed to determine the phase of the disease and course of action. For chronic cases, a liver biopsy may be needed. Two are injectable interferons, while the other five antivirals are tablets that must be taken every day to suppress viral growth and reduce liver swelling and damage. * Immunomodulators, such as conventional IFN-a2 and PEG-IFN-a2, aim to enhance the host immune response but are limited by significant side effects and variable efficacy. Using MAGPIX multiplex analysis, the researchers found that macrophage colony-stimulating factor, FLT-3 ligand, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, epidermal growth factor and transforming growth factor alpha had potential as diagnostic biomarkers. A decision-tree analysis indicated that combined detection of macrophage colony-stimulating factor and FLT-3 ligand was more valuable diagnostically than the individual measurements considered in that model. Occult hepatitis B infection, abbreviated OBI, is defined by the presence of hepatic hepatitis B virus DNA despite the absence of detectable serum hepatitis B surface antigen, or HBsAg. The study initially enrolled 6,773 healthy volunteers, with individuals under 18 excluded. Screening for hepatitis B markers then identified 57 cases of OBI. The comparison group comprised 37 donors selected from the same initial cohort who had no viral hepatitis markers, HIV or somatic diseases. The investigators measured cytokines, chemokines and growth factors in blood plasma to characterize the immune-mediator profile associated with occult infection. The group also showed elevated concentrations of six growth factors: epidermal growth factor, FLT-3 ligand, transforming growth factor alpha, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, macrophage colony-stimulating factor and vascular endothelial growth factor. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Book Lab Tests Find Cancer Care Rather than indicating a uniformly reduced inflammatory response, the pattern combined anti-inflammatory activity with some concurrent elevation of pro-inflammatory signals. The authors characterized occult hepatitis B as having a dominant anti-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic background, a profile they said could facilitate viral persistence and promote liver fibrosis. Receiver operating characteristic analyses indicated diagnostic potential for five measured mediators: macrophage colony-stimulating factor, FLT-3 ligand, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, epidermal growth factor and transforming growth factor alpha. The decision-tree results further supported measuring macrophage colony-stimulating factor together with FLT-3 ligand as a combined diagnostic approach. These findings represent associations and model-based estimates within the screened cohort, not proof of clinical performance in routine use. The supplied study abstract does not provide sensitivity, specificity, confidence intervals or independent validation, so the strength of the proposed biomarkers cannot be fully evaluated from the reported information alone. The authors interpreted the elevated growth-factor response as a feature of aberrant tissue repair. They linked transforming growth factor alpha and epidermal growth factor to incomplete regeneration and scarring, while the broader cytokine environment was described as favoring persistence of the virus. FLT-3 ligand appeared to have a potentially dual role, associated with hepatoprotection on one hand and fibrotic progression on the other. These are mechanistic interpretations of the observed pattern rather than demonstrated causal effects. The study was an observational comparison of circulating immune mediators, not a treatment trial or longitudinal analysis, so it does not establish that the measured cytokines preceded infection or fibrosis. Its strongest supported contribution is the identification of a blood-based cytokine and growth-factor pattern associated with occult hepatitis B, including a combination with potential diagnostic value that requires further validation. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Blood Counts Fall Uniformly During Peginterferon Therapy for Chronic Hepatitis B, Small Study Finds by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Blood Counts Fall Uniformly During Peginterferon Therapy for Chronic Hepatitis B, Small Study Finds Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Peginterferon alfa-2b remains one of the few finite treatment options available for selected patients with chronic hepatitis B, particularly in strategies aimed at durable immune control of the virus. Yet the drug carries a well-recognized hematologic price: leukopenia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia are among its best-documented adverse effects and can shape treatment tolerability, monitoring intensity, dose decisions, and the need for supportive care. A new exploratory analysis, published in Frontiers in Medicine, has now tracked these blood count declines in detail within a small, prospectively followed cohort of 21 Chinese patients, quantifying how uniformly and how deeply counts fell during the first ten weeks of therapy, and asking whether the pattern differed between patients who showed an early serological response and those who did not. The study, conducted at the Second Affiliated Hospital and Yuying Children’s Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University between July 2024 and February 2025, enrolled adults with chronic hepatitis B who received peginterferon alfa-2b at 180 micrograms subcutaneously once weekly, with or without background oral nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy. The investigators classified patients operationally by early serological response through Week 15: among those with detectable hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at baseline, response required either a decline of at least 1.0 log10 IU/mL from baseline or a fall of HBsAg below the assay’s lower limit of detection; among those already below that limit, response required anti-HBs seroconversion to at least 10 mIU/mL. Thirteen patients met response criteria and eight did not. Because the cohort size was set by the available parent study rather than by a formal sample-size calculation, the authors framed the entire analysis as hypothesis-generating. The central clinical finding was strikingly uniform. White blood cell count, absolute neutrophil count, and platelet count all declined from the first visit to the third visit in both response groups, and every single paired change was negative. Among the 13 responders, the median paired changes from Visit 1 to Visit 3 were −2.430 × 109/L for white blood cells (bootstrap 95% confidence interval: −2.530 to −1.530), −1.730 × 109/L for neutrophils (−1.990 to −1.094), and −67.0 × 109/L for platelets (−83.0 to −55.0), each with a matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation of −1.00. Among the 8 non-responders, the corresponding medians were −2.745 × 109/L for white cells (−3.570 to −2.190), −1.870 × 109/L for neutrophils (−2.260 to −1.110), and −97.5 × 109/L for platelets (−112.0 to −64.0). Visit 2 occurred at a median of 34 days after Visit 1, and Visit 3 at a median of 70 days, corresponding roughly to weeks 5 and 10 of treatment. Discover more Check Symptoms Book Lab Tests Study Biology Get Health Tips Find Treatments The observed nadirs told a similar story of broad, treatment-associated myelosuppression. Median white cell nadirs were 2.29 × 109/L in responders and 3.25 × 109/L in non-responders; median neutrophil nadirs were 1.10 and 1.69 × 109/L respectively; and median platelet nadirs were 86.0 and 112.0 × 109/L. However, when the investigators formally compared the two groups, the estimates were imprecise. The responder-minus-non-responder Hodges–Lehmann shift for white cell nadir was −0.810 × 109/L with a confidence interval spanning −1.240 to 0.160, and for neutrophil nadir −0.391 × 109/L (−0.830 to 0.330); the platelet nadir shift was −20.0 × 109/L (−39.0 to 7.0). None of these comparisons established a response-group-specific toxicity pattern, and the authors were careful to note that the wide intervals preclude any claim of equivalence between the groups as well. Binary thresholds underscored how common the cytopenias were. At Visit 2, white blood cell counts below 4.0 × 109/L occurred in 19 of 21 patients, or 90.5% (exact 95% confidence interval: 69.6% to 98.8%). Neutrophil counts below 1.0 × 109/L were seen in 7 of 21 patients (33.3%), and platelet counts below 100 × 109/L in 10 of 21 (47.6%). The near-universality of the white cell threshold led the team to treat it as a pragmatic clinical-management context rather than a discriminating molecular endpoint: when almost every patient crosses a cutoff, that cutoff carries little information for distinguishing molecular subgroups within the cohort. Discover more Seek Counseling Save on Rx Find Cancer Care A methodologically notable feature of the study was its handling of supportive care. Oral leukocyte-support medication was given to some patients after their counts fell, which raises the question of whether later blood counts reflect the drug’s toxicity or the mitigation of it. The team reconstructed treatment timing from deidentified records and built a post-documented oral-support-date indicator, classifying each complete blood count as before or after the first documented treatment date. In a random-intercept model covering 60 planned-visit observations from all 21 participants, the post-date term was −0.008 × 109/L for white cells (P = 0.979) and −0.105 × 109/L for neutrophils (P = 0.632), meaning the indicator did not materially alter the fitted decline. Boundary analyses coding ambiguous same-day visits as exposed or unexposed, and a strict pre-support paired set of five responders and four non-responders, all remained directionally consistent with decline. Crucially, because support was initiated in response to low counts, these non-randomized analyses cannot estimate treatment efficacy or remove confounding by indication. The second half of the study turned to whole-blood RNA sequencing, asking whether baseline host molecular state was associated with the hematologic endpoints. Blood samples collected in PAXgene tubes at Weeks 0, 5, and 10 were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, and gene-level counts were normalized using the variance-stabilizing transformation in DESeq2. Hallmark pathway activity was summarized with gene set variation analysis across 50 pathways per endpoint family, with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction applied within complete families. The result was a disciplined null: across 350 baseline associations in seven endpoint-specific families, no Hallmark pathway reached the prespecified exploratory threshold of q < 0.10, with a minimum q of 0.251. No baseline candidate-gene association met the threshold either (minimum q = 0.417). In paired Week-10-minus-Week-0 analyses among the 20 patients with both time points, none of 150 Hallmark associations reached q < 0.10. Because whole-blood expression reflects both cell-intrinsic transcription and shifts in circulating cell composition, the researchers ran a sensitivity analysis using xCell2, a reference-based tool that infers cell-type enrichment from bulk transcriptomes. The inferred neutrophil enrichment score showed only modest and imprecise concordance with measured neutrophil counts at baseline (Spearman rho = 0.382, confidence interval −0.110 to 0.732), but tracked measured counts much more strongly across matched visits (rho = 0.693 for neutrophils, 0.559 for white cells) and for within-person changes over time. Composition adjustment changed several pathway estimates, and a few adjusted platelet-endpoint signals nominally crossed q < 0.10, but none reached q < 0.05, four of seven had nonconverged confidence intervals, and the intervals were extremely wide. The authors declined to interpret these unstable signals as pathway discoveries, emphasizing that the enrichment scores are relative measures derived from the same bulk data as the pathway scores, leaving residual confounding and mathematical coupling as live concerns. The discussion places the findings in biological context without overclaiming mechanism. Type-I-interferon receptors and signaling have been demonstrated in CD34-positive hematopoietic progenitor cells, and interferon exposure can rapidly suppress hematopoiesis, supporting a marrow-production component for the leukocyte and neutrophil declines. For platelets, experimental type-I-interferon signaling can reduce platelet production and function, and prior small studies in chronic hepatitis B and other viral hepatitides have suggested impaired platelet production rather than antibody-mediated destruction. The authors note, however, that they did not measure bone-marrow function, endogenous G-CSF, antiplatelet antibodies, or thrombopoiesis in their own cohort, so these mechanisms remain contextual rather than demonstrated. The study’s limitations are substantial and openly stated. It is an exploratory secondary analysis of a single-center cohort of 21 participants with no independent validation; the between-group confidence intervals are wide; only one participant was HBeAg-positive, limiting generalization; and whole-blood transcriptomics cannot be read as liver-intrinsic biology. What the analysis delivers is a carefully quantified clinical picture: during peginterferon alfa-2b-based therapy for chronic hepatitis B, white cell, neutrophil, and platelet counts fell in every patient studied, the decline was not clearly modified by early serological response status, and a near-universal white cell threshold is more useful for clinical management than for molecular stratification. The transcriptomic null results, reported with complete multiplicity control, serve as a cautionary benchmark for future biomarker claims in this space, and the authors stress that all findings require confirmation in larger, independent, preferably multicenter cohorts with orthogonal measurements of cell composition and hematopoietic function. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health ORC1 Protein Rises with HBV Liver Disease Progression and Flags Poorer Survival by October 27, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 ORC1 Protein Rises with HBV Liver Disease Progression and Flags Poorer Survival Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The research, conducted by a team at The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University in Nanning, China, examined ORC1 in HBV-related liver disease and assessed whether it could serve as a marker of disease stage and prognosis. The study enrolled 178 participants divided into two groups. The HBV-positive cohort comprised 124 cases: 49 patients with HBV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma, 33 with HBV-related cirrhosis, and 42 with chronic hepatitis B. The HBV-negative control group included 54 individuals, consisting of 35 patients with non-HBV hepatocellular carcinoma and 19 with hepatic hemangioma. This design allowed the investigators to compare ORC1 expression across the spectrum of HBV-driven liver disease while controlling for cancer that arises without viral infection. ORC1 in liver tissue was detected by immunohistochemistry. In a subset of 17 HBV-HCC patients for whom serum samples were available, the researchers also measured circulating ORC1 by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with high ORC1 expression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to compare how well tissue ORC1, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), and des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin (DCP) discriminated HBV-HCC from other disease states. The central finding was that tissue ORC1 was significantly upregulated in HBV-positive patients, and HBV infection itself was independently associated with high ORC1 expression, with a statistical significance of P<0.001. Expression followed a clear gradient across disease stages: ORC1 levels increased progressively from chronic hepatitis B to cirrhosis to hepatocellular carcinoma. This pattern suggests that ORC1 tracks the proliferative activity that intensifies as HBV-related liver disease advances toward cancer. Because AFP and DCP, the conventional biomarkers for hepatocellular carcinoma, have well-recognized limitations in detecting early-stage disease, the researchers tested whether ORC1 could add diagnostic value. Tissue ORC1 showed only moderate discrimination between HBV-HCC and HBV-related cirrhosis, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.64, and between HBV-HCC and chronic hepatitis B, with an AUC of 0.66. The serum measurements added a cautious note of interest. In the 17 HBV-HCC patients with available serum, tissue and serum ORC1 were moderately correlated, with a Spearman rank correlation coefficient of 0.554 (95% confidence interval 0.085 to 0.822, P=0.021). The wide confidence interval reflects the very small subset size, so the relationship between circulating and tissue ORC1 requires confirmation in much larger cohorts before any clinical use of serum ORC1 could be considered. Not every association held up. ORC1 expression was not significantly associated with tumor diameter (P>0.05), meaning that within the HCC group, larger tumors did not necessarily express more ORC1. This suggests that ORC1 reflects the proliferative state of the underlying liver disease rather than the physical size of an established tumor. For prognostic information, the team turned to external validation using TCGA-LIHC, the liver hepatocellular carcinoma dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas. In that dataset, high ORC1 expression was associated with poorer overall survival, with a hazard ratio of 1.7 and P=0.0026. This independent cohort analysis supports the interpretation that elevated ORC1 marks a more aggressive disease course, although the survival analysis was performed in a public database cohort rather than in the Chinese patient cohort itself. The authors conclude that ORC1 upregulation is independently associated with HBV infection and increases with disease progression across HBV-related liver disease. They characterize ORC1 as primarily a proliferation- and progression-related marker rather than a stand-alone diagnostic biomarker, given its only moderate discrimination for HBV-HCC. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer TIGIT receptor drives NKT-like cell exhaustion in high-HBV liver cancer patients by October 27, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 TIGIT receptor drives NKT-like cell exhaustion in high-HBV liver cancer patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Patients with hepatocellular carcinoma who carry a high hepatitis B virus load show a distinctive form of immune dysfunction in a rare but important population of circulating immune cells, according to a new study published in Cancer Immunology, Immunotherapy. The research focuses on CD3-positive CD56-positive NKT-like cells, which bridge features of T cells and natural killer cells and contribute to both antiviral defense and tumor immune surveillance. In patients whose serum HBV DNA exceeded 10,000 IU per milliliter, these cells displayed clear signs of hypofunction, raising questions about how chronic viral replication shapes antitumor immunity in the liver. The researchers found that TIGIT levels on peripheral blood NKT-like cells rose in parallel with HBV DNA concentration, so the higher a patient's viral load, the more TIGIT their NKT-like cells carried. Functionally, the high-HBV group's NKT-like cells secreted reduced amounts of antiviral effector cytokines, indicating that the cells were present but blunted in their ability to respond. To test whether TIGIT itself was responsible for the impaired activity rather than merely a marker of it, the team compared the behavior of TIGIT-positive and TIGIT-negative NKT-like cells within the same patients. The TIGIT-positive subset showed significantly lower immune activity, supporting the idea that expression of this receptor tracks with a functionally exhausted state rather than simply accompanying it. A second layer of the mechanism involves plasmacytoid dendritic cells, or pDCs, which present the ligand CD155 that engages TIGIT. In patients with high HBV DNA, CD155 expression on pDCs was markedly upregulated compared with HCC patients whose viral loads were low. The most direct evidence came from co-culture experiments in which NKT-like cells and pDCs from patients were grown together and stimulated with hepatitis B core antigen, the viral protein that NKT-like cells would normally recognize. When the investigators blocked the TIGIT pathway, the effector function of the patients' NKT-like cells was restored, demonstrating that the receptor-ligand interaction was actively suppressing the cells rather than simply correlating with their dysfunction. The new data provide a rationale for developing TIGIT-directed immunotherapy specifically for hepatocellular carcinoma patients with high HBV loads, a group whose disease is driven by both chronic viral infection and tumor progression. The clinical context matters. Persistent HBV infection can lead to chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, and high serum HBV DNA is recognized as a major risk factor for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma. The study's scope should be kept in mind. The work examined peripheral blood cells rather than tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and the functional restoration was demonstrated in co-culture assays rather than in patients. Whether TIGIT blockade would improve clinical outcomes in high-HBV HCC patients remains an open question that would require clinical testing. Nevertheless, by linking viral load, receptor expression, ligand upregulation, and reversible dysfunction in a single mechanistic chain, the study offers a coherent account of how chronic HBV replication may undermine one arm of antitumor immunity and identifies a concrete molecular target for future intervention. The audit, published in AIDS Research and Therapy as a Brief Communication, examined 183 patients with current or prior HBV exposure. Of these, 12 patients were switched to HBV-inactive antiretroviral therapy, meaning regimens that do not include drugs with activity against hepatitis B. According to the authors, there were significant variations in the testing practice performed before and after the switch to monitor potential HBV activity. This suggests that clinicians managing these patients did not follow a uniform approach to checking whether hepatitis B remained suppressed once HBV-active drugs were removed from the regimen. The authors note that consistency between guidelines would enhance implementation efforts in their context. The finding highlights a practical question raised by the study: how HBV-inactive antiretroviral therapy affects clinical monitoring in patients co-infected with HIV and HBV, and what optimal monitoring practices should be for HBV exposure in HIV patients on antiretroviral therapy. As an audit of clinical practice rather than an intervention study, the work describes what was observed at a single service setting and does not establish outcomes of any particular monitoring approach. The authors frame their conclusion around the need for greater guideline consistency to support implementation in their context.
